#2728. The Sixers’ NBA Cup dreams come down to Friday

For the first three years of the NBA Cup, the Sixers failed to advance past the group-play stage. This season, they have a chance to make it to the knockout round for the first time ever.

Wednesday unfolded exactly how the Sixers needed it to. Despite being without Joel Embiid and losing Jaylen Brown to a hamstring injury in the first half, the Sixers held on to beat the Miami Heat, 111-104. A few hours later, the New York Knicks pasted the Cleveland Cavaliers, 121-102. (Can someone please stick a fork in the Cavs? For their own sake?)

Here's an updated look at the East Group B standings heading into Friday:

For the Sixers, it's simple: win and they're in. If they beat the Indiana Pacers, they'll clinch East Group B no matter what happens in Knicks-Heat. The Knicks already have two losses, and the Sixers now have the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Heat courtesy of Wednesday's victory. The Cavs have the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Sixers, but that's no longer an issue since they're locked in at 2-2.

If the Sixers lose to the Pacers, their minus-12 point differential will keep them out of the wild-card mix. You might not think that's a big deal, but as Joe Flynn noted on Bluesky, the stakes are sneakily high.

Given the three-year sample size, you might be inclined to discount that as a meaningful correlation. Fair enough. With that said, there's also a financial prize for advancing to the knockout round and beyond, which actually is a big deal for a number of players on the Sixers' roster.

This was the financial breakdown last year, according to Colin Salao of Front Office Sports:

Advance to the knockout round: $53,093 per player

Advance to the semifinals: $106,187 per player

Advance to the NBA Cup final: $212,373 per player

Sure, LeBron James and Joel Embiid might not bat an eye at an extra half-million, but most of their teammates are earning $6 million or less this year. Hell, even LeBron is only earning $3.9 million on his contract. Winning the NBA Cup would be more than a 10 percent bonus!

In years past, stars like LeBron, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander have spoken about how their lesser-paid teammates give them extra motivation to advance deep into the Cup's knockout round. For young players such as Labaron Philon Jr. ($3.6 million), Dominick Barlow ($3.4 million), Ariel Hukporti ($3.4 million), Jabari Walker ($2.6 million) and Adem Bona ($2.3 million), the Cup prize is a hefty portion of their salary.

For a basketball history buff like LeBron, there's extra incentive to reach the Cup final this year. The Cup semifinals and finals were held in Las Vegas in each of the first three years, but the NBA changed it up this year by moving the semifinals to normal NBA team markets and hosting the final at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. LeBron gushed about the Palestra earlier this year, and it's easy to imagine him getting fired up to play at another iconic non-NBA venue.

The Sixers very well might have to beat the Pacers without Brown, who aggravated his hamstring injury and is set to undergo imaging Thursday. If Embiid can return, they're likely headed for an all-time schedule loss against the Houston Rockets on the second night of a back-to-back Saturday, as both LeBron and Embiid will be more incentivized to suit up against Indiana to clinch a spot in the Cup's knockout round.

If the Sixers take care of business Friday, they'll earn at least $50,000 per player. Not bad for a day's worth of work.

#2726. Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture.

But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.

On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day.

Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions.

Perps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.

Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies.

Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now.

Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.

Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house.

"We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."

Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months.

At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.

Others have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets.

Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets.

While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S.

"That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."

Kalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived.

Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders.

But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition.

"What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama dunks against the Portland Trail Blazers in Portland, Ore., Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Craig Mitchelldyer

#2723. AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns

AI credit markets are shuddering again with Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia.

Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom.

Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points. Credit default swaps are insurance against nonpayment and are considered a barometer of perceived risks. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday after stepping down on Nov. 12 amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. His reinstatement on Monday was cheered by investors, who pushed stocks higher, yields lower and spreads on CDS tighter. However, stocks retreated, bond yields rose and CDS spreads widened on Tuesday.

Ben Emons, founder and chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, called it a waning of the "Jensen effect."

The moves suggest "markets see government intervention as 'moral suasion' that carries credit and interest-rate risks," he said.

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back.

CoreWeave wasn't the only name seeing heightened concerns in CDS spreads. Oracle's five-year CDS spread jumped 7% to 355.68. Even highly rated hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Amazon.com saw spreads widen by more than 2%. Nvidia's CDS added 3.4%.

Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds, believes the drama that unfolded with Huang's return to Nvidia won't necessarily sit well with credit investors.

"A lot of old school credit people are going to look at what kind of materialized there, the administration's involvement in putting him back in, and I think a lot of credit participants are going to step back and tiptoe away from that a bit," he said. "Credit market investors typically don't like that type of drama or uncertainty."

While Nvidia has commitments across the AI ecosystem, it is the neoclouds that have been under the most scrutiny. Many of the companies, which rent out AI computing power and cloud capacity, are highly leveraged and have relied on Nvidia financing to reduce their exposure to the bond market.

With so much riding on Nvidia's funding, Huang's next move is being closely watched.

During his brief absence, chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call that Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments" and will remain disciplined in how it commits capital.

That suggested Nvidia was going to be more judicious with financing, says Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"That concern should be put to rest with Jensen [Huang] back," he said.

Investor Steve Eisman, of "Big Short" fame and host of "The Real Eisman Playbook" podcast, believes Huang feels emboldened now that he's back in charge.

"[H]e'll double down on the circular financing," Eisman predicted on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday.

After Huang's departure, Eisman believed that the ecosystem the CEO created by pouring money into AI companies would likely unwind and leave some of the companies in "big trouble."

"Now that he's back, they're not," he said.

Others are not so certain the level of funding will continue.

"Given scrutiny of disclosure around financing and guarantees … we do not expect Mr. Huang's return to bring a quick reversion to broader customer financing," Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a note Monday.

Nvidia said on its earnings call that it has $118 billion in guarantees, as of Oct. 25, to back AI projects.

Concerns about the level of debt to fund the AI infrastructure buildout had already taken hold before Huang's departure and reinstatement.

"These issues have not disappeared just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate Jensen Huang," said economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research.

John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson Investors, believes having Huang back at the helm "reaffirms his existing go-to-market strategy." However, the credit market is still taking a cautious look at the neoclouds as it waits for more clarity on long-term supply/demand dynamics.

Still, Lloyd is cautiously positive on CoreWeave, which he owns in portfolios he manages, and noted all the data point to a "pretty healthy environment right now." That includes strong residual values on graphics processing units and spot compute rates, he noted.

"The company is doing everything in its power to execute," he said. "They don't need the high yield market at this time."

In the meantime, investigations into Nvidia and Huang are ramping up. Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his activities, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a probe. At the federal level, President Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"There's other shoes to drop," Rosenberg said. "I don't think that the book has been closed on this file."

#2721. Chase Elliott: Strong Start Gone Sour Raises Questions for 2027

CONCORD, N.C. -- Is it time for one of NASCAR's longest-running driver-crew chief combos to split up after their worst season yet? Maybe.

Chase Elliott started the season strong, getting his first win in the seventh race of the season. The win at Martinsville Speedway in March was the earliest Elliott had ever won in a season and was the first of two victories in the first 11 races. After the 11th race, which he won at Texas Motor Speedway, he was third in the points standings.

After 14 races, Elliott had eight top-10 finishes, including five top-five finishes.

Then in the 21 races after getting in a hard crash at Michigan International Speedway, Elliott could only muster five top-10s, including three top-fives.

When the season ended, Elliott had eight top-fives, 13 top-10s and an average finish of 15.1. All of these ranked low in the context of Elliott's career, only earning fewer top-fives in a season where he missed seven races (eight top-fives in 29 starts). In no season had he ever earned fewer top-10s or a worse average finish. His laps led (318) is also the second-worst that Elliott has ever had in a single season, behind only 325 in 2018.

Coincidentally, that was the year that most closely mirrored what 2026 was like for Hendrick. They needed time to adapt to a new body and struggled in the process.

What's different is Kyle Larson, William Byron and even Alex Bowman took somewhat of a step forward with the further-developed body while Elliott took a step back.

Elliott had four top-10 finishes in the final 10 races: Eighth at Kansas Speedway, seventh at Las Vegas Motor Speedway, third at Phoenix Raceway and second at Martinsville Speedway. However a 22nd-place finish at Homestead-Miami Speedway, a 12th-place finish at Charlotte Motor Speedway and a 23rd-place finish, three laps down on speed at Bristol Motor Speedway showed cracks in their speed.

When Hendrick named new crew chiefs for Alex Bowman (Rudy Fugle) and William Byron (Adam Wall), many hoped Elliott something would happen for Elliott. However, the plan was set in stone and Gustafson and Elliott are coming back.

Gustafson has been in the Cup Series for 22 years, including 11 with Elliott who has earned essentially all of his stats with him. Momentum carries over so the duo will need to start strong to not let that hangover spike.

If not, it may be time to reassess Elliott and Gustafson.

#2720. Tom Brady doesn't approve of Aaron Rodgers' comments on Mike McCarthy: 'Nobody wins when the family feuds'

Aaron Rodgers ended his Pittsburgh Steelers career in a way that will be remembered long after his time as a player ends. Tom Brady does not appear to approve.

The former New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers star and current Fox Sports broadcaster weighed in on Rodgers going scorched-earth against Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during the Philadelphia Eagles-Dallas Cowboys Thanksgiving game on Thursday, suggesting Rodgers should have taken a more graceful route out of Pittsburgh:

"The sanctity of an NFL locker room, it's a very sacred place. We shouldn't ever lose track of that as players. It's a privilege to be in that locker room. You're fighting with your teammates, you're fighting with your coaches, you're always acting as a team together. Shouldn't always be the place for private things to become public, that's what I'll say."

The trouble for the Steelers began late Tuesday night, when the team announced it was benching Rodgers and starting backup quarterback Mason Rudolph against the Denver Broncos on Thursday. Rodgers responded by going onto his friend Pat McAfee's show and unleashing a torrent of claims about McCarthy's aptitude for the job.

The Steelers officially released Rodgers soon after the interview. Subsequent reports indicated Rodgers demanded the team either give him play-calling duties or release him, with McCarthy later confirming Rodgers "made an ultimatum."

Brady praised Rodgers' career, but again indicated there wasn't much to be proud about this week:

"Certainly a Hall of Fame career and he's a tremendous player and it has nothing to do with his play-style. I was fortunate to be around a lot of great teammates over the years, and what made a great teammate to me was you cared about your teammates and your coaches, and you cared about what your team was trying to accomplish. That supersedes any individual aspect of your game that you want to promote.

"Again, I was very fortunate. It was a great locker room. I played for my teammates, I played for my coaches. Nobody wins when the family feuds."

Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady both had tension with a longtime head coach. The two situations ended very differently.

For his part, Brady played under a grand total of three head coaches during his NFL career: Bill Belichick with the New England Patriots and Bruce Arians and Todd Bowles with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Perhaps reinforcing his point, it's well-known that Brady and Belichick had their friction while working together. Brady acknowledged last year that "a natural tension" developed and only ended when he left New England, but there was no public blow-up and Brady has otherwise supported and defended the coach since their split.

Rodgers' time with McCarthy goes back to his sophomore year in the NFL in 2006, two years before his first career start. McCarthy's hire in Pittsburgh reportedly wasn't intended as a way to lure back Rodgers for another year, but it felt like a natural reunion for a pairing that once won a Super Bowl together.

#2717. Hull City unlikely to keep Vaz beyond January

From a future investment to a potential transfer problem: Robinio Vaz's time away from Roma risks ending sooner than expected.

The French striker, who moved to Hull City during the final days of the summer transfer window, has failed to establish a significant role in the English side.

According to Tuttomercatoweb.com, the Premier League club is even considering terminating his loan deal early.

Roma acquired Robinio Vaz from Marseille last January for approximately €25 million, banking on the qualities of the 2007-born striker, considered an interesting prospect.

The deal was designed with the player's future development in mind, but the size of the investment also suggested a potential immediate contribution.

In the second half of the season, however, the Frenchman failed to convince Gian Piero Gasperini, finding very few opportunities to shine. After spending the summer in Rome, the club therefore chose to send him out on loan to help him develop through increased use.

The agreement with Hull City included a €2 million loan with a €30 million option to buy, a deal that could have guaranteed Roma a significant financial return in the event of positive performances. However, things aren't going as expected.

Vaz continues to find little playing time, and the English club isn't reportedly considering a permanent purchase of the player.

Instead, the possibility of terminating the deal during the next transfer window has emerged, potentially returning the striker to the Giallorossi early.

Roma is also reportedly dissatisfied with the situation, especially since the lack of playing time risks further slowing the young Frenchman's development and compromising his value.

The initial goal of the loan was to allow Vaz to gain experience and demonstrate his qualities more consistently, but so far the move to England hasn't yielded the desired results.

#2715. The Jordan Clarkson moment that shows why Knicks’ unique bench works so well

It was a guy who didn't play who served as a catalyst for the Knicks' most all-around win this year.

Coach Mike Brown used 12 players in the team's 121-102 win over the Cavs on Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden. Without OG Anunoby (calf strain) and Miles McBride (adductor tightness), it meant end-of-the-bench reserves got a rare chance to see some action.

Pacôme Dadiet had seven points in 14 minutes. Rookie Tyler Nickel, making his NBA debut (he has spent this year in the G League), got nine minutes and had five points. Mohamed Diawara got four minutes and chipped in three points. James Wiseman saw six minutes of action and helped seal the win with a few crucial rebounds late — he finished with six offensive rebounds.

Under Brown's anything-goes system, nobody is too far away from getting a chance. His love of experimentation, particularly early in the year, means players seemingly out of the rotation will get their opportunity to prove themselves at some point.

Jordan Clarkson of the New York Knicks smiles before an NBA basketball game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

It has cultivated an ego-less culture among the bench players, where they know the minutes will look different every night. It's a system of basketball socialism of sorts. But it's only possible because one member of that group set the tone for the rest.

"As a coach, you could want to do that, but you have to have others around you that will at least support it initially to see how it turns out," Brown said. "And a huge, huge, huge catalyst for that was Jordan Clarkson. Jordan Clarkson was the one, if you're talking about giving 100 percent out there to what allows me to do that, I think Jordan Clarkson gave me at least 90 percent of the opportunity to do it, because here's an accomplished veteran that could be in the rotation for almost any team out there, let alone a championship team, and I can literally play him six straight games and then sit him 10 straight games and he's gonna be the same dude every fricken' day. And he's gonna talk the same way to his teammates. Not 'can you believe what Mike Brown did?' Nah, he's gonna be the same dude, uplift the group, and then when I call his number again, he's gonna be ready to go.

"He's a guy that, even when he gets done playing, it's one of those things where you hope that he can just be a part of this organization in some way, shape or form until he doesn't want to be part of this organization. He's that type of person, in my opinion."

Clarkson missed Wednesday's game — the fourth straight he's been sidelined due to plantar fasciitis. But it was he who helped Dadiet — who has largely underwhelmed, now in his third year after the Knicks drafted him in the first round — deliver his best game as a pro.

"JC is always big on that, telling guys to stay ready," Jose Alvarado said. "He was in [Dadiet's] ear the whole shootaround [Wednesday morning]. Just telling everybody to stay ready because you never know when your name is called."

New York Knicks forward Pacome Dadiet (4) puts up a shot against the Cleveland Cavaliers at Madison Square Garden in New York, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

Alvarado himself had his best game of the year with 21 points in 19 minutes. But it wasn't long ago that he was out of the rotation, with Tyler Kolek having usurped him as the backup point guard.

But Brown has recently been experimenting with having Alvarado on the floor at the same time as Jalen Brunson, in order to allow Brunson to play off-the-ball more. And Brown has liked the results.

That has meant Alvarado is now cutting back into Kolek's minutes, despite Kolek continuing to play well. That could rub other players on other teams the wrong way –— losing minutes despite not doing anything wrong, simply because the coach wants to try something new and see how it works out. For the bench players, nothing is set in stone, regardless of how you play.

This team embraces it, though. Brown compared the way this bench pulls for one another to the championship Spurs and Warriors teams he was an assistant on.

"We care about each other," Landry Shamet, currently the top dog of that bench unit, said. "We want to win for each other. We're willing to take on different roles and we know that we've got each other's back. If Jose's got it going and my minutes are shortened, awesome. And vice versa. All of us, Deuce [McBride] included in that, I would throw him in that as well, all of us kind of feel that way. That's really cool.

"I've been saying it, I've been a broken record about it, but you don't see that — that's very rare where no ego or ulterior motives get involved. That's something special that you want to be a part of."

Something special, sparked by a special personality in Clarkson.

#2714. 2026 Week 13 American Conference Previews and Predictions

The final week of the regular season here, and the American Conference championship race still has nine of 14 teams technically alive.

UTSA (9-2, 6-1 American) is the only team that controls its own destiny for the championship, and the Roadrunners can secure hosting duties with a win over Tulsa on Black Friday. Memphis (8-3, 5-2 American), North Texas (7-4. 5-2 American), and East Carolina (7-4, 5-2 American) are currently tied for second place, and since all three teams did not play each other, a three-way tiebreaker would be determined by computer rankings. Thus, UTSA is the only team that controls its own destiny for the championship.

If Memphis, North Texas, and East Carolina all lose, that opens the door for five three-loss teams — Army (5-5, 4-3 American), Tulsa (7-4, 4-3 American), Florida Atlantic (7-4, 4-3 American), Tulane (6-5, 4-3 American), and UAB (6-5, 4-3 American).

Six of the seven Week 13 matchups feature teams still mathmetically alive for the title game. Here's a preview of the final week of American play:

Tulsa (7-4, 4-3 American) enters as a slight road favorite, and that's a testament to how the Golden Hurricane have played lately. Tre Lamb's team has won three consecutive matchups, defeating Tulane by 50, Florida Atlantic by 17, and Charlotte by 28, finding an offensive rhythm down the stretch of November. Quarterback Baylor Hayes has registered the highest, second-highest, and fourth-highest passing totals of his college career during this three-game win streak, accounting for 11 total touchdowns during the span. Wide receiver Oran Singleton Jr. is also emerging as a star, and he's on the precipice of a 1,000-yard season coming off his second 100+ yard, 3-touchdown outing of November. The Golden Hurricane defense, which famously stonewalled Oklahoma State in Week 1, has also returned as Tulsa is only allowed 15.0 points per game during this win streak. Also, no American team has decisively defeated — all three conference defeats were all by one score, and the Golden Hurricane led by double-digits in two of them.

UTSA (9-2, 6-1 American) may be the underdog, but history suggests it's dangerous to doubt Jeff Traylor in the Alamodome. The head coach is 28-1 at home against conference opponents, most recently upsetting North Texas in 35-16 fashion. UTSA will look for an offensive resurgence after scoring just 19 points against UAB last week. The status of A'Marion Peterson, who averages 8.3 yards per carry and ranks fifth nationally with 16 rushing touchdowns, is unknown, but the Roadrunners still field strong running back depth with Will Henderson III and Brandon High Jr. UTSA also looks for a strong performance from Owen McCown, who will be recognized on senior day after serving three years as the starting quarterback. UTSA's defense has been quite volatile this season, surrendering 60 to Florida Atlantic but holding North Texas to as few as 16. The Roadrunners generate frequent takeaways but often struggle generating pressure, ranking 15th-to-last nationally in sacks.

Temple (2-9, 1-6 American) owns the longest losing streak in the American. The Owls dropped their sixth straight game against Rice, squandering a 10-point lead in the final two minutes of regulation. That wasn't the first time Temple lost after holding a double-digit lead after the two-minute timeout either, in a year defined by crunch time struggles. One of the few bright spots in an otherwise-lost season is the play of outside linebacker Curly Ordonez, whose 111 tackles rank fourth nationally. But the Owls will need to step up in other areas defensively against this explosive Memphis offense, especially after allowing north of 30 points in five of their last six. Offensively, Temple relies heavier on the run game. Keveun Mason is coming off his highest rushing output against an FBS opponent this season, producing 98 yards against Rice. Temple ranks 97th in scoring offense but could find a spark against a Memphis defense that has surrendered 38+ points in two consecutive contests.

Memphis (8-3, 5-2 American) likely remains in control of its own destiny to qualify for the American Championship Game, given its spot above North Texas and East Carolina in the computer rankings the conference uses to settle tiebreakers (a composite of SP+, SportSource TR116 TSR, ESPN SOR, and KPI). The Tigers are coming off a tough loss, however, surrendering a fourth down in the final seconds against Navy to fall 38-34. Still, the Tigers field one of the nation's top offenses, ranking first in yards per game and ninth in scoring. The unit is balanced and explosive, as Marcus Stokes ranks eighth in the FBS in passing, while Jaylin Carter ranks ninth nationally in rushing. Memphis ranks atop the FBS in 50, 60, and 70-yard plays, proving the ability to score from anywhere on the field. But to make its first conference title game since 2019, improvement will be need to seen defensively. The Tigers are 111th in total defense, most recently allowing 41 points to South Florida and 38 to Navy, struggling particularly with quarterback mobility.

Navy (4-6, 3-4 American) registered a very on-brand win last week. For the third consecutive year, the Midshipmen played the role of spoiler, unseating a ranked team despite entering the matchup unranked. Even though Navy won't qualify for bowl eligibility for the first time since 2023, the team remains dangerous thanks to the dominance of Jackson Gutierrez. The mobile quarterback ranks first nationally with 140.5 rushing yards per game, and he enters this Charlotte matchup coming off his third performance with at least 220 rushing yards and two touchdowns this season. Thanks to Gutierrez's mobility, Navy has scored at least 34 points in each of its last five conference matchups. But the Midshipmen aren't as sturdy on defense as they've been in the previous two seasons, surrendering at least 34 points in five consecutive matchups. Linebackers Coleman Cauley and MarcAnthony Parker will lead the charge defensively as Navy aims to extend its winning streak to three prior to the Army-Navy Game.

Charlotte (1-10, 1-6 American) can improve upon last year's record with a win on senior day. The 49ers have endured a difficult season, but they've demonstrated progress in recent weeks, defeating Temple on Oct. 17, taking Tulane to overtime on Oct. 30, and falling by one point to East Carolina on Nov. 14. Charlotte is at its best when Conner Harrell is at his best, but the team will also need to pick up its 122nd-ranked run game heading into the finale. The 49ers' defense was at its best in early November, holding ECU to 17 points and UAB to 23, but the unit took a step back last weekend. The unit, led by middle linebacker Gavin Willis, will be tested with a high-powered run game, hoping its 113th-ranked run defense can provide enough stops to upset the Midshipmen.

Florida Atlantic (7-4, 4-3 American) offers the superior offense in this matchup. The Owls rank 11th nationally with 38.0 points per game, fielding the nation's 14th-best total offense and 3rd-best passing offense. Zach Kittley's air raid offense has thrived this year, largely due to the connection between Caden Veltkamp and Easton Messer. Veltkamp, the nation's leader in touchdown passes with 33, has eclipsed 300 passing yards in six of seven conference matchups — and the other was a 60-29 win over Florida Atlantic where the run game thrived. Meanwhile, Messer is the FBS receptions leader, ranking seventh in yards and second in touchdowns. Kelby Valsin also has over 1,000 receiving yards in this offense that often substitutes the run game for quick throws. The Owls defense has been a concern for much of the year, ranking third-to-last in the country in yards allowed per game. However, the unit has improved in recent weeks, limiting UTSA to 29 and South Florida to 14. Takeaways have fueled that, and FAU has come up with seven in its last three outings.

East Carolia (7-4, 4-3 American) offers the superior defense in this matchup. The Pirates ride a four-game win streak, and they haven't surrendered more than 17 points during that timeframe, most recently stifling Army in a 10-6 decision. The Pirates are the ultimate backfield invaders, ranking first in the FBS in tackles for loss with 9.2 per game, and Kieran Davis leads the team with 12. ECU will need to rely more on the passing defense against Florida Atlantic, and that unit has been stellar too. The Pirates surrender 182 passing yards per game, and they've recorded more interceptions (11) than they have allowed passing touchdowns (8). But to compete with Florida Atlantic, ECU will need to unleash more of an offense that hasn't scored more than 20 during its four-game win streak. The main source of offense is a ground game led by TJ Engleman Jr., who is coming off his sixth 100-yard performance in his last eight games.

Prediction: Florida Atlantic 28, East Carolina 16

Army (5-5, 4-3 American) must win this week to secure bowl eligibility and reach the six-win mark for the 10th time in 11 years under Jeff Monken. The Black Knights were in excellent position for their second American championship in three years several weeks ago, but they've dropped three consecutive matchups — two by one score. Close games have been a theme for Army, which has competed in 13 one-score games across its last 13 FBS matchups. Monken's No. 2 ranked rushing offense is led by quarterback Cale Hellums, who is 30 yards away from his second straight 1,000-yard season. Additionally, running back Godspower Nwawuihe has provided a boost to the option attack lately, producing two 100-yard games in late October. However, Army has been burdened by miscues lately, committing four of its six turnovers this season in the last three weeks. The Black Knights aim to improve ball security as well as defense that ranks 97th against the run, allowing over 5.1 yards per carry.

Rice (2-9, 1-6 American) counters Army with an option attack of its own, although the scheme is different. The Owls are coming off their first FBS win of 2026, and it was a triumphant yet unorthodox one. Rice deployed three different quarterbacks during a late double-digit comeback at Temple, utilizing Gael Ochoa as the primary option, Jacurri Brown as the short-yardage specialist, and Patrick Crayton Jr. as the long-distance passing threat. The strategy worked, and Rice's offense was at its best under the atypical arrangement. Thus, anything is on the table for the Owls in their season finale. While Scott Abell's team was a strong finisher against Temple, the team is typically a strong starter, especially on defense where it hasn't allowed more than 10 first half points since Oct. 24.

Saturday, Nov. 28 at 3:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+)

Tulane (6-5, 4-3 American) clinched bowl eligibility for a fifth straight season last week, storming back from a 10-point fourth quarter deficit to upset North Texas. While mathematically alive, the Green Wave likely will not qualify for their fifth conference championship in five years, but they've saved their best for the elite teams in the conference, knocking off both Memphis and North Texas. True freshman Trace Johnson started both of those victories, and he's showing signs of development, producing the best performance of his career with 283 yards and four touchdown deliveries last week. Tulane also provides firepower in the run game with a deep running back corps of Jaylin Lucas, Maurice Turner, Johnnie Daniels, and Jamauri McClure — and three of those tailbacks have exceed 100 rushing yards this year. While the Green Wave thrive on the ground, their opponents do the same. Tulane ranks second-to-last nationally in run defense, surrendering over 223 yards per game.

South Florida (6-5, 2-5 American) was the only team in the American to sweep its non-conference slate, but the Bulls have struggled mightily against their conference peers. USF enters its final home game at Raymond James Stadium riding a three-game losing streak, suffering close defeats to East Carolina and Memphis before a multifaceted struggle at Florida Atlantic. The Bulls' defense has been respectable for most of the season, ranking 35th in fewest points allowed per game. But the team will need more offense to secure its fourth consecutive winning season. Two weeks ago, USF had its best offensive showing of the season against Memphis when quarterback Luke Kromenhoek threw for 271 yards and rushed for 146. After parting ways with offensive coordinator Tim Beck this week, the Bulls look to unearth that version of Kromenhoek one final time before leaving Raymond James Stadium.

UAB (6-5, 4-3 American) enjoyed one of the most successful rebuilding efforts in the American this year, locking up bowl eligibility in the first full season under head coach Alex Mortensen. That dramatic improvement can be traced to the defense led by coordinator Todd Grantham. Last season, UAB ranked second-to-last in scoring defense. This year, the Blazers are 47th in scoring defense, 20th in total defense, and first in passing defense. Edge rusher Marlin Dean, a candidate for the conference's defensive player of the year, has led the charge with 11.5 sacks (third in FBS) and five forced fumbles (first in FBS). The star talent on defense translates to the back end where cornerback Delvon Gulley has deflected a conference-best eight passes while picking off two — including a game-sealing pick-six against East Carolina. The defense provided enough stops to upset conference leader UTSA last week, but ultimately fell 19-17, needing more offensive contributions to win. Running back Rod Robinson II, who has 371 rushing yards and five touchdowns in November, hopes his contributions will be enough at North Texas.

North Texas (6-5, 4-3 American) had the clearest path to the American Championship two weeks ago as the last remaining team with a perfect conference record. In two weeks, the Mean Green's spectacular season was derailed by UTSA, Tulane, and quarterback injuries. Losing starter Tayven Jackson (sixth nationally in passing yards per game) due to an upper body injury was a significant blow, but things went further south for the Mean Green when backup Chris Jimerson Jr. exited last Saturday's contest with an injury, causing the team to finish with wide receiver James Tyre at quarterback. While North Texas' QB situation remains unclear for Saturday, the Mean Green know they can rely on a run game headlined by Jahiem White, who ranks fifth nationally in rushing. A shorthanded North Texas will need any offensive firepower it can get to qualify for a second consecutive championship game. After scoring 45+ points in six consecutive games, Neal Brown's team has been held to 16 and 24 in the past two weeks.

#2713. Eagles, ex-Cowboys QB Joe Milton III overcome 21-point deficit to stun Dallas: 'I know that defense like the back of my hand'

The Philadelphia Eagles stunned the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving, kicking a 59-yard game-winning field goal with two seconds left to clinch a 39-38 victory for their second consecutive win in a crucial divisional matchup.

The 21-point comeback marked the largest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history.

It looked like the Eagles were done for, unable to muster much offense and unable to stop the Cowboys' offense. Dallas led 31-10 with 15 seconds left in the third quarter, but Philadelphia stormed back thanks to quarterback Joe Milton III's arm.

The momentum swung in a big way when Milton launched a 45-yard touchdown pass near the goal line, finding DeVonta Smith for the score.

That was the duo's second long touchdown of the game; they connected earlier on a 50-yard score.

The Eagles claimed Milton after the Cowboys cut him from their practice squad on Oct. 16. Thursday was his third start for the Philadelphia, and he finished the great comeback 21-for-31 passing for 331 yards, 3 touchdowns and 1 interception.

"I know that defense like the back of my hand," Milton said, per the Forth Worth Star- Telegram's Nick Harris.

After the 45-yard Smith score, the Eagles' special teams unit blocked a punt and recovered it for a touchdown. In a minute and a half, Philadelphia went from trailing by 21 to seven.

Dak Prescott led a Cowboys touchdown drive, ending it with an impressive quarterback keeper as he lunged to the end zone, got hit, and still managed to carry the ball across the goal line while in bounds.

Milton answered, almost identically, with a rushing touchdown of his own on the following drive, though his didn't have to withstand a big hit from a defender.

After a Dallas punt, it looked like the Eagles had the chance they needed, but Milton made one of his few mistakes with an interception he threw into triple coverage.

The only harm came from time lost on the clock as Brandon Aubrey missed a 40-yard field goal.

Milton put the team on his back again and fired a laser to the end zone, finding first-round rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon leaping into the end zone.

The Eagles went for 2 and converted, but it was called back due to holding. Philadelphia's second attempt at a 2-point conversion fell to the ground.

Prescott and the Cowboys tried to run out the clock, but they faced fourth-and-1 on the Eagles' 39-yard line. Prescott was sacked for a 9-yard loss, giving the Eagles a chance to get into field-goal range and go for the win.

Milton got the Eagles to the Cowboys' 41-yard line, which was enough to put Elliott in range.

After the field goal, Prescott's Hail Mary attempt fell incomplete.

"Yeah, it's pretty stunning," Prescott said via the team's website. "I said that about the Cardinals game, but this one takes the cake."

Philadelphia won its first two games of the season, and then dropped seven in a row, leading to a Week 10 bye. Philadelphia beat the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday and has now notched its second consecutive victory, moving to 4-7.

Dallas (5-7) has now alternated wins and losses since Week 6.

After getting the ball back thanks to a turnover on downs at their own 48-yard line, Eagles QB Joe Milton found DeVonta Smith twice for a combined 14 yards, but a crucial false start set them back five yards.

On fourth and 10 from the Cowboys' 41-yard line, the Eagles sent out kicker Jake Elliott to attempt the game-winning field goal from 59 yards … and it was GOOD.

Dallas got the ball back, giving Dak Prescott one pass attempt to make some magic, but it was intercepted by safety Andre Mukuba. BALL GAME.

Holding just a two-point lead over the Eagles, the Dallas Cowboys decided to go for it on fourth-and-1 with just over a minute to go in the fourth quarter.

However, it didn't go as planned, as Dak Prescott took a nine-yard sack versus DT Ty Robinson, setting up the Eagles at their own 48-yard line with under a minute to go.

Joe Milton is playing motivated football against his former team.

Milton fired another laser to the end zone and this one went to a leaping Makai Lemon, the Eagles' first-round rookie.

Philadelphia went for two, and converted but there was a flag on the play for offensive holding. The Eagles opted to still go for it, but the pass was knocked away.

Dallas will get the ball with just over 2 minutes left, clinging to a 2-point lead.

Brandon Aubrey, one of the best kickers in the league, missed a 40-yard field goal.

The ball wasn't tipped, but it took off toward the uprights and then screamed left. The replay showed the laces of the ball were facing in toward the kicker, which could have played a factor.

Eagles take over with 3:23 left, trailing by 8.

The Eagles were facing third and 15. Milton tried to find a receiver down the field, but he threw into triple coverage and it was picked off.

It was a wild play for Dallas who had a late sub and the player had barely come on the field and blitzed from the sideline, causing pressure on Milton.

Dallas takes over with just over 7 minutes left in the game, leading by 8.

Smith only missed one play and is back in the game after an extended delay while a Cowboys defender was tended to by trainers for an injury of their own.

Eagles quarterback Joe Milton was again trying to throw a deep pass to DeVonta Smith.

The wideout was in double coverage, and he went into the air to try to catch it, but got turned and landed hard on his back.

He remained down and was reaching at his back. Trainers helped him to his feet and off the field. Smith left the field, jogged a little on the sideline and then went into the medical tent.

Eagles punt returner Britain Covey took a hard hit on the punt return and it looked like the ball may have become dislodged.

It looked like it could have been a fumble in real time, but replays showed that Covey either was down before losing it, or had regained possession.

Regardless, Dallas threw the challenge flag, for real this time.

The Cowboys ran a trick play on third and 18. Dak Prescott hit George Pickens for a quick pass.

Pickens then all of a sudden passed it across the field to Hunter Luepke who weaved through defenders and ran the field all the way for a touchdown, even jumping into the Salvation Army red kettle.

There was a flag on the play. Pickens' pass was ruled to be a forward pass. Not only did the touchdown not count, but it resulted in a loss of down so the Steelers had to punt.

"Anything you can do, I can do better" - Joe Milton probably.

All of a sudden this game got interesting.

After Dak Prescott's rushing touchdown, the Eagles took over. Philadelphia needed just three plays after a big kick return to score.

Quarterback Joe Milton hit DeVonta Smith for a four-yard gain, and then on the next play the duo picked up 23 yards.

Milton and the offense was on the 15-yard line and the quarterback took it himself and ran the ball in.

The Eagles opted to go for two, but the conversion failed. Dallas leads 38-30 with 9:09 left in the game.

The Cowboys once had a 21-point lead and watched it nearly disappear as Dallas' most recent drive started with just a 7-point lead.

Dak Prescott leaned on CeeDee Lamb to get the Cowboys down the field as the star wide receiver came down with a huge 39-yard reception to flip the field. Lamb then added a 12-yard gain later in the drive.

The Cowboys found the end zone as Prescott took off down the sideline. He dove for the end zone and managed to get the ball to cross the goal line in bounds while absorbing a hit for the 14-yard score.

Dallas leads 38-24 with 10:11 left in regulation.

Dallas was facing third-and-one, and the handoff went to Javonte Williams. He was stuffed at the line and couldn't convert.

The Cowboys offense lined up to try to get the Eagles to jump but they didn't. Dallas took the delay of game and lined up to punt.

The Philadelphia special teams unit got home and blocked the punt. It bounced in the Eagles' favor and Philly was able to recover it and walk it in for the touchdown.

After the extra-point game it is all of a sudden a 7-point game.

Joe Milton and DeVonta Smith have been must-watch in this game.

Milton rolled to the right on this play and threw a rocket while on the run. He hit an open DeVonta Smith who was able to come back, catch the ball and get into the end zone.

With the extra point, Philly now trails 31-17.

Cowboys rookie wide receiver Camden Brown had his first career reception to start the drive, and it was a big one for 19 yards.

That was the highlight of the possession, though, as Dallas got into Brandon Aubrey's field goal range. The star kicker was good from 59 yards out, and Dallas now leads 31-10 with 3:30 left in the third quarter.

After the Cowboys' latest punt, the Eagles had a chance to try and spark some momentum. Will Shipley picked up 10 yards on two carries, but that is where the drive ended.

Milton was sacked for a loss of 10, Shipley picked up three yards on a carry and then Joe Milton had a deep incompletion bringing up the punt.

Dallas had scored touchdowns on back-to-back drives to end the first half. That momentum was not sustained starting the second half.

The Cowboys had a big splash play with Dak Prescott hitting CeeDee Lamb for 22 yards. After that though, it was a loss of five on a run, a gain of eight on the next play and then a sack to force a punt.

Joe Milton began the second half by finding DeVonta Smith for a five-yard gain. On second down, he was sacked for a nine-yard loss, then missed Elijah Moore on third down.

Milton's touchdown pass at the end of the first half set a team record.

According to Next Gen Stats, his pass traveled 64.4 yards in air distance, making it the longest pass TD for an Eagles QB in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016).

We head to halftime with the first half being all Cowboys.

Dallas leads 28-10, and the Eagles will get the ball coming out of the half, following an extended halftime show featuring country music singer Miranda Lambert.

#2712. Matt LaFleur on Packers' run-game struggles: "We're trying"

The Packers weren’t able to stop the run on Wednesday against the Rams. To apply a twist to a classic line from John McKay, they made up for it by not being able to run.

“Right now, we’re a pass-heavy offense and we’re trying to sneak in some runs there to at least keep the defense honest,” coach Matt LaFleur told reporters after the 26-13 loss when asked about his team’s offensive identity.

“We’re trying, for sure,” LaFleur said. “We’re trying.”

He also was asked whether they tried to run it enough.

“Obviously not, not when you lose the game like that,” LaFleur said. “So I would say the answer to your question is no. I mean, you’ve got to convert third downs too. You’ve got to get those opportunities to get some first downs. And the second half, I think we had one drive that was a seven-play drive or whatever and everything else was like three-and-out or two-and-out and we turned the ball over.”

On a night when the Rams had 241 yards rushing against only 132 yards passing, the Packers mustered only 55 rushing yards on 14 attempts.

Not having Josh Jacobs didn’t help matters. Without Jacobs (who’s recovering from a broken finger), the Packers’ backfield consisted of Kaleb Johnson (eight carries for 13 yards), MarShawn Lloyd (one carry for 10 yards), and Chris Brooks (one carry for four yards).

Receiver Savion Williams ran the ball twice for 18 yards, making him the leading rusher for Green Bay. Quarterback Jordan Love added one for seven, and receiver Bo Melton ran one time, for three yards.

And, no, that’s not good enough. Especially on a night when receiver Christian Watson was lost early to a concussion.

Even if the Packers can muster enough wins over the final six weeks to qualify for the postseason, it will become very hard to win in January if they can’t run or stop the run.

#2709. James Cook makes NFL history on Thanksgiving night

Buffalo Bills running back James Cook III has a share of another NFL record. Cook has now rushed for at least 75 yards and a touchdown in 10 consecutive games, tying a record Terry Allen set across the 1995 and 1996 seasons with Washington.

Cook found the end zone against the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night during the second quarter to put the Bills up 7-0. He then eclipsed the 75-yard mark in the third quarter on a five-yard run that put him at 79 for the night.

It's been 30 years since Allen put together his streak of 10 games. Since then, we've watched some pretty impressive running backs come through the NFL. LaDainian Tomlinson, Adrian Peterson, and Derrick Henry have all had their share of record-setting performances, but none of them managed to do what Cook just did.

And unlike Allen, who needed parts of two seasons to put together his streak, Cook has done it all in the same season. In fact, the Bills' season opener was the only game this year in which Cook didn't meet both statistical requirements.

Cook entered Thursday night's game having rushed for 1,003 yards and 10 touchdowns over the course of his nine-game streak, averaging 111.4 yards per game and 5.1 yards per carry. He eclipsed the century mark in five of those nine games, including a season-high 157-yard performance against the New York Jets.

Remember when we spent so much of the offseason in 2025 talking about whether the Bills should pay Cook? Buffalo eventually gave its running back a four-year, $48 million contract extension, and Cook has spent the better part of two seasons giving us reasons to talk about what a good decision that was.

The Bills will head to Foxborough next week for their second meeting of the season with the New England Patriots. Cook rushed for 75 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries in their first matchup.

Another 75 yards and a trip to the end zone next week, and Cook will have an NFL record all to himself. Considering we've been watching him do just that every week since September, it might be time to start wondering just how big a number he's going to leave for the next running back to chase.

#2708. Ex-Steelers’ Mike Tomlin Gets Brutally Honest About Rodgers-McCarthy ‘Dumpster Fire’

Offering the most unique perspective possible, former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin spoke open and honestly about what's going on within the franchise he presided over for 19 years.

And to be as candid as possible, the coach turned NBC analyst labeled the current state of the once-proud Pittsburgh Steelers as a "dumpster fire" before finishing his commentary on a 24-hour period thats saw Mike McCarthy bench Aaron Rodgers and then the future Hall of Fame quarterback take the opportunity Pat McAfee provided to unleash on the coach in a way that aired out "dirty laundry" that occurred behind closed doors, leading to his subsequent release.

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events," Tomlin admitted at halftime of NBC's broadcast of the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills. "To see laundry aired out that way in a public form ran counter to NFL norms."

Tomlin hoped for a better end to a legendary career for Rodgers, the quarterback who led the Steelers to his final playoff game with the franchise last year. He also said he was surprised to see Rodgers reveal information the public wouldn't otherwise know – Rodgers accusing McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, saying "1-2-3, go Packers!" at halftime and being disinterested in getting to know members of the defense.

"I think the prevailing one is just general sadness – sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career, the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers. And just on a macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum – those are things that kinda run counterculture to professional football."

And to top matters off, Tomlin even contradicted what Steelers owner and team president Art Rooney II said about Rodgers. After Rooney II told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette's Gerry Dulac, the longest tenured Steelers reporter on the beat, that Rodgers was a bad teammate earlier on Thanksgiving Day, Tomlin closed the night by characterizing the 42-year-old quarterback's relationship with his teammates as someone who was "beloved" and stressed he's not exaggerating that compliment.

All in all, Tomlin expressed a sadness most Steelers fans can relate to. But to be fair to McCarthy and all involved, Tomlin did admit it was far from smooth sailing drama wise during his tenure. Tomlin even said as much, placing the "dumpster fire" label on several of the scenarios he dealt with as well.

#2706. Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But investigations into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts.

"Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders."

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday.

Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia. A separate securities class action targets the company and Huang, its co-founder.

Now the board’s insurance choices are part of the story. A risk advisor with direct knowledge of Nvidia’s coverage says the company built an approximately $1 billion D&O tower, insurance jargon for directors and officers insurance policies from different companies that combine to cover one massive risk.

Nvidia "loves insurance," the advisor said. “They buy insurance as if they have no balance sheet.” A billion-dollar tower would essentially mean Nvidia "bought the market," purchasing all the coverage it could get, according to an industry expert with 25 years working in financial insurance. The expert asked not to be named out of concern for past or potential future clients.

But Nvidia directed all that coverage to Side A only, according to CNBC's source. Side A protects directors and officers personally when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B covers the company for legal defense costs or settlements on behalf of directors and officers, and Side C protects the company when it's named as a defendant in a suit such as a securities claim.

The risk advisor says Nvidia believed it had "the war chest" to protect itself against a securities class action suit.

That choice is raising questions about whether the board protected itself at the company’s expense. CNBC asked Nvidia for comment but received no response.

An insurance CEO characterized a billion-dollar policy as a lot of coverage, but said a Side A-only allocation was a surprising move because it results in imbalanced coverage, protecting only directors.

That structure is not automatically a governance failure, according to a D&O insurance expert with long experience in coverage for banks, drugmakers and other businesses that often face litigation. Side A-only programs are common among companies with the capital to manage the corporate risk internally.

"For a company with Nvidia’s resources, retaining the company-side risk can make financial sense," the advisor said. It's Side A D&O that's "imperative to corporate governance."

"It is a capital-allocation decision," the expert told me. The company decides that buying insurance for its own balance sheet is not worth the premium. In other words, Side B and Side C are considered too expensive for the coverage the company gets.

The question for shareholders is whether the board’s decision to hold that risk was a sound use of the company’s resources and whether the company can absorb the costs if the claims grow.

A shareholder derivative complaint filed Nov. 11 names Huang, directors and other officers. It alleges that they failed to oversee risks involving Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and made misleading statements. It also alleges that some defendants sold roughly $2 billion in Nvidia stock while holding material nonpublic information. Those remain allegations, not findings.

A separate securities class action, filed Nov. 9, names Nvidia and Huang. It seeks damages for investors who bought Nvidia shares between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, alleging the company and Huang misled investors.

The distinction matters: The derivative suit is brought on Nvidia’s behalf, while the class action seeks recovery for investors.

"Insurance is already at work," says Michel Léonard, chief economist at the Insurance Information Institute, describing standard policy mechanics, not Nvidia’s specific policy. "Once the suit is filed, D&O starts paying defense costs, long before anyone proves anything."

A claim still has to meet the policy’s terms, and defense costs can reduce the remaining limits. Nor does a drop in Nvidia’s market value by itself establish an insurable loss. Plaintiffs would need to prove legally recoverable damages; the policy would respond only to covered losses.

The board has already taken steps it says are aimed at accountability. Nvidia announced an independent investigation on Nov. 8, and independent directors retained outside counsel two days later. Huang resigned as CEO and a director on Nov. 11; the board appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised by Huang's extramarital relationships.

Atkins, who joined the board of Wynn Resorts in 2018 after founder Steve Wynn resigned, argues that allegations are not conclusions and that boards should also weigh governance concerns against the value a founder brings to a company’s innovation. Nvidia's investigation is continuing even as Huang resumes leadership.

“Will companies’ hyper-accelerated innovation speed be the same without them? I don’t think so,” said Atkins, author of "Don't Waste a Board Seat: A Decision-Maker's Guide to Choosing Directors Who Create Value."

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy also says the company has indemnity agreements with its directors and officers — separate from its insurance. Those agreements provide for the company to cover certain costs and liabilities when the law permits.

#2700. Bears stun Lions on late Rome Odunze TD

The Bears suffered an agonizing defeat in Detroit on Thanksgiving a couple of years ago, but they found themselves on the other side of things this time around.

Caleb Williams hit wide receiver Rome Odunze in the back corner of the end zone for a six-yard touchdown with three seconds left on the clock. The extra point gave the Bears a 39-35 lead and the game came to an end after the Lions’ attempt to lateral down the field failed to produce a miracle.

It was the first time the Bears led all day, but that’s all it took for them to end the day in sole possession of first place in the NFC North. Odunze’s score capped a wild second half that saw the two teams put up 55 combined points in one of the most entertaining games of the season.

The game-winning touchdown drive came after Lions head coach Dan Campbell passed on a 51-yard field goal with 2:22 to play in the game and went for it on fourth-and-4. A pass to running back Jahmyr Gibbs was complete, but he was yanked down by linebacker T.J. Edwards and stopped short of a first down.

Campbell’s decisions on the previous possession will also merit a second look. The Lions chose to have Jared Goff roll left to throw on a third-and-1 while in field goal territory and Goff’s pass behind Jameson Williams wound up being intercepted by Bears safety Dillon Thieneman. The Lions chose to run with Sione Vaki rather than Gibbs on the previous play, which was a curious choice on a day when Gibbs ran 21 times for 205 yards and three touchdowns.

That aggressiveness has been a hallmark of the Campbell era, but the calls backfired on a day when the Lions led by as many as 11 points. The defense coming up with big plays to thwart Campbell’s gambles deserves credit for the ultimate result and so does Williams, who finished the day 30-of-44 for 345 yards and two scores despite losing tight end Colston Loveland to a knee injury early in the first quarter.

Williams proved his mettle in big spots several times last season and Thursday’s win is the latest reminder why the Bears are building their future around him. They’ll return home next week for a date with another division leader in the Jaguars and these two teams will do it again in Chicago in Week 17.

The Lions will try to rebound in Atlanta next Sunday and they can’t afford too many more stumbles in a jam-packed NFC playoff race.

#2699. What are Spurs fans thankful for this Thanksgiving?

The Spurs had a tough loss in Portland before the Thanksgiving break and will face arguably their biggest challenge yet when they face the West-leading Lakers after it. We are getting close to a quarter of the season being on the books, and games are starting to feel more meaningful as most teams round into shape.

As the season progresses, it gets harder to sit back and just enjoy San Antonio basketball without any concerns, but fortunately Thanksgiving offers the perfect opportunity to think about all the good times it has provided already and to reflect on how lucky fans of the Silver and Black really are.

Lee Dressie had a fantastic post about it that you should check out, but it would be interesting to see what you, the readers, are thankful for. Here's my list, as a way to get things started.

This one is self-explanatory. Wembanyama is the most tantalizing talent to hit the league in a generation, and he's a Spur. Luck got him to San Antonio, but he embraced the fanbase and seems to be happy to be in the city. He's lived up to the hype and seems like a perfect fit for the franchise, adapting to its traditions and ways while staying eager to forge his own path.

Watching Wemby is a joy for anyone who loves basketball, but it's extra special to watch him dominate while wearing Silver and Black.

The Spurs will be without Dylan Harper due to a hip injury for a while longer. Fans have not even gotten to see how Tobias Harris looks on this team, as he's been out since before preseason with a calf strain. A dirty play by Jeremiah Fears has forced De'Aaron Fox to sit out a few games. San Antonio has had its share of injuries.

Fortunately, none of those injuries have sidelined anyone for the rest of the year and, if everything goes well (knocks frantically on wood), all three players should be back relatively soon. Other contenders have not been so lucky, so it's important to be thankful for the injury luck the Spurs have had so far.

Sometimes fans are forced to root for players that, while talented, are not particularly likable. Whether because they are out of touch after becoming rich and famous or because of their personalities or bad behaviour, it can occasionally be hard to actually like the guys wearing the jersey. Luckily, that's not a problem with the current Spurs.

Sure, Wembanyama can come off as arrogant, but he also seems to have a good moral compass and is boring in a good way, putting basketball above everything. De'Aaron Fox always has a smile on his face and has adapted to any role asked of him. Harrison Barnes is the ultimate professional and a very charitable person. The young guards are hard workers who are willing to continue to improve instead of relying on talent and athleticism alone. Devin Vassell is soft-spoken but committed to winning, no matter what it takes.

Even the guys who have struggled, like Keldon Johnson and Luke Kornet, have great personalities that make them lovable. It's really hard to find someone to dislike on the roster, which makes watching the Spurs a lot more fun.

This one is important to remember, especially after rough losses. The Spurs have fallen short in four games this season and have had some close calls against inferior opponents. It's completely understandable to have some concerns about the team during the bad times, and occasionally even during the good times. The good news is, while there are some issues, none seem unsolvable.

The Spurs have a ton of talent, so they can overcome some mistakes, which is great. The three-point shooting has been so bad that it's bound to improve. The bench play has been poor, but it shouldn't be impossible to find some lineups that work better. Having Harris back will certainly help the second unit. And if all else fails, a trade or a signing could give the team a boost if it needs one. San Antonio is in a great place already, but things could realistically get even better.

Now let's get to the important part. What are you thankful for as a Spurs fan? Let us know in the comments.

The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data.

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.

"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.

The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s.

Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt.

Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle.

The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.
