#2689. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2684. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2677. LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'

LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over 'Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was another eventful week for LeBron James.

That's why we started the LeBron Log in the first place.

The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft.

This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson.

James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers' latest team outing.

He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone's fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character.

"I mean, it's Rocky. We in Philly," James said. "I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I've got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool."

The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona.

"Movie night, courtesy of LeBron," the team wrote.

The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3.

Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players.

"They went, they said it was very good, they loved it," Nurse said. "The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same."

James' first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition.

James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting.

The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball.

"I'm a guy who don't like shooting against the laces," James said. "So sometimes I'll come up on a quick stop and I'm about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I'll turn that into a pump fake."

The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix.

James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night's meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games.

James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69.

Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear.

James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee.

The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them.

Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration.

James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames.

James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called "Bron."

The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with "Bron" across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos.

It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players.

The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed.

"The integrity of NBA competition, and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans," the complaint said. "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer.

PlayVision renamed it "Evie" on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York.

CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images)

James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup.

On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland's 108-95 win over Philadelphia.

Donning the Cavs' old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes.

Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench.

James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history.

The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson's original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later.

James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure.

Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson's No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

#2675. Eagles mount furious comeback, beat Cowboys 39-38 in Thanksgiving classic

It was a Thanksgiving Day classic in Dallas.

In a wild game that went from an apparent blowout to a thrilling comeback, the Cowboys jumped out to a 31-10 lead and then lost 39-38 when Eagles kicker Jake Elliott hit a 59-yard field goal with two seconds left.

Eagles quarterback Joe Milton played by far the best game of his career, throwing for 331 yards, with three touchdown passes and a touchdown run. We’ve always known Milton had a strong arm, but he showed today that he’s more than just a thrower. He can lead an NFL offense as a quarterback.

But Dak Prescott is a good quarterback, too, and he turned in a big game of his own. He threw for 291 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions.

Prescott’s favorite receiver was CeeDee Lamb, who finished with 134 receiving yards, and running back Javonte Williams ran for two touchdowns and also caught a touchdown pass.

The Eagles, however, got a monster game from wide receiver DeVonta Smith, who had 11 catches for 200 yards and two touchdowns. Smith was sensational while the Eagles were coming back in the fourth quarter.

Special teams miscues killed the Cowboys: The Eagles blocked a punt for a touchdown, and Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey missed a 40-yard field goal in the fourth quarter. Aubrey, who became the highest-paid kicker in the NFL this offseason, is having the worst season of his career.

The loss drops the Cowboys to 5-7 and is devastating to their playoff hopes. The 4-7 Eagles aren’t contenders, but they played like contenders today.

#2673. Bills beat Chiefs on deflected punt, Tyler Bass' 57-yard field goal at the buzzer

The Bills overcame a sluggish offensive game in rainy, windy conditions to beat the Chiefs on Thanksgiving in Buffalo, winning 13-10 on Tyler Bass' 57-yard field goal as time expired.

The kick came after a Bills defensive stop deep in the Chiefs' own end and a partial block of Matt Araiza's punt. Local hero Joe Andreesen got a piece of Araiza's punt, and Greg Dortch bravely returned it to the Kansas City 39-yard line, setting up Bass' game-winner in an ugly offensive night.

It was Buffalo's sixth straight regular-season victory over the Chiefs, dating back to 2021.

The Chiefs had a chance to run out the clock in a 10-10 game with less than 30 seconds left, but Patrick Mahomes fumbled the first-down snap, derailing the drive, and Travis Kelce dropped a well-placed pass that likely would have sent the game to overtime. The Bills then deflected Araiza's punt and returned it to the Chiefs' 39-yard line.

The Chiefs also had a huge first-down catch by Rashee Rice controversially wiped out by replay with just under two minutes left that could have tilted the game in Kansas City's favor.

The two teams combined for 471 yards of offense in the poor weather, which kept up for the duration of the game.

The Bills moved to 10-1, maintaining their lead on the rest of the AFC. The Chiefs fell to 8-3, half a game behind the first-place Broncos in the AFC West.

Buffalo increased its probability of winning the conference's No. 1 seed to 63%, according to The Athletic. Kansas City's fell to 3%.

Josh Allen struggled through one of the poorest passing games of his career, throwing for 81 yards and two interceptions. His legs got the Bills out of some jams, but they mainly had to lean on the running of James Cook, who ran for 117 yards and their only touchdown of the game on 32 carries, which tied his career high.

Mahomes, the hotter quarterback coming into the game, had more success Thursday, throwing for 174 yards on 16-of-29 passing. But the Chiefs punted on their first four possessions and came up empty on their final four series, with Harrison Butker's missed field goal with just over six minutes left looming large.

The first half was a mess — cold, rainy, windy — and a stark contrast to the high-scoring first two games on Thanksgiving. Both teams traded a pair of punts in a scoreless first quarter. The Bills struck first, laboring down the field to get in the end zone on Cook's 5-yard run, overcoming an overturned TD and a questionable false-start call at the goal line.

Buffalo's suddenly hot defense took advantage of the elements and KC's four straight punts to open the game. It appeared that the Bills would take a two-score lead as they drove to the Chiefs' 9-yard line, but Allen's pass was tipped by George Karlaftis and intercepted in the end zone by Alohi Gilman to thwart that drive.

The Chiefs finally got going before halftime, driving to the Bills' 8-yard line, but Mahomes' end-zone pass to Rice was incomplete, and the Chiefs settled for a short Butker field goal to cut Buffalo's lead to 7-3.

Kansas City came out of halftime with renewed focus, looking the best they had offensively all game. Emmett Johnson, starting again for an injured Kenneth Walker III, capped the drive with a 1-yard TD run. It was an impressive drive despite the rain continuing to fall, giving the Chiefs a 10-7 lead. It was Johnson's fifth straight game with a touchdown. That score ended a streak of 49 drives without allowing a TD by the Bills' defense.

Allen, who had only 41 first-half passing yards, was working through his issues gripping the ball, and the Bills penetrated the Chiefs' red zone on their opening drive of the third quarter. But Allen's on-target pass to Khalil Shakir deflected off his hands and went down as Allen's second interception, this time by Nohl Williams.

The Bills' defense muscled up again and pushed the Chiefs back, giving Buffalo good field position again. Another labored drive — its fifth of the game of at least four minutes — bogged down, as the Bills had to settle for Bass' 54-yard field goal, tying the game at 10-10.

Mahomes was under fire on the ensuing drive, but he completed a third-and-15 pass under heavy pressure — vintage Mahomes — throwing back against his body for 19 yards and a clutch first down.

But penalties were a problem all game for the Chiefs, and consecutive flags pushed them back 15 yards. The Chiefs settled for a Butker field-goal try from 46 yards, but he pushed it to the right for his eighth miss of the season. That is two more than he's had in any single season in his 10 years as a Chief.

"I'm not going to make any decisions," Reid said when asked about Butker's struggles, according to The Athletic's Nate Taylor.

The Chiefs' defense showed it could flex its muscles, too. After Cook moved the chains, the Chiefs sacked Allen just as the Bills moved into Kansas City territory. It was that kind of night for the offense and for Allen.

Backed up inside his own 10, Mahomes hit Rice with an 11-yard pass on third-and-10, taking a big hit from the Bills' Amani Hooker. But the play was reviewed, and it was determined that the ball came loose and touched the ground, forcing the Chiefs to punt.

Allen got the ball back at his 47-yard line with plenty of time to mount a game-winning drive but had a first-down completion wiped out by penalty and took a massive sack on third down, and the Bills punted with less than 40 seconds left in regulation.

Instead, the Chiefs watched the Bills pull out the ugly game in the waning seconds.

The Bills won a game in which Josh Allen went 10-for-21 for 81 yards, 0 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. It began as a slog, but then every stop began landing like a haymaker.

All three games today were decided in the final three seconds.

Tyler Bass is good from 57 yards out and that will do it. This game seemed destined for overtime, until a catastrophic play put the game in the Bills' hands. That missed 46-yarder by Harrison Butker looms large.

A Chiefs three-and-out, a tipped punt and a quick return has the Bills attempting a 57-yarder for the win.

Patrick Mahomes fumbled the shotgun snap in the Buffalo cold and rain, but he got the ball back before the Bills defense could get there.

The Bills appeared to move into field goal position, but Dalton Kincaid got called for a blatant offensive pass interference, then Josh Allen got sacked on 3rd-and-9. The Bills are punting with 38 seconds left.

It's a short punt for the Chiefs too. Buffalo will get the ball at the Kansas City 37-yard line needing only a field goal with 1:40 left.

The Chiefs were facing 3rd-and-10 deep in their own territory, but Patrick Mahomes found Rashee Rice for 11 yards and a first down. However, replay overturns the catch — Rice didn't have the ball secure when it hit the ground — and that makes this a three-and-out for Kansas City.

The Bills' next drive goes nowhere quickly, with Nick Bolton and Christian Roland-Wallace combining to sack Josh Allen on third down. The Chiefs will get the ball back at their own 9-yard line with two minutes left.

Harrison Butker lined up for the 46-yard attempt, but his kicking woes continued.

He was not able to handle the weather conditions and pushed the kick wide right.

The game remains tied at 10 with 5:56 left in regulation.

Bad weather isn't keeping Patrick Mahomes from pulling some magic.

After scrambling toward the right sideline, he threw across his body, and Cyrus Allen came out of nowhere to pick up 19 yards on third and 15.

The fourth quarter began with Buffalo getting some extra yards, but not being able to sustain the drive.

Even with the bad weather, Tyler Bass lined up for the 54-yard attempt. He nailed it as it hooked right through the uprights to tie the game at 10.

12 minutes to go in a brand new ballgame.

#2663. Sabres Finally Get Much-Needed Production From Veteran Trio

The Sabres could be turning a corner at the American Thanksgiving checkpoint. One reason? An uptick in scoring from some struggling forwards.

With Jiri Kulich heating up in recent games, a few veteran forwards could end up joining him. In Wednesday night's 5-1 win over the New York Rangers, Josh Doan and Jason Zucker provided assists on Joshua Norris' goal at 2:37 in the second period to put the Sabres up 2-0.

While the trio linked up just once on Wednesday, it could serve as a catalyst for more production in the closing days of November. So far, the Sabres have been top-heavy, with six of their forwards averaging over a half-point per game.

As for Doan, Zucker, and Norris, the returns haven't been anywhere near as encouraging. Doan, who is in his first year of a seven-year deal that carries a cap hit of $6.95 million, has just eight points, four goals, and a 9.8 shooting percentage in 25 games.

Norris hasn't fared any better, with eight points and five goals in 25 contests. Norris, however, is posting a 20.0 shooting percentage. He just doesn't shoot the puck enough, with 25 shots on goal this season. Norris, with a $7.950 cap hit, is Buffalo's highest-paid forward.

Zucker has just two goals and three points in 16 games. Zucker enjoyed two solid seasons with the Sabres, posting 53 and 45 points in 2024-25 and 2025-26, respectively. That said, he is in his age-35 season, and isn't expected to be as effective as he once was.

Norris may be the more frustrating case this season. He appeared in 47 regular-season contests between when he was traded to Buffalo in Mar. 2025 and April 2026, posting 14 goals and 36 points.

Now that he's finally healthy and has seen 25 games, the points production has yet to follow a quarter of the way through the season. If Wednesday night marked a turning point and if he can follow up on Friday against the Pittsburgh Penguins, he will further drive home how deep this Sabres team can potentially go.

Norris has shown flashes earlier in the month. The consistency must follow.

The same applies for Doan, whose 52 points and 25 goals in 2025-26 gave fans a reason to believe Buffalo found a young forward capable of putting up at least solid numbers. But Doan has been up and down throughout his career — with nine points in 11 games in 2023-24 and 19 in 51 in 2024-25.

He has lacked year-over-year consistency. If he can find it, he too will help transform a solid top six in Buffalo into a solid top nine. That could make the Sabres dangerous between the quarter and midseason marks.

The Sabres are heading into an important part of their schedule. Following their Nov. 27 matchup with the Penguins, Buffalo will embark on a Western Conference road trip between Dec. 1 and Dec. 6.

The first matchup in that slate of games will be against the Edmonton Oilers. When Buffalo returns home on Dec. 10, they will face the Oilers again. Then, they will have showdowns with the Anaheim Ducks and Ottawa Senators.

Those are four excruciating matchups that may end up in high-octane play for both sides. If Norris and Doan can keep turning a corner, with Zucker providing supplementary help, Buffalo will match up well against their toughest upcoming opponents.

#2662. James can still take over ‘any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots

James can still take over 'any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James isn't oblivious to the calendar and the clock.

He knows he'll turn 42 years old next month, he's ancient by NBA standards and decline is inevitable.

James also knows who he is and what he still can do, whatever the norms are for players of a certain age.

"I think his battle against Father Time is one of the most impressive things he's done over the course of his entire career," Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra said Wednesday before Miami's loss to the Sixers. "We all know and everybody always says that Father Time always wins. But right now he's giving Father Time hell."

James went on to record his first triple-double with the 15-4 Sixers, posting 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds. The four-time MVP is at 126 regular-season triple-doubles and counting in his career.

Only Russell Westbrook, Nikola Jokic, Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson have more in NBA history. James is 17 above Philadelphia native and Sixers legend Wilt Chamberlain.

With Joel Embiid sidelined by illness for a second consecutive game and Jaylen Brown ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness, James' do-it-all performance was timely. Tyrese Maxey's 30-point, six-assist outing was essential, too.

"I'm just trying to play the game the right way," James said. "I don't think my job is to dominate the game every night for this ball club. We have a Finals MVP (Brown), we have a regular-season MVP (Embiid), we have an up-and-coming superstar at point guard, we've got a young fella in VJ (Edgecombe) who's up and coming as well.

"My dues are paid with what I've done. If they need me to dust off the cape from time to time, then I can still accomplish that. But that's not my job. … But if they need it, I can do it at any given moment."

James' night featured a flurry of very deep three-pointers in the second quarter.

He started the season 10 for 46 beyond the arc (21.7 percent), but his percentage has risen to 31.6 with two sweet-shooting games in a row.

"The work has been put in and I'm not ever worried about anything as far as my game," he said. "The difference between the start of the season and now is that my legs are feeling better, my ramp-up is feeling better.

"I'm about to be 42 years old in a month. S—, it takes a little bit longer for the ramp-up, but I've been feeling pretty good as of late. I don't ever second-guess myself … because I know the work that I put in."

While James' rebounding was perhaps the least spectacular aspect of his game, Sixers head coach Nick Nurse appreciated his work on the boards.

James has remained a statistically solid defensive rebounder into his 40s and he's one reason why the Sixers have made a major improvement in that department. According to Cleaning the Glass, the Sixers' opponents have grabbed 28.4 percent of their own misses, which ranks sixth in the NBA. The team ranked 27th last season.

Asked about James' cape comments, Maxey shouted out, "Dust it off then!" with a grin.

Maxey's not sure exactly when James will dramatically elevate his game, but he trusts the 22-time All-Star to pick the right spots.

"I don't know," Maxey said. "Early in the game, he was telling me he was tired. I said, 'Well, we don't have time for you to be tired.'

"But he does a good job of just managing the game. He knows when he needs to score, he knows when he needs to pass. We're going to need a lot from him. I know he's seasoned, but we expect a lot of him and he does that."

#2658. Jeffery Simmons: I didn't simulate snap count on false starts, Lions are "crying" about a them problem

Long before the Bears beat the Lions on a last-second touchdown catch by wide receiver Rome Odunze, one of the storylines of the game was a run of false start penalties by the Lions.

Center Juice Scruggs was called for back-to-back false starts and then picked up a third later in the half. Left guard Christian Mahogany was flagged for another one before the next snap and there were indications from the Lions that Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was simulating the snap count to get them to jump.

Mahogany made that accusation explicit after the game that the Bears “find out the snap count of the quarterback and they use it” while adding that Lions linemen were wearing microphones that he believes will back him up. Simmons was not penalized, but was seen speaking to the referee during a break in play. He denied Mahogany’s allegation after the 39-35 win.

“We don’t have to. We don’t have to,” Simmons said, via Dave Birkett of the Detroit Free Press “We line up and play football. They quarterback check. I said, ‘Run.’ I didn’t say, ‘Hut.’ I mean, their cadence, they say, ‘White 80, white 80.’ I mean, when you lose football games, it’s a lot of complaining and a lot of crying. I mean, there was a couple times that they false start, we didn’t say a word. So that’s their problem, not ours. . . . If I say, ‘Run,’ I’m telling my defense, run. Think I care to tell them what they about to do? I’m talking to my guys. So all the crying that they’re doing, that’s a them problem, not me.”

Mahogany was flagged for taunting Simmons during a 70-yard Jahmyr Gibbs touchdown run in the fourth quarter and kicker Jake Bates missed the ensuing extra point to leave the score 35-24. The Lions would not score again and the Bears headed back to Chicago with an improbable victory.

#2656. 4 instant takeaways from the Chiefs’ last-second loss in Buffalo

The Kansas City Chiefs fought to the end of a messy, low-scoring game against the Buffalo Bills, but ultimately fell 13-10. Here are four takeaways from Thanksgiving night:

From the jump, Kansas City's defense was ready for a long evening of containing James Cook and taking on the battering ram that is Josh Allen. On a rainy evening, Buffalo used a high-volume run game to control the contest, but the Chiefs never allowed Cook to gain more than 10 yards on any of his 32 carries.

Buffalo's running backs were held to 3.4 yards per carry, but quarterback Josh Allen gained 43 yards on the ground and found room for a 17-yard gash at one point. However, the Chiefs' coverage was tight and held Allen to just 81 yards and two interceptions on 10 of 21 passing; he finished with an 18.3 passer rating.

The Bills were able to march in the red zone a couple of times that Kansas City eventually forced to a screeching halt with clutch interceptions by cornerback Nohl Williams and safety Alohi Gilman.

As a low-scoring game came to a close, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo dialed up the blitz to contain Allen in the pocket and bring him to the ground multiple times. From start to finish, the Chiefs' defense played winning football on Thanksgiving night…

… and the special teams unit did not play winning football. If you thought the conditions of the game were sloppy, the performance of the special teams topped it.

Whether it was a dropped kickoff, a dropped punt, a misfielded punt backed up deep, netting eight yards on a punt or the various penalties, it was a typical first half for the Chiefs' special teams unit. Unfortunately, the miscues kept coming, including a 46-yard field goal missed by the over-trusted Harrison Butker.

At the very end, punter Matt Araiza was backed up and had his punt tipped, setting up enough of a return for the Bills' game-winning field goal. It was a gross night for long-time special teams coordinator Dave Toub's unit.

From the opening drive, an apparent miscommunication between rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson and left guard Kingsley Suamataia left edge defender Bradley Chubb unblocked to make the third-and-one stop, it was a rough showing for the Chiefs' offensive line.

Backups Hunter Nourzad and Fred Johnson were inserted into the game and had costly penalties in the second half, but those were not the only two flags on the Chiefs' offensive line. One of the most crucial was called on left guard Kingsley Suamataia after the snap, which took Kansas City from a manageable third down to a third and long they were unable to convert.

Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and running back Emmett Johnson found space to make plays enough times to give the Chiefs a fighting chance, but the offense was overcoming backups up front as much as the rain in this one.

After the football world had its mind blown with Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington's non-catch a few weeks ago, wide receiver Rashee Rice's catch on the field being overturned was the latest in the storied history of "what is a catch?"

No one will seemingly ever have a confident answer to that question. Alas, it wasn't the reason Kansas City lost this game, just an insane call.

#2653. Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup

Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James posted his first triple-double as a Sixer on Wednesday night and led his team to a 111-104 win over the Heat at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

James notched his 126th career regular-season triple-double with 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds for the 15-4 Sixers.

Tyrese Maxey scored 30 points and dished out six assists.

Giannis Antetokounmpo recorded 32 points and 14 rebounds for the 10-7 Heat.

The Sixers improved to 2-1 and Miami fell to 2-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup.

Jaylen Brown was ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness. He had six points on 2-for-8 shooting over 17 minutes.

"He'll get some imaging and we'll get the update tomorrow," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said.

Joel Embiid (illness) missed his second game in a row. The Sixers are set to visit the Pacers on Friday night in their final Cup group game.

"He's ill," Nurse said of Embiid. "I do not know whether he's going to Indiana yet or not. I guess we'll find that out late tomorrow afternoon."

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory over the Heat:

Nurse emphasized pregame that the Sixers needed an improved defensive performance.

"We've got to compete much better at the defensive end than we did Monday (against the Trail Blazers)," he said. "It's as simple as that."

The night did not begin in especially promising fashion on that front. Antetokounmpo powered through Brown and scored inside for the game's first bucket. His transition layup put Miami up 6-0. The Heat scored nine fast-break points in the first six minutes.

As he had Monday in the Sixers' loss to Portland, Jabari Walker started at center. He was among the Sixers who shared the daunting defensive assignment of Antetokounmpo.

Walker took a charge on the 10-time All-Star in the first quarter, but Antetounkmpo had a stellar start. He forcefully orchestrated Miami's offense, often plowing through the middle of the floor and finding efficient answers.

The Sixers' defense was better late in the first quarter and it didn't hurt when Antetokounmpo took a seat.

Maxey had an aggressive, productive first period, scoring 13 points. Dominick Barlow's tip-in gave the Sixers a 27-26 edge.

James drained three three-pointers early in the second quarter, including a confident, deep jumper that fired up a high-volume home crowd. He's shown that he remains capable of flipping a world-class switch and taking over games in a vast array of ways.

There's no question the 22-time All-Star is out of his early-season outside shooting slump. James has gone 8 for 11 from long range over his last two games. He's scored at least 20 points in four straight.

"I just play the game as it unfolds," James said. "I had a couple of opportunities and I was able to connect on them. I kind of know when my hand is feeling pretty good, especially from the outside. We'll see how long I can keep it going."

Adem Bona checked in early in the second quarter. He provided a string of excellent defensive possessions against Antetokounmpo, including an emphatic block and several well-guarded missed jumpers, although Bona did get called for three fouls in the second period.

Nurse was pleased with what he received defensively from both Bona (two blocks, six rebounds) and Barlow (nine points, eight rebounds) off the bench.

"They used their gifts," he said. "They're quick side to side, both of them. When they're in that kind of fighting mode like that … they did a good job. We tried to get Bona in there when Giannis was in, just for the rim protection. And Dom just played really, really (well) all over the place … on the defense, on the rebounding, on the running, on the cutting."

The Sixers played effective zone defense at the tail end of the second quarter and held a nine-point halftime lead. That grew as high as 16 points in the third quarter.

Miami pulled back within single digits, but the Sixers maintained a healthy advantage and James kept on making highlight plays. He lobbed the ball up to Edgecombe early in the fourth quarter and the second-year guard skied high to lay it in. James later connected with Barlow on an alley-oop.

Once the Sixers have a substantial lead, James' presence is a massive help offensively. He's very well-accustomed to conducting methodical half-court offense, identifying favorable matchups and turning to fruitful actions over and over. James will also still steam forward on the fast break when he sees the chance.

Maxey buried a step-back three to extend his team's lead to 111-95 with 2:29 on the clock and the Sixers polished off a professional win. The fans roared when James snatched the rebound required to reach his triple-double.

"We came out tonight with a different mentality, different energy," Maxey said. "Nurse got on us a little bit in the film (session) yesterday. He lit a fire for a lot of us, which is good. We needed it."

#2648. Mike Tomlin on current Steelers situation: "It's a dumpster fire"

Many folks in and around football have had opinions about the recent brouhaha between former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Steelers coach Mike McCarthy. Few have the insight and perspective that former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin brings to the table.

Appearing on NBC’s Chiefs-Bills halftime show on Thanksgiving night, Tomlin shared his thoughts on the situation in a conversation with Mike Tirico. (A portion of it was on the live broadcast; the full interview is here.)

“I had a range of emotions watching those course of events yesterday,” Tomlin told Tirico. “I think the prevailing one is just general sadness. Sad on a micro level, sad on a macro level. And by that, I mean, you know, just from an individual perspective, sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career of the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers, and just on the macro level, whether it’s organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum.

“Those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football. So, just a lot of emotions, but probably more than anything, man, general sadness on a lot of levels.”

Tirico asked Tomlin if he was shocked by Rodgers’s decision to air dirty laundry in a public forum.

“It certainly did,” Tomlin said, “but, you know, and particularly because I know both men involved, certainly had a lot of intimate work and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years, and have known and competed against Mike, you know, respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time. But I don’t — what I acknowledge is I don’t know them as a collective, the nature of their relationships, and so certainly I was surprised by that.”

Regardless of Rodgers’s conduct on the way out the door, Tomlin explained that Rodgers was viewed favorably by his teammates in 2025.

“He was beloved, and I’m not, you know, over-exaggerating that,” Tomlin said. “He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates, and particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years and at times they lose a little patience for the process, or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys, et cetera. Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real, natural way. He was a tireless worker regarding the process.

“I called early-morning quarterback meetings on Wednesday and Thursday. He was always early and engaged. Did a heck of a job in terms of engaging and developing, assisting in the development of young players. Specifically, Will Howard was always in that meeting, and, shoot, man, [Rodgers] and I were shoulder-to-shoulder in terms of the development of Will and challenging Will to develop professional habits. And so, you know, it was early and extremely consistent during my time with him, in terms of his willingness to work in those areas, and I think that’s why he’s so beloved in that locker room, as been reported by multiple sources in light of this incident. That is real. The guys in that locker room love and appreciate Aaron Rodgers.”

Had Tomlin gotten any sense that things were so close to breaking down?

“Absolutely none, but it’s a really specific reason why, to be honest with you, man,” Tomlin said. “One of my cultural mantras, when I worked there for the 19 years, is don’t talk to people about your problems unless they can be a component of the solution. Because if you do, it’s counterproductive, and people know where I stand there. And by that I mean if you have a problem with your playing time, don’t talk to your teammate about it. Talk to somebody that can do something about it. That’s problem solving.

“And so everybody understands my posture on some of that stuff, and so although I have really good, fluid communication with many of those guys, particularly, the more veteran guys, they know me and know me well enough to know that I didn’t want to hear about any potential issues, because I’m not a component of the solution. And so although, particularly, like, Cam Heyward, he and I spent a little time together doing his bye week. Man, we had no mention of anything bubbling under the surface, if you will.”

Can McCarthy effectively lead the team, given what Rodgers said?

“You know, it certainly created some challenges and challenges is probably an understatement if all of those things are true,” Tomlin told Tirico. “And certainly the ‘1-2-3 Packers’ is, because he acknowledged that. But his ability to overcome that or inability to overcome that in my opinion is based on relationships and the depth of those relationships and how those guys feel about him, or how those guys buy into what he’s selling. And so, certainly, he’s been there a short period of time. And so it makes you wonder, the level of that challenge. But it’ll be relationship-based, his ability to overcome the things that you mentioned.”

How does Tomlin think the Steelers will fare against the Broncos on Friday?

“Based on my knowledge of the men, particularly the leaders, the longstanding guys, they’ll do a great job of getting hyper-focused on what really matters, and that’s that football game,” Tomlin said. “They’ll use it as a mantra to bring them together. I expect those guys to fight. Now, fight and quality play are two different things. I’m certainly not gonna expect those guys not to fight. I think they’re gonna fight and fight extremely hard. What I’m interested in is quality of play, quality of execution. And those are things that could be impacted by the level of distraction that they had on a short week in particular.”

Tirico then asked Tomlin how he feels, overall, about what has transpired this week.

“I’m upset about it, you know, it’s a dumpster fire,” Tomlin said. “And I don’t say that in a judgmental way. I presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years. But it certainly is upsetting, and I’m sure Steeler Nation is upset.”

If owner Art Rooney II calls Tomlin for advice, what would Tomlin say?

“Hey, Mike, that’s a hypothetical, because I know he wouldn’t and, and because I know how he’s trained,” Tomlin said. “You know, Art is a guy that’s not a hedge fund guy that bought a football team. He’s not a, you know, artificial intelligence guy that bought a football team. This is a family business. It’s generational. Any advice or thought process in that way, I imagine he just says, ‘What would my dad do?’ Or, ‘What would my grandfather do?’ Their mode of operation is time tested, it’s generational. And so, I doubt, very, very seriously, that he called anyone for outside advice.”

Finally, Tirico asked whether Tomlin believes Rodgers will get another NFL opportunity this season, if he wants one.

“There’s certainly a possibility for that,” Tomlin said. “And I just say that based on the 19 years that I held the position that I held. It’s a 32-team league. All it takes is one. Over time, I’ve laughed and watched that people talk about, you know, ‘No, that could never happen.’ In a 32-team league, when everybody is highly competitive and there’s some real challenges, particularly as you get to this portion of the journey from a player availability standpoint, there’s certainly a possibility if he desires that he could play again, because all it takes is one suitor.”

Having cleared waivers, Rodgers is available to that one suitor, if/when that one suitor calls. Still, that one suitor will need to be willing to accept the risk that, if Rodgers doesn’t have things go the way he wants, he’ll choose to do again the same thing he did this week.

#2639. Chiefs’ Andy Reid sends stern message to Kingsley Suamataia after crucial penalties in Bills game

Chiefs' Andy Reid sends stern message to Kingsley Suamataia after crucial penalties in Bills game appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Kansas City Chiefs let a big one slip away on Thanksgiving night, and Andy Reid made it clear that Kingsley Suamataia's penalties played a part in it.

The Chiefs fell 13-10 to the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium, with Tyler Bass drilling a 57-yard field goal with four seconds left to win it. Suamataia, who has been playing left guard, was flagged three times by the third quarter, including two holding calls and an unnecessary roughness penalty.

After the game, Reid didn't mince words about his young lineman's mistakes.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"He can't have that. He's a young guy. He's gotta continue to grow. But you surely can't have the penalties that he had. Nobody knows it better than he does. Can't do that. Big game. You gotta play and control whatever you've gotta control," Reid said, via Sam McDowell.

Suamataia's first hold came in the final two minutes of the first half and wiped out a Patrick Mahomes scramble, though Kansas City still managed to get a Harrison Butker field goal out of the drive. His unnecessary roughness flag in the third quarter was even more costly, turning a manageable second-and-3 into a much tougher situation.

It wasn't the first time this season the third-year pro has been in Reid's doghouse. The Chiefs benched Suamataia twice earlier in the year, though Reid insisted at the time that it "isn't punishment."

The penalties were painful in a game where yards were hard to come by. Kansas City was flagged eight times for 68 yards and managed just 241 yards of total offense.

The defense did its part, picking off Josh Allen twice and holding Buffalo to 230 total yards, but the offense couldn't build on its 10-7 lead after Emmett Johnson's third-quarter touchdown before Bass tied it from 54 yards out.

The loss dropped the Chiefs to 8-3, while the Bills improved to 10-1. Kansas City will try to bounce back against the Los Angeles Rams next Thursday.

#2635. Tyler Bass hits walk-off 57-yard field goal, Bills beat Chiefs 13-10

The weather in Western New York delivered nasty conditions with freezing rain for Thanksgiving night.

Buffalo's kicker sent a walk-off, 57-yard field goal through the uprights to give the Bills a 13-10 victory over the Chiefs, putting the club further in the driver's seat for the AFC's No. 1 seed.

The game was not without controversy, particularly late in the contest. But the weather conditions also affected both teams, as neither offense got much going.

Josh Allen finished the game 10-of-21 for 81 yards with two interceptions, rushing for 43 yards on seven attempts. Allen's passer rating of 18.3 is the second lowest of his career in any regular-season game.

Patrick Mahomes completed 16-of-29 passes for 174 yards with no touchdowns or interceptions.

James Cook ended up pacing the offense for Buffalo, rushing for 117 yards on 32 carries with Buffalo's only touchdown — a 5-yard run in the second quarter.

The Chiefs got a 26-yard field goal from Harrison Butker to close the first half and a 1-yard touchdown from Emmett Johnson to open the second half. But the team was not able to score again.

After Bass connected on a 54-yard field goal in the fourth quarter to tie the game at 10-10, Butker missed his eighth field goal of the year — this one going wide right from 46 yards out.

Kansas City had the ball with another shot to get Butker in field goal range. But what looked like a third-down completion from Mahomes to Rahsee Rice was overturned on replay, allowing Buffalo to field another punt.

The Chiefs got yet another opportunity to possess the ball after Allen was sacked for the second time on the night. But the club's special teams continued to have issues, with Josh Downs fielding a punt inside the 10, returning it to just the 11-yard line.

And when Mahomes' third-down pass to an open Kelce fell incomplete, Matt Ariza's punt was short and skipped to Greg Dortch, who returned 17 yards to the Kansas City 39 with four seconds on the clock.

Somehow in the weather conditions, that was enough for Bass, who sent the 57-yard attempt through the uprights to give the Bills their 10th win of the season.

Between Butker, Downs' returns, and Ariza's punts, the Chiefs special teams had a rough night, arguably costing the team the game.

On the injury front, Chiefs receiver/returner Jalen Royals (ankle) exited and was not able to return.

With the win, the Bills are now 10-1 and will have at least a one-game lead on the rest of the conference entering Week 13 for the No. 1 seed. Buffalo will play division-rival New England in Week 13.

The Chiefs are now 8-3 and won't have extra rest in the coming week, as they'll be in Los Angeles to face the Rams next Thursday night.

#2634. Kenny Smith Pays Backhanded Compliment To LeBron James When Explaining His Longevity

Philadelphia 76ers superstar LeBron James' longevity is quite remarkable, and he made history yet again on Wednesday. James broke his own record for the oldest player to record a triple-double in the 76ers' 111-104 win over the Miami Heat at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

It shouldn't be possible for a 41-year-old to play this well, and Kenny Smith thinks the rules are helping James. Smith explained the 22-time All-Star's longevity on Inside the NBA on Wednesday.

"We can't forget, without Luka [Doncic] in the playoffs, he dominated the first round of the series," Smith said. "And he still has that ability because the way the game is played today, obviously, with the lack of hand-checking, it is a parallel game. And so what happens is if you're like a track star, and he can just stay in track shape, and he's pushing the ball like a track star and not getting touched, not getting slowed down.

"And he's still 6'9″, 240 lbs, and can still move on a track pace," Smith added. "And the NBA is still in danger with him on the floor."

The NBA banned hand-checking in 2004, and Smith believes James wouldn't be as effective at his age were it still allowed. The 61-year-old thinks his athleticism and size are enough to succeed in today's league, which is quite the backhanded compliment.

Yes, James being a very good athlete helps, but he is still very skilled, and his mind remains sharp. It's the combination of all three that still enables him to dominate games.

James shone for the Los Angeles Lakers in Luka Doncic's absence in the first round of the 2026 NBA playoffs against the Houston Rockets. The Lakers had been written off going into the series, but he led them to victory in six games.

We saw that version of James again against the Heat, as he had 25 points (9-15 FG), 10 rebounds, 12 assists, and one steal. He scored 14 points in a row for the 76ers at one point in the second quarter, and we're so blessed to still see him in action. James doesn't always have to take over with all the talent around him, but made it clear he can dust off the cape when need be.

The 76ers improved to 15-4 with this win over the Heat and remain atop the standings in the Eastern Conference. They are definitely a serious title contender, and James has his eyes set on winning his fifth championship. While some believe this would help his GOAT case, others don't. Smith likely falls in the second category. He has made it clear that Michael Jordan is his GOAT.

Smith has also said James is touching the Magic Johnson-Larry Bird "fiber," not the Jordan "fiber." He believes defense is what separates his former UNC teammate from LeBron.

James isn't going to get any better defensively at his age, of course. He'll continue to be a big threat on offense, though, and he'll be in action next when the 76ers take on the Indiana Pacers at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Friday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

#2631. Game Preview #20: Wolves vs Grizzlies Game Thread

Happy Thanksgiving, everyone. As your holiday winds down, I'm pleased to bring you a brief preview of the next Minnesota Timberwolves game, which is against the Memphis Grizzlies.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (14-5) at Memphis Grizzlies (14-5)

This matchup will be the final game of the group stage for the NBA Cup, and the winner will get an automatic place in the cup playoffs. The Wolves have yet to reach that stage of the tournament, so putting together a win to make it there would be yet another great chapter within the storybook of this resurgent season.

A loss would not be ideal, though it would not be the end of the world as far as the Cup is concerned. Minnesota is in a pretty good position to make it in as a wildcard team over the Denver Nuggets based upon point differential. Obviously winning any game is the best-case scenario, though the Wolves have multiple paths towards competing for the increasingly-coveted NBA Cup title.

Regardless of Cup implications, this should be yet another good matchup between two teams that have been consistently strong in the Western Conference. Minnesota took the last matchup at home 104-95 which featured strong performances from Jaden McDaniels, Ayo Dosunmu, Jonathan Kuminga, and Terrence Shannon Jr. The Wolves will need to keep up their positive momentum from all of those guys if they look to clinch the group and pass the Grizzlies in the Western Conference standings.

That said, it may still be tough sledding for an already-injured team that may be dealing with another one for the foreseeable future. Keeping that in mind, here are a couple things I'm looking for in the game tomorrow:

Watching LaMelo Ball gingerly limp off of the court against the Oklahoma City Thunder was not a welcome sight. We got the win, but everyone is hoping that his turned ankle does not turn out (pun intended) to be anything serious.

It would not be out of the realm of possibility for Ball to miss this game. However, the team that used to boast significant guard depth is looking considerably weaker if we have the quadrio of Ball, Anthony Edwards, Donte DiVincenzo, and Jaylen Clark all sidelined.

As it were, this means that Bones Hyland should get a sizable helping of playing time. I would not be shocked to see G-League stud Zyon Pullin also get a fair bit of run to ease what would otherwise be a hefty serving of minutes for Hyland and Dosunmu. We've learned this season just how important adequate point guard play is with the addition of Ball, and I do not think Chris Finch would overwork the two guards left that are capable of stuffing that position.

On the other side of the scorer's table, the Grizzlies also have their share of injuries to deal with. Rookie forward Cameron Boozer is still out with injury, and Zach Edey is a game time decision after picking up a knock in their last game against the Los Angeles Clippers. With Jerami Grant, GG Jackson, and Scottie Pippen Jr. all still on the injured list as well, Memphis has had plenty of guys step up and give the team quality minutes in their absences. They may need more help if they are looking to defeat the Wolves on Friday.

What can't Jaden McDaniels do? Nothing, apparently. The guy has been a machine as of late, averaging 26 points per game while shooting the ball well over 67% from the floor and 69% from deep across his last five games. Those are some nice numbers.

On top of that, Jaden is continuing to put the clamps on opposing teams' best players. He locked up Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at the end of the game last evening, and McDaniels never appears to tire across the course of the game. He's doing it all for the Timberwolves, and that production has been necessary in the wake of the Edwards injury.

There is a legitimate argument to be made regarding Jaden as an All Star candidate this season. That argument will be bolstered if he can continue to control games with Ball sidelined. It's not McDaniels's fault that he is in this position to carry the team on his back, though his admirable performances are earning attention league-wide.

Next man up is always the mentality, and Jaden has been doing his part in keeping this injury-addled team afloat. Adding another injury to that mix certainly changes the dynamic of the team, though McDaniels has been playing strong enough that he should be able to overcome the absence of Ball.

I've mentioned in past articles that while Ball hasn't had the most statistical significance across the last couple weeks, he is unquestionably controlling the game and making the offense easier for everyone else. With him out, someone else will have to step up to make some shots and draw the defense in their direction. That person should be Terrence Shannon Jr.

He's had a few up-and-down performances lately, and his last game against the Thunder saw him score only eight points on 2/10 shooting while turning the ball over three times. Minnesota won the game, but they will need more production out of TJ with Ball being out against a tough opponent in Memphis.

A brief positive for TJ could be conceptualized with the news of Ball's absence, as the ball will likely be in the hands of Shannon more during his minutes. Last year gave the film buffs tons of evidence about how effective TJ can be as a scorer if he is initiating the offense. If he has more opportunity to control the lineups when he is deployed, he should be able to find a rhythm quickly.

Efficient scoring performances from TJ are always welcome sights. He has already been an integral part of this team with the current injury situation, and that importance will be inflated with yet another injury to a key player that plays heavy minutes. Expect Finch to lean on Shannon early and often in this contest.

This one is going to be a nail-biter, but I can't bet against the Wolves no matter who we play against. Expect TSJ to have a strong scoring night and, ideally, a grand re-opening of the Bone Zone. I think the Wolves take this one, but not by much.

#2628. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2627. Melton hit 8 threes on Kings, joined an exclusive Warriors’ club

De'Anthony Melton nailed eight threes against Sacramento on Wednesday night and sent me down a rabbit hole (brought to you by Stathead) that ate up a lot more of my Thanksgiving than I planned.

Melton tied his career high with eight threes and scored 24 points in the 129-110 NBA Cup win over the Kings, and he did it with Steph sitting out with a torn oblique. He went 8-for-12 from deep, 8-for-14 overall, and never took a free throw.

With those eight treys, Melton walked into one of the most exclusive shooting clubs in franchise history. All of which got me wondering how often the Warriors lose when somebody does that. The answer is: almost never.

Since Coach Steve Kerr took over in 2014, there have been 120 regular-season performances where a Warrior hit eight or more threes, spread across 119 games because Curry and Wiggins share one, and the Warriors are 92-27 in those games. That's a .773 winning percentage, a 63-win pace, and the average scoring margin across all 119 games, wins and losses together, is almost plus-10.

Melton is the eighth different Warrior to do it under Kerr. The other seven are Curry, Klay Thompson, D'Angelo Russell, Jordan Poole, Wiggins, Brandin Podziemski and Moses Moody, and if you squint, that list doubles as a decade of Warriors history.

By the way, if I told you two Warriors once hit eight threes apiece in the same game during the Steve Kerr era would you bet on that being the Splash Brothers? Wrong, dear reader. Twas' Curry and Andrew Wiggins.

But let's find some more fun facts. During the first five seasons of the Kerr era, 2014-15 through 2018-19, the Warriors went 50-4 when somebody hit eight threes. Since then they're 42-23. A 92.6% winning percentage turned into 64.6%. Remember when Steph would hit his sixth three and you'd start figuring out how to beat the traffic out of Oracle? Nowadays a sixth three means you're hoping the Warriors can get a stop at the other end.

In the 73-9 season they went 20-1 in these games, which means somebody hit eight threes in roughly one out of every four games that year. The one loss took history to pull off. On April 1, 2016, Curry hit eight threes against Boston and the Celtics still won 109-106, ending the 54-game home winning streak, an NBA record. Even the losses from that era came with a plaque.

Those dynasty teams had the defense, depth and talent to turn a hot shooting night into an early bedtime for everybody watching on the East Coast.

Curry has 88 of the 120 performances, and Steph and Klay have a combined 111 of them, 92.5% of the entire club. The Warriors are 68-20 when Steph hits eight. Through age 34, the Warriors were 56-10 in his eight-three games. Since he turned 35, they're 12-10. Since he turned 37, they're 3-3.

He's still having these nights, and that's what gets me. In January 2025, at 36, he went 8-for-8 from three against Philadelphia, the only perfect night in the entire dataset. He dropped 31 with eight threes on the Lakers a month ago at 38 years old. The miracle nights keep coming, but they used to be a guaranteed win and now they're closer to a coin flip. The worst one to look back on is February 2024 in Atlanta, when he scored 60 with 10 threes and lost in overtime. He's lost 57-point and 50-point games too. The Warriors are 10-3 when Curry scores at least 50 points and makes at least eight threes, and they went 4-0 when Klay did it. When Steph has gone nuclear lately, he's usually been making up for everything around him.

Across his whole Warriors run under Kerr, 2014-15 through 2023-24, Klay went 19-4 in his eight-three games and 13-1 at home. He scored 60 points in 29 minutes against Indiana and sat out the fourth quarter. He hit 14 threes in 27 minutes in Chicago, which is still the franchise record, and he once went 10-for-11 from deep against the Lakers.

Not counting Steph and Klay, the record is 6-3. Two of those losses belong to D'Angelo Russell, who hit nine threes against Dallas on Dec. 28, 2019 and nine more against Indiana on Jan. 24, 2020, and lost both. The Dallas game was a 20-point loss, still the worst in the whole dataset. That's the most 2019-20 Warriors thing imaginable, and I say that with love for everyone who suffered through that season.

Poole went 1-1 and Wiggins went 2-0. Podziemski went 1-0 against the Lakers in April 2025, and Moody went 1-0 last November in New Orleans when he hit seven threes in one quarter and joined Steph and Klay as the only Warriors ever to do it.

A 6-3 record for the non-Splash Brothers isn't a big enough sample to call it a new formula, and one bench explosion against Sacramento doesn't change the math from the last few years. These days the shooting is sometimes the only thing keeping the Warriors in the game.

That's why Wednesday night felt so good. Steph was in street clothes nursing a torn oblique, somebody else got to be the reason an opposing coach was staring at the ceiling wondering what he did to deserve this.

#2626. How Fury and Joshua changed British boxing forever

They have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.

Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.

They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.

Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.

Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.

We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.

Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.

Britain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas.

Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.

In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight.

"Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.

Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard.

"I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.

By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA.

"The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."

Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.

Fury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.

Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night.

"You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for £2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.

Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.

Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.

Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.

Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."

Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.

Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".

Yet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, the one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?

After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".

For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.

In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.

Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place.

"Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says.

But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved.

"Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.

The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff.

But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.
