#2625. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni pulled back from fans after Thanksgiving win over Cowboys, team claims he was celebrating

Emotions were high following the Philadelphia Eagles' comeback win over the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving. Especially for Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni.

The immediate aftermath of the game saw Sirianni approach a group of field-level Eagles fans and exchange some high-fives, before looking at another group and getting pulled back by a pair of staffers. It's unclear what happened, but Sirianni appeared to maintain eye contact with someone and tried to force his way back before getting pulled to the field.

It was only a few seconds, but it drew attention on social media.

The simple explanation appeared to be Sirianni, who wears his heart on his sleeve in the best of times, was trying to get into it with the opposing fan base. The team and coach are claiming that wasn't the case.

While speaking with reporters postgame, Sirianni said he was only trying to celebrate with Eagles fans and that he was pulled back to the field to shake hands with Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer:

"There were a lot of Eagles fans back there, I was excited to celebrate with those Eagles fans and our team and everything like that. It was fun … I'm sure there were some [Cowboys fans] in there but at that point it felt like there was only Eagles fans, we were able to high-five.

"I had to shake everybody's hand out on the field and wanted to be able to celebrate with everybody, and also shake Schotty's hands and their players' hands."

An Eagles representative apparently backed up this account with Pro Football Talk, contending that Sirianni was only celebrating. We'll see if anything else comes of that, but Sirianni is the head coach with less to worry about following that game.

Philadelphia's win went down as the biggest comeback in NFL Thanksgiving history. The Cowboys led 28-10 at halftime and by as many as 21 points late in the third quarter, only for a superb performance by former Cowboys practice-squad QB Joe Milton, now playing for the Eagles, and some brutal mistakes by Dallas to trigger a wild comeback.

Eagles kicker Jake Elliott made a 59-yard field goal for the win, improving the Eagles' record to 4-7 in what has been a trying season for a team that won a Super Bowl less than two years ago.

#2623. Egor Demin’s standout outing leaves Nets wanting more

TORONTO — To say the Nets have had a disappointing start to the season would be an understatement.

But on Thanksgiving, the Nets can at least be happy about struggling Egor Dëmin having a bounce-back performance. Probably the best outing of his heretofore underwhelming campaign.

"The guys off the bench, Egor, Noah [Clowney], they were amazing," coach Jordi Fernández said after the Nets' slump-busting victory in Milwaukee.

The Nets snapped their five-game skid that had been tied for the worst in the NBA. And Dëmin showed promising signs of snapping out of his own not-unrelated malaise, coming into Friday's game in Toronto.

Perhaps most auspicious was the fact that it wasn't just a hot shooting showing, but an all-around night.

Part of Dëmin's allure as the eighth overall pick was his size, a 6-foot-9 guard who could not just space the floor but rebound and use his wingspan on defense.

That's happened all too infrequently so far. But it did Wednesday against the Bucks.

Dëmin finished with 15 points, four assists, three rebounds and a game-high plus-15. And despite being 0-for-5 from deep, Dëmin — who has struggled horribly inside the arc — was 5-for-6 from 2-point range. He even added feisty defense.

For a player too often faced with the question of "What can he do but shoot?" this was the answer. One that has to get repeated, starting against the Raptors.

Egor Dëmin, who scored 15 points in the Nets' win over the Bucks, drives past Ryan Rollins during the victory. AP

"Yes, he went back to the simple things and started with this physicality on defense," Fernández said. "They felt him the whole game, his length. Then he can rebound. He can be in the gaps. And then offensively, just simple.

"And I know he's capable of [hitting] every shot. Every 3 that he takes, I think it's going in. He was 0-for-5, but guess what? I think all his shots were great. So that's the way I want him to play: with energy, touching the paint, chasing the ball with his teammates, four assists. Proud of him, for sure."

Three games ago, Fernández had pulled Dëmin from the starting lineup for the first time since November of his rookie campaign.

Egor Dëmin rises up for a layup during the Nets' win over the Bucks in Milwaukee. Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images

Dëmin went into Milwaukee having averaged 11.6 points on just 32.2 percent shooting over his prior five games.

And his woes were the worst on the other end of the court, posting a horrid 137.9 defensive rating during that skid. Dëmin was an aggregate minus-57, with Fernández admitting the Russian needed to be better in terms of his physicality.

Dëmin acknowledged a need to improve and did so against the Bucks. His defensive engagement helped spark a game-changing third-quarter spurt and helped the Nets run — his blown dunk notwithstanding.

"Before anything else, I've got to be present mentally for this team, especially because I'm trying to step in front as a leader role, and help Julius [Randle] out from that standpoint — from that kind of perspective — and help Mike [Porter Jr.] and older guys out with the leadership role," Dëmin said.

"So first off, I've got to be in my own mind out there present, and enjoy the game. And for me, it all came from the defensive side of the game. I was locked in with that, and everything else came to me naturally. Because we were getting stops and getting in transition — not counting that missed dunk — but we were getting wide-open opportunities that we were able to execute."

Dëmin had a block and a steal in the same game for the first time this season. He had three deflections and got in passing lanes.

And when Dëmin checked in with 5:16 left in the third and the Nets down 65-60, he helped ignite a 13-2 run. He had five points and two assists in just 1 ¹/₂ minutes, giving them the lead for good.

"Everybody was able to just put their minds together and not just focus on team defense but their own island, how we say 'guard your yard,' " Dëmin said. "That's where it came from."

The next goal is for Dëmin and the Nets not to lose it before Friday's game in Toronto.

#2621. ‘Done & Dumb!’ Cowboys Lose In Historic Fashion To Eagles On Thanksgiving

The semi-tanking Philadelphia Eagles – playing backyard football with little real motivation – somehow erased a 21-point deficit on Thursday to mount the largest Thanksgiving Day comeback in NFL history, beating the heavily favored Cowboys 39-38.

Dallas' loss dropped the Cowboys to 5-7, bringing on the reality of their slim-to-none playoff hopes. They have mastered the art of failing to win back-to-back games, and there has been another season-long constant under pack-your-bags head coach Brian Schottenheimer:

This is the dumbest football team I've ever seen.

Once again, reasons for me to testify to that same thing I've said in the last couple of weeks (which has caused an army of Cowboys-lovin' fans to come hard at me) are everywhere.

Want just one crunch-time mini-bundle? Multiple times in the final seconds, Eagles QB Joe Milton – the Cowboys' third-string practice-squad reject, if you will, who made Dallas look foolish for letting him go to Philly this season – was simply trying to throw the ball out of bounds to eat clock … and not even move closer for the eventual game-winning field goal.

Let me repeat: Philly, down by 2, had no designs on bothering to risk moving closer for the kick.

And yet multiple times, Cowboys defenders interfered with the intended receivers … even though the intended receivers weren't even intending to receive!

Said Prescott: "Pretty stunning. … (Numb) is a good description of how I'm feeling right now."

#2617. Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations rules between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.

Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"

Sheikh Mansour's control of Manchester City has come into question [Getty Images]

When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."

Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football £20.3m annually.

Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

The IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

City have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

#2614. What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players -have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.

But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.

Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.

Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is said to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.

That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.

The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.

When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.

Bayern boss Vincent Kompany (left) has himself recently been diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord [Getty Images]

Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.

As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.

The release clause of £125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.

Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.

Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.

Whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2612. NBA's eight biggest disappointments through one month: Injury bug, same old East and an underwhelming champ

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're roughly one month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and things are going pretty well in certain respects. Luka Dončić and the Lakers are off to a hot start in Los Angeles. Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs have picked up right where they left off after last season's Finals trip. And the Celtics are battling the new-look Sixers at the top of the Eastern Conference.

In other areas, things are going … not so well. Below are the eight biggest disappointments so far this season.

There have been so many players impacted by various injuries that it's almost hard to keep track. Jalen Duren (hamstring) has missed almost the entire season in Detroit. Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are still recovering from knee injuries and have yet to play for Golden State, while Steph Curry is now out with an abdominal tear and Kristaps Porziņģis stepped away from basketball. After sitting out all of last season with an Achilles tear, Tyrese Haliburton is currently dealing with a hamstring issue. Brandon Ingram (Achilles) hasn't made his debut for the Clippers. Austin Reaves is out with a heel injury. Anthony Edwards underwent knee surgery and will miss a chunk of time for the Wolves, and it seems unlikely that Donte DiVincenzo (Achilles) will play this season, even though he remains hopeful that he will. Paolo Banchero remains sidelined with an ankle sprain. Ja Morant is out with a hamstring strain. Ben Simmons didn't play a single game for the Kings before tearing his Achilles. Kawhi Leonard (knee) is once again on the shelf in Toronto. And the reeling Jazz are without Jaren Jackson Jr (knee), Lauri Markkanen (hand) and Jusuf Nurkic (toe).

It's all a huge bummer for the players, their teams and fans of hoops in general. But no team has been hurt more on the injury front than the Thunder.

The disappointment here is how unkind fate has been to OKC. The Thunder were close to fully healthy when the season started — and then far from it not long after it began. When OKC beat the Spurs in San Antonio in the season opener — after losing four of five regular season games to them last season, as well as falling to the Spurs in the Western Conference Finals — it felt like a statement that the Thunder were back and we were in for an epic battle between the two teams over who would rule the West.

And then all of that was stripped away. Just three games into the season, Jalen Williams — who missed much of last season due to injury — suffered a gruesome fall and had to undergo surgery for a fractured fibula as well as reconstruction of ankle ligaments. In that same fateful game, Cason Wallace tore his labrum and later had shoulder surgery. They haven't been officially ruled out, but if either of them plays basketball again this season, it will be a surprise. Making matters worse, Chet Holmgren tore a tendon in his knee and "underwent a biological treatment" to address it. He'll miss approximately two months, but the Thunder do expect him to return. That's what passes for good news in OKC these days.

The Thunder are — or were — the deepest team in the NBA. That's a credit to what Sam Presti built. But even OKC has its limits. Losing three of five starters is tough to overcome, even when you're led by the reigning back-to-back MVP in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. That doesn't mean the Thunder (currently 9-6 and eighth in the West) can't still make a deep playoff run, but the odds of them doing so — and of them fighting the Spurs all season for the top spot — got a lot longer.

We were told that this was finally the season that the East returned to its former glory. We were told that the conference would be loaded. We were wrong. (Full disclosure while putting a palm to my face: I might have done some of that telling.)

Through the first month, the East has been mostly underwhelming. Eight of the 15 teams are below .500. The conference has a combined 17-37 record against the West. Only one of the top seven teams in net rating — the Celtics — plays in the East. Five of the top six teams by point differential play in the West.

The defending champion Knicks are 8-6. The Cavaliers, who made it to last season's Eastern Conference Finals and had championship aspirations of their own, are 8-8. The Magic, Raptors and Pacers — who currently occupy the eight, nine and 10 seeds — all have losing records. By contrast, the worst play-in team in the West right now is Golden State at 8-7. That record would be good enough for the seven seed if they played in the East.

But maybe we shouldn't be surprised. Since the 1999-2000 season, the West has had the better overall record in all but three campaigns. Maybe next year the East will finally snap out of its funk, but don't bet on it.

The Jazz just picked up back-to-back road wins in L.A. over the Lakers and Clippers, but that doesn't begin to dig them out of the deep hole they've made for themselves. The Jazz were gearing up to be competitive in the West this season. So much for that. Like the Thunder, injuries have not been kind to them. Nurkic has yet to play a single game this season, while Markkanen and JJJ have missed significant time with maladies of their own. What looked like a formidable frontcourt has been decimated.

Still, it's hard to believe how bad the Jazz have been in pretty much every facet. Their first win came in the second game of the season, a one-point squeaker over the Pelicans. It took until mid-November to end an ugly 12-game losing streak and pick up their second and third wins. They're 25th in net rating and point differential. The season has barely begun, and it's already basically wait until next year for the Jazz.

The NBA panicked and tried to solve for a problem that wasn't actually an issue, except for a small fragment of people who care more about optics than the product itself. And so the league enacted lottery reform and the new 3-2-1 system was put in place. This was ostensibly designed to prevent tanking, incentivize winning and bring greater parity to the league. Oops.

The Hornets, Wizards, Bulls, Nets and Bucks are all well underwater in the East. The Pelicans and Clippers are drowning in the West, while the Kings and Jazz are even worse. What the league failed to account for is that some of these teams are just organically bad — and now they will have decreased odds at getting better.

Under the old system, the Grizzlies would be pretty thrilled to see the Jazz struggling since Memphis has Utah's first-round pick in the upcoming draft as part of the JJJ trade. Alas, after making that move, the league changed the rules, which means the Grizzlies can pick no higher than sixth now as a consequence of the new system preventing a team from picking in the top five in three consecutive drafts. Since the Jazz picked in the top five in each of the last two drafts, that means the Grizzlies are now out of luck with that Utah pick this time around. Womp, womp for them.

And on top of it all, fans of bad teams were robbed of the entertaining-in-its-own-way race to the bottom to maximize lottery odds, giving supporters a small silver lining in the otherwise gray clouds of their season. RIP Tank Watch.

When aren't the Kings disappointing? Aside from their unsightly 1-13 record, the Sacramento front office continues to make baffling decisions. The Kings originally acquired Nique Clifford from the Thunder for a Spurs 2027 first-round pick. Sacramento held onto Clifford for 83 games — choosing to bury him on the bench this season and play him barely six minutes per game — before shipping him back to the Thunder for two second-round picks.

So the Thunder ended up with the player and a first and the Kings ended up with two seconds.

One of these organizations is savvy and opportunistic, and the other is the Kings. It's a miracle they nailed the Darius Acuff pick.

Oof. It has not been a good season to date for Bridges. After going cold to begin their first-round playoff series against the Hawks, Bridges found his form and played well, helping the Knicks go on an epic run that ended with New York's first championship in 53 years.

If that hope was that Bridges would snap out of his early-season funk in similar fashion, the Knicks seem somewhat less patient these days. While head coach Mike Brown has insisted that Bridges is a starter, he has sometimes hedged his bets in crucial situations, going with Landry Shamet or Deuce McBride over Bridges when things get tight and the Knicks need more reliable offense on the floor.

Through 14 games, Bridges is averaging 7.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists on 40.2/28.9/75 shooting splits. It's the lowest scoring output and the worst shooting numbers of his career. As a result, his minutes have dipped to 25.6 per contest. That's also a career low. Bridges is still a plus defender. And he's only 30. The Knicks obviously hope he'll figure it out, as he has in the past. If not, his new four-year, $150 million extension that kicked in this season will start to look worrisome.

Why are we still subjected to … [motions at everything below in the most pejorative fashion possible] ... this?

ALL 30 TEAM COURTS FOR @EMIRATES NBA CUP 2026 pic.twitter.com/RgBqe1VJCB

Why can't whoever came up with the gorgeous GTA VI crossover court in Miami be in charge of the Cup floors instead?

The Miami Heat are rolling out the “Vice City” hardwood 😮‍💨👏(via @MiamiHEAT) pic.twitter.com/AFcyK2akaV

Respecting the Cup would be so much easier if they'd give us more of this. Maybe they could dream up some sweet new jerseys while they're at it.

#2611. Andy Reid disagrees with overturned Rashee Rice catch after Chiefs' loss to Bills: 'That was not clear and obvious'

Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice appeared to have a much-needed first down against the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving. The NFL's replay center disagreed.

With the game tied 10-10 and two minutes left in the fourth quarter, the Chiefs got the ball deep in their own territory. A pair of incompletions left them facing third-and-10, at which point Patrick Mahomes appeared to connect with wide receiver Rashee Rice for 11 yards and the first down.

However, the play was surprisingly overturned on replay, with the official only saying, "After review, the ball hit the ground, it's an incomplete pass."

The call was popular at Buffalo's Highmark Stadium, but not so much on social media.

The video replay indeed showed the ball hit the ground while pinned between Rice's right hand and shoulder, but that alone doesn't make the play an incomplete pass. The ball must also come loose while hitting the ground before Rice establishes possession, and that was very much up for debate.

Additionally, the NFL maintains a "clear and obvious" standard for overturning plays. So the replay officials in New York City not only believed Rice hadn't completed the catch, they also decided it was clear to anyone watching.

Chiefs head coach Andy Reid very much didn't seem to think that was the case after his team's 13-10 defeat, via Kansas City's KSHB 41:

"Not [a call] that I agreed with, but yeah. This came from New York, so it's not from these guys. Our guys called it a completion, the guys who were working the game. I'm not quite sure what they saw. I saw he had control of the ball and his elbow hit and then the ball hit, but he had control.

"Normally, in those kind of situations, it's gotta be clear and obvious. To me, that was not clear and obvious."

Rashee Rice appeared to have a first down for the Chiefs. The NFL's replay center disagreed.

Mahomes' wife Brittany, meanwhile, used the occasion to dispute the idea the Chiefs have benefited from calls during their recent run, writing the following on her Instagram story:

"Guess we can't even play football without getting it called against us… not sure what an actual catch is after that I guess? I don't wanna hear s*** anymore from anyone"

She also posted a collection of social media posts criticizing the call to her story.

NFL vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth spoke to a pool reporter, pointing to Rice's hand moving up the ball as evidence that he lost control.

To be clear, this play did not singlehandedly cost the Chiefs the game, though it's undeniably frustrating. Had the Rice catch stood, they still would have needed to travel half the field to reach field-goal range, on a day in which struggling kicker Harrison Butker made one field goal from 26 yards and missed another from 46.

Facing fourth-and-10, Kansas City was instead forced to punt out of its own end zone. The teams immediately exchanged three-and-outs and appeared headed to overtime, only for field position to bite the Chiefs again when a disastrous punt sequence put the Bills in field-goal position for the final play.

#2610. Luciano Spalletti hails Juventus star Andrea Cambiaso as catalyst for four-goal Europa League comeback against Omonia

Luciano Spalletti has credited Andrea Cambiaso with transforming Juventus' fortunes during their Europa League victory over Omonia. The Bianconeri manager admitted that his side struggled early on before the versatile Italian international sparked a dominant four-goal response.

Juventus secured a vital victory in their quest for Europa League progression, but the night did not start according to plan for Luciano Spalletti's men. An early defensive lapse involving goalkeeper Neto allowed Lubomir Satka to give Omonia a shock lead, leaving the Turin giants facing an uphill battle. However, a stunning strike from Cambiaso shifted the momentum entirely, allowing the hosts to settle into their rhythm and eventually overpower their opponents.

Reflecting on the early difficulties and the subsequent turnaround, Spalletti was quick to highlight the impact of his star man. "At the beginning, we made a couple of mistakes that the others exploited. Things got a bit messy like that. Then Cambiaso put everything right with a great goal and the team played more calmly," the manager said, as quoted by Tuttosport.

Acknowledging that Cambiaso initially showed "moments of apprehension," Spalletti highlighted how quickly the player settled into the contest and stepped up when his side needed a spark. Spalletti was quick to underline the complete technical toolkit that makes Cambiaso such a threat in the final third. From sharp one-touch combinations to taking on defenders directly, the manager made it clear that Cambiaso's attacking instincts set him apart.

"He made decisions, untangling problems for the team, like the goal into the top corner," the boss noted. "As things went well for him, he gradually came into possession of his qualities. He knows how to play football, he knows how to play first time, he's good at getting into the box, he's good at one-on-one, and he has a high level of quality in his proposition," Spalletti added.

Spalletti was also left pleased after his decision to rotate the squad paid dividends on the European stage. Having handed opportunities to several players who have struggled for consistent minutes of late, the manager saw his fringe options rise to the occasion and highlight the depth at his disposal.

Reflecting on the performance, Spalletti acknowledged how difficult it can be to find rhythm immediately after a spell on the sidelines, while praising his side's intensity off the ball. "Did the new players on the pitch respond? Yes, and it's not easy to find your form straight away when you've been away for a while," he said. "We scored beautiful goals, we were good on the pitch, we pressed well."

With their Europa League fate firmly in their own hands, Juventus must now shift focus back to Serie A and translate that clinical European form into domestic momentum as they look to surge up the standings. Spalletti's side face a genuine banana skin on Sunday with a daunting trip to an in-form Como outfit that has been turning heads across Italy. This weekend's clash is already shaping up as a make-or-break crossroads for the Bianconeri's entire season.

#2608. MLB rumors: Mets to meet with NPB star, plus latest on Ketel Marte, Cubs, Mariners, Nationals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're one week away from Thanksgiving and the offseason has started to pick up a little bit in Major League Baseball. We've seen an All-Star pitcher sign (Sonny Gray to the Twins) and a trade involving an All-Star (Maikel Garcia to the Mariners). The White Sox also signed a mid-rotation starter while the Red Sox grabbed a first baseman fresh off a World Series title. Is there enough time for a flurry of moves before the owners lock the players out when the CBA expires on Dec. 1?

In theory, there sure is. We can hold out hope, as there has been enough movement to keep belief alive.

It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are willing to trade All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. A big hurdle might be his 10-and-5 no-trade rights and questions about which teams Marte would approve in a potential deal. Further, the asking price on Arizona's end is "very high," reports FanSided. Still, plenty of teams are said to be interested.

Marte, 33, has five years and $91.75 million left on his deal. He finished third in MVP voting in 2024, was a highly productive All-Star in 2025, but some issues arose in 2026, including several no-shows. He hit .249/.316/.432 (107 OPS+) with 2.5 WAR and some possible clubhouse baggage.

The Mets are planning a Zoom meeting with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the New York Post. This won't have an impact on their pursuit of Tarik Skubal, just in case anyone is curious.

Taira, 27, has been one of the top pitchers in Japan's NPB for years. Last season, in 23 starts, he had a 1.36 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 141 strikeouts in 146 innings. He's had a sub-2.00 ERA four of the last five seasons, with the exception being a 2.40 in 2023.

CBS Sports ranked Taira as the No. 19 free agent available this winter:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Seibu announced on Oct. 30 that Taira will be posted this offseason.

Because of the expected lockout, international free agents are working under an artificial Dec. 1 deadline to sign, rather than the normal posting window.

For now, the Mets' rotation starts with Nolan McLean and Christian Scott.

The Cubs' main focus is on pitching, as well it should be after having one of the worst pitching staffs in baseball along with one of the best collections of position-player talent. Still, both corner outfielders (Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki) have hit free agency along with catcher Carson Kelly, so they can't just ignore the offense. On that front, the ballclub has "extensively scouted" Teruaki Sato, according to The Athletic.

Sato has played mostly third base, where the Cubs have Alex Bregman, but also has outfield experience and could simply serve as DH. In 143 games last season in NPB, Sato hit .306/.383/.609 with 40 doubles, 39 home runs and 106 RBI. His strikeout numbers are high, but sometimes that's the price to be paid for top-level power.

CBS Sports ranked Sato as the No. 4 free agent this winter:

He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.

After being one of the most disappointing teams in 2026 and having an active general manager, of course the Mariners weren't going to just sit around after one move. Sure enough, Jerry Dipoto told reporters on Wednesday that they are still looking to add a right-handed bat (remember, Randy Arozarena is a free agent) along with a veteran infielder and a left-handed reliever even after acquiring Garcia. And perhaps most importantly, Dipoto insisted that they do have the payroll flexibility to add all of this.

Further, he also said the rotation is set and no other starting pitchers will be moved. So it'll be Logan Gilbert, George Kirby, Bryan Woo, Emerson Hancock and Kade Anderson heading into next season.

Fresh off signing right-handed starter Dustin May, the White Sox are looking to add another starting pitcher "of similar magnitude," reports the Chicago Sun-Times.

Though the White Sox were one of baseball's best stories last season and made the playoffs, the rotation was very thin. Right now, they have Sean Burke, May, Taylor, Davis Martin and Anthony Kay as their top five and are looking to add another of May's ilk. Things are already looking much better.

The Nationals finished third in the majors in runs scored last season, believe it or not. They trailed only the Cubs and Brewers, scoring more than the Dodgers. The problem was that the pitching staff was mostly a mess. As such, it's no surprise they are after starters and The Athletic names three targets: lefty Kris Bubic, righty Brady Singer and Japanese import Kona Takahashi.

Bubic, 29, has battled shoulder and elbow injuries the past two seasons, but the upside was flashed in the first part of 2025. He made the All-Star team and had a 2.55 ERA through 20 starts and 116 ⅓ innings.

The 30-year-old Singer was 6-15 with a 5.85 ERA for the Reds last season in a disaster of a contract year, but he was productive in the previous two seasons.

Takahashi, 29, was 9-7 with a 2.64 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and 118 strikeouts in 143 ⅓ innings in NPB last season.

#2607. NBA rumors: Suitors emerging for Dejounte Murray, demand for Anthony Davis and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 NBA season is barely a month old and trade season won't officially begin until December 15 when players signed this summer are eligible to be moved, but that doesn't stop the rumor machine from churning in the Association.

The first 15 games of the season have been enough for some teams to learn the harsh truth about not being a contender this year, while others are off to surprisingly good starts that could turn them into midseason buyers. That's how the trade market starts to take shape, and with a trade request already made in New Orleans by Dejounte Murray and a handful of expiring contracts known to be open to moving, we can start piecing together an early look at what trade season may look like.

The one unknown this season is how the league's lottery reform will affect the in-season trade market. Fewer teams will have incentive to completely bottom out, but even with teams not trying to sell everything off, there will still be enough teams trying to buy to create a market.

On Thursday, we got a fresh batch of rumors, starting with some updates on potential suitors for Murray after being sent home by the Pelicans.

Murray makes $32.8 million this year and has a player option for $30.8 million next year that he will almost assuredly pick up. That means he's not exactly a coveted asset, and even for teams with a potential need at point guard, so far no one seems to be jumping at the opportunity to trade for the disgruntled Pelicans guard.

Two teams that were quickly connected as potential destinations for Murray were the Suns and the Heat, both with glaring point guard needs and a desire to contend this season. However, neither team is desperate to make a move right now, according to Jake Fischer in the latest Stein Line newsletter.

Murray and Klutch Sports see Phoenix as a good landing spot, but the Suns view center as a bigger need than point guard and would demand that the Pelicans send back draft capital to take on Murray's salary, Fischer reports. Miami, meanwhile, has shown little appetite for Murray and he is not expected to be one of its trade targets because of his player option for next season that would severely limit their ability to retool the roster around Giannis Antetokounmpo.

With the two most obvious potential suitors for Murray not exactly showing a lot of excitement for bringing him in, it seems likely that Murray's trade request and absence from the Pelicans will extend for quite some time and could last all the way to the trade deadline.

The Washington Wizards are 5-11 to start the season, which makes it increasingly unlikely they will be trying to work out a long-term extension for Davis. The early returns on Washington's commitment to Trae Young have not been good, and if the Wizards are looking to acquire some assets this season, Davis makes the most sense as an expiring contract.

On the latest episode of the Hoop Collective, ESPN's Brian Windhorst offered an update on Davis' market and desires for his next contract.

"I think people have demand for Anthony Davis," Windhorst said. "They just don't want to give him a max extension, and I don't think he's looking for a max extension, but I do think he's looking for a lot of money."

That's not exactly groundbreaking information and any team exploring a trade for Davis will want to know what, exactly, he's looking for in his next contract. Below the max is a start, but teams are growing wary of giving out massive money to aging stars in the second apron era. Davis brings an additional level of risk to any long-term contract discussions with his injury history.

That said, he has been quite good this season -- averaging 24.6 points and 10.1 rebounds per game on solid efficiency -- and the Wizards should be shopping him to teams desperate for a center upgrade. If Phoenix is less interested in a point guard but has an appetite for a star center, perhaps the Suns could be a trade partner to offload Jalen Green's contract -- to be clear, that's not a rumor, just connecting dots between a few recent rumors.

Everything with Davis' market will come down to what Davis and Rich Paul tell teams about what they want his next contract to look like.

With Murray on the block and the Pelicans at 5-11, it's fair to wonder (again) if some of New Orleans' more intriguing players could find their way onto the trade market.

The player most teams around the league covet in New Orleans is Trey Murphy III. Even though he's in the midst of a slow start to the season and currently dealing with knee tendonitis, other teams still covet his potential as a star on the wing given his abilities as a scorer and defender. The Pelicans also believe strongly in Murphy's upside, and unfortunately for other teams, Fischer reports Murphy -- unlike Murray -- has no desire to make a trade request.

As such, he's going to be quite expensive to pry from the Pelicans, who "remain reluctant" to discuss trades for Murphy. Given he's their best potential trade chip, that's probably a wise approach, and New Orleans will hope some hopeful contender is desperate enough to give up a haul of assets before they consider moving him.

#2606. 10 Eagles things I think I think after incredible comeback vs. Cowboys

There's no other way to describe the Philadelphia Eagles' comeback victory over the Dallas Cowboys — which was way more enjoyable than any meal you could consume on Thanksgiving. This is an Eagles game that's going to be remembered forever, just like the Christmas Day win over the Cowboys in 2006 and the Miracle at the Meadowlands comeback in 2010.

The victory is that improbable, especially when the Eagles were down 31-10 with 3:35 left in the third quarter. They had no business being in this game, yet they found their way back to make it a game — and stole a victory away from the Cowboys on Thanksgiving.

This was a game the Cowboys should have won handily. Instead they choked it away, thanks to the hands of a resilient Eagles team that didn't let their 3-7 record stand in the way of what seemed to be an insurmountable deficit.

No matter how the rest of this season goes, that was one heck of a win. This victory will be talked about amongst generations of Eagles fans.

A Thanksgiving miracle — that may have ended the Cowboys season. The Eagles are good at ruining seasons all of a sudden.

Milton delivered one of the greatest performances my a quarterback in Eagles history. What Milton did against the Cowboys was absolutely incredible, and this was more than a quarterback showing off his ridiculous arm talent.

The final stat line: 21-of-31, 311 yards, 3 TD, 1 INT, 10.7 YPA — 121.8 rating. 3 carries, 15 yards, TD.

There are only two quarterbacks in Eagles history with 300+ passing yards, 3+ passing TD, 1+ rushing TD, and average 10+ YPA in a game — Milton and Michael Vick (2010 at Commanders). That's how well Milton played on Thanksgiving — in just his third career start.

Once the Eagles trailed 31-10, Milton went 11-of-16 for 181 yards with 2 TD, 1 INT and a 120.1 rating (averaging 11.3 YPA). He also had 15 yards and a rushing touchdown in that stretch to bring the Eagles back from three scores.

This level of play was throughout the game. Milton used his arm strength to keep the Eagles offense moving, going 11-of-19 for 278 yards with 3 TD, 1 INT and 14.6 YPA on throws that traveled 10+ air yards — finishing with a 120.1 passer rating. He was 2-of-6 for 95 yards and 2 TD with 0 INT for a 121.5 passer rating on throws that traveled 25+ air yards. Any completion on passes that traveled 25+ air yards was a touchdown.

The Eagles had some exciting performances from Jalen Hurts over the years, but that was arguably the most exciting passing performance by a quarterback since Nick Foles threw for 471 yards against the Houston Texans in 2018 (and that was an Eagles' win too).

Impressive performance by Milton, finally giving life to an Eagles offense that badly needed it.

Milton had a touchdown pass that traveled 64.4 yards in air distance, and that wasn't the most impressive aspect of his performance. He threw an interception into triple coverage with 7:14 to play when the Eagles were trailing 38-3, which seemed to be the backbreaker with how the defense was playing.

The Eagles got the ball back and Milton goes 4-of-4 for 70 yards and a 24-yard touchdown to Makai lemon on the ensuing drive — netting a perfect 158.3 passer rating. The poise and ability to forget that interception immediately following the interception spoke more volumes about who Milton is as a player than anything else he accomplished on Thanksgiving.

When Milton made a boneheaded play, he responded in the way winning quarterbacks respond. He hasn't even been on his team for two months and was able to shake that play off and perform at an even higher level.

Since the interception, Milton finished 6-of-9 for 84 yards with a touchdown and a 133.6 passer rating. He led the Eagles to victory with a touchdown drive and set Jake Elliott up with his game-winning field goal.

Want to know how to stick around as a starting quarterback in the NFL? Moments like that.

One of the few things I wanted to see in the remainder of the season was if Milton could play well enough to be the QB2 next year. Judging Milton through two starts was tough, given the state of the offense and the changes the Eagles were making to accomondate his game.

Milton didn't get to throw the deep ball much, and he missed when he had his opportunity last week to DeVonta Smith. He didn't miss any of those opportunities on Thanksgiving, hitting two of them for 95 yards and two touchdowns.

On throws that traveled 20+ air yards, Milton went 6-of-11 for 188 yards and 3 TD with 0 INT — a 139.2 passer rating. The arm strength was clearly on display, along with the accuracy on the deep ball.

Milton was relentless facing pressure too, finishing 7-of-10 for 154 yards with 3 TD and 0 INT for a 152.1 passer rating — while also being sacked five times. He was 6-of-8 for 145 yards with 3 TD and 0 INT on throws from outside the pocket — 156.3 rating.

Backup quarterbacks don't have games like this. QB5's — which is what Milton was when he signed — really don't have games like this.

This performance may have locked up QB2 for Milton next year. If Milton can stack up good-to-solid performances, he'll be the QB2 on the Eagles (at least).

Milton may get a starting opportunity elsewhere too (he is a restricted free agent), but the Eagles can control his fate there as well. The situation needs to play itself out, but Milton is certainly on the radar around the league.

When Milton was making incredible throws against the Cowboys, I couldn't help but think of his journey to get to this point. Over the last four months, Milton was cut by the Cowboys after losing the QB2 job to Sam Howell —toiling on the practice squad for five weeks.

Any team could have claimed Milton when he was waived, and no team did. Any team could have signed Milton from the Cowboys practice squad to the active roster, and no one did.

The Eagles signed Milton to the active roster when Jalen Hurts was lost for the season due to blood clots in his lungs. If Hurts wasn't done for the year, the Eagles wouldn't have brought in Milton.

He literally was their QB5, the fifth quarterback to make the active roster. Tanner McKee got three starts before the Eagles turned to Milton, Andy Dalton told the Eagles he had a better opportunity with the Atlanta Falcons.

Milton wasn't considered by the Cowboys and 31 other teams until the Eagles needed a quarterback. To have a performance like that against a team that cut him and chose Sam Howell over him had to be bittersweet — especially since he led the Eagles to a 21-point comeback on the road against that team on Thanksgiving in just his third start.

Certainly Milton will soak that all in at some point, but the battle to succeed and have a moment like that are why sports are so great. Even when Milton was counted out, he wasn't.

There were questions whether DeVonta Smith was a WR1 earlier this season. There shouldn't be any following Thanksgiving.

Smith finished with 11 catches for 200 yards and two touchdowns in the win over the Cowboys, the first Eagles' player to get 200+ receiving yards in a game since DeSean Jackson in 2010. He had the most receiving yards on Thanksgiving since 1945 — and the second-most by any player on the holiday in NFL history.

Smith had two touchdown catches of 45+ yards, the first player to do that on Thanksgiving since Randy Moss in 1998. He had more receiving yards on Thanksgiving (200) than A.J. Brown has the whole season (128).

How good was the Milton-Smith connection? Milton was 11-of-14 for 200 yards with 2 TD, 0 INT and a 158.3 passer rating when targeting Smith — 14.3 yards per attempt. He hit Smith on throws of 24, 50, 45, and 23 yards of those 11 completions, and also hit him six times on throws of 10+ air yards.

When Smith is healthy, he's very good. He wasn't even fully healthy in this one, injuring his lower back trying to make an insane catch in the fourth quarter on a Milton deep ball. Smith could barely run at full speed the rest of the way, yet still was able to go out and make plays.

Smith has 42 catches for 551 yards and 4 TD in six games. He's averaging 91.8 receiving yards per game, a 17-game pace of 1,561 yards. With the injuries, Smith is still on pace for 851 receiving yards (and those numbers will go up if he's good enough to play).

Milton has an excellent chance to stick around with Smith on the field. That connection was brilliant on Thanksgiving.

Hard to state the claim the Eagles have given up on Nick Sirianni based on the last two games.

A win against the Pittsburgh Steelers to end a seven-game losing streak is a gut-check victory. Stealing a game on Thanksgiving against the Dallas Cowboys is in unchartered territory.

The Eagles were down 21 points with 3:35 left in the third quarter. They had eight plays in the quarter that went for 1 yard at that point, while the defense allowed 31 points on seven possessions and 6.7 yards per play.

They could have packed it in and allowed Dallas to continue to roll. They didn't.

The Eagles not giving up in a season that has experienced injury after injury (including the multiple starters that left the game), team captains and long-time starters getting traded, the handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots, and the uncertain future of the coaching staff speaks volumes of how Nick Sirianni prepares his team during the week.

No matter what Sirianni does during a game (and after), his players are still playing for him. The message is still getting across to the players in that locker room and the Eagles don't believe their playoff chances are dead yet.

If Sirianni is back after this season, this is the reason why. This locker room has no checked out on him, and they are demonstrating that with their performance on the field.

Any team could have called it a day down 31-10 late in the third quarter. Not the Eagles, who had their biggest comeback in 16 years.

I understand why Sirianni acts like he does. Sirianni is a very emotional individual and a competitor who puts his heart and soul into coaching.

Going on a seven-game losing streak took its toll on Sirianni, who spent weeks trying to figure out what was going on with his football team. This is a head coach who was 59-26 (.694 win percetatge) after his first five seasons, making the playoffs all five years and winning a Super Bowl while appearing in another one.

Sirianni is fighting for his team — and his job. The last two months have been brutal.

The Eagles head coach gets caught up in the moment with fans a little too much. He lets his emotions get the best of him. I'm not even sure if he was interacting with Eagles fans or taunting Cowboys fans, but it was enough where he had to be pulled away by Dom DiSandro.

Sirianni shouldn't be putting himself in that situation, and he's done it far too much. I like that he's authentic, but that is taking it too far.

The Eagles head coach shouldn't care what the fans think of him, good or bad. It's clear Sirianni hears what's said of him and acts on it when he wins.

Sirianni gets over the top with this stuff, a silly distraction after the massive win. The Eagles have enough issues to worry about inside the Jefferson Health Training Complex.

Can't speak enough on how good Jake Elliott has been all season. Elliott's two field goals on Sunday were the reason the Eagles won, and he gave the Eagles their first lead of the game on a 59-yard field goal with two seconds left — and the kick would have been good from 65 yards.

Elliott had ice in his veins when making that kick, just like the majority of clutch kicks he's made in his career. Elliott is 14-of-14 on field goals in the final minute of a game in regulation or overtime, 5-of-5 on kicks of 50+ yards in one-score games.

He's 2-for-2 in those situations this season, and 1-of-1 on game-winning field goals.

Elliott has improved to 5-of-5 on 50+ yard field goal attempts, after being 5-of-15 (33.3%) on those kicks over the previous two seasons. Elliott is 8-of-9 (88.9%) on 40+ yard kicks this season after going 20-of-34 (58.9%) on those kicks over the previous two seasons.

The comeback is incredible, and why the Eagles chose to adamantly defend Elliott this offseason. Just an amazing season from Elliott, who might be in line for an All-Pro campaign.

This Eagles comeback doesn't happen without Robinson, who made the most of his opportunity when his number was called. Robinson had three pressures in seven pass-rushing snaps, an insane pressure rate of 42.9%.

One of those pressures was the fourth-down sack on Dak Prescott on 4th-and-1 with 55 seconds left — the first one of Robinson's career. This was a player who wasn't even guaranteed to make the roster once training camp started, and earned his way onto this team with his play in training camp.

That play set the Eagles up to steal the game, and set off a fire in Dallas on whether Brian Schottenheimer should have punted or went for it — enough where his job is in question. Robinson was able to make that massive of a presence as a pass rusher, and deserves more playing time going forward.

Oh, and Robinson also blocked a punt that was recovered by Kenny Moore for a touchdown. That play was massive in the Eagles' comeback, and cut the deficit to 31-24 with 13:53 left in the game. Robinson should have been credited with a forced fumble in this game too, but I digress.

Robinson is the first player in Eagles history to record a sack and a blocked punt in the same game. This is a player that logged just 73 defensive snaps this season prior to Thursday.

The Eagles have something with Robinson. They traded Jordan Davis for multiple reasons.

The Eagles entered this game with the worst second-half offense in football. The 4.6 point average in the second half was last in the NFL. So was the yards per play (3.6), average yards in second half (110.1), and net yards per attempt (4.3). The only major statistic that wasn't 32nd was yards per carry — 30th at 3.3.

This week was significantly different. The Eagles scored 22 offensive points in the second half (29 total), averaging 6.9 yards per play and gaining 200 yards of offense. They averaged 5.4 yards per carry and 8.5 net yards per attempt — all this while only converting 20% of third downs.

This was the worst team in football in the second half, and they're still last in the league in offensive points scored (6.2), yards per play (3.9), and average yards in second half (118.3). yards per carry moved up to 29th (3.4) and net yards per attempt improved to 31st (4.8).

The Eagles even scored in the third quarter! Milton's touchdown pass in the third quarter was just the second touchdown scored by the Eagles in the third quarter all season — the other one was against the Cowboys. They improved their third quarter scoring average to 30th in the league (2.1 points).

This offense in the second half underwent a complete 180, and it didn't start out that way (first eight plays went for a yard). Amazing turnaround once Milton hit Smith on that 45-yard touchdown with 24 seconds left in the third quarter.

Can the Eagles build off this? Hopefully.

Bonus: Enjoy this win (enjoy all of them). This is one the city of Philadelphia will talk about for a long time, even better since this season has been a disaster and this matchup seemed like a easy victory for the Cowboys (I didn't even think the Eagles could score 20 points when I was watching Dallas film on Monday).

You'll remember where you were and who you were with when the Eagles pulled off this comeback.

The Eagles are 4-0 against the Cowboys on Thanksgiving and Christmas — all games in Dallas. Happy Thanksgiving everyone!

#2604. Luis Castillo trade grades: White Sox give up steady back-end starter to offload salary; Rockies get creative

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Two days after adding Dustin May to their rotation, the Chicago White Sox have subtracted Luis Castillo and Davis Martin. The White Sox are sending Castillo and Martin to the Colorado Rockies for lefty Sean Sullivan and minor-league catcher Douglas Veliz, the teams announced late Thursday. The Rockies will take on Castillo's entire contract.

Castillo, 33, joined the White Sox in a deadline trade with the Seattle Mariners. He struggled badly after the deal, allowing 30 runs in 31 innings, and he finished the season on the injured list with a shoulder issue. Castillo has one year remaining on his contract at $22.75 million, though a $25 million option for 2028 will vest if he throws 150 innings in 2027.

The 29-year-old Martin threw 146 innings with a 3.95 ERA in 2026, but it was a 3.41 ERA in the first half and a 5.12 ERA in the second half. The White Sox kept him at arm's length in the postseason despite running bullpen games almost nightly. Martin allowed two runs in one inning in his only postseason appearance.

Neither Sullivan nor Veliz are significant prospects. For all intents and purposes, the White Sox are attaching Martin to Castillo as a sweetener to get the Rockies to take Castillo's salary. The Rockies are essentially buying Martin, who is under team control through 2030, by taking on the rest of Castillo's contract.

Here now are our trade grades for this two-for-two swap.

Fair or not, I'm going to lump the two Castillo trades together. Chicago stepped out to acquire Castillo at the deadline and absorbed the $30 million or so remaining on his contract to do it. Seranthony Domínguez, who had about $15 million left on his deal, went the other way in the trade, so the White Sox took on about $15 million total, and also gave up a pretty good prospect in Boston Smith.

Four and a half months later, the White Sox had to give up a steady back-end starter in Martin to clear Castillo's money. They ended up saving about $7 million in 2027 in this series of moves, but it cost them Martin and Smith (and Domínguez), and they had to endure 31 awful innings from Castillo. Unless Sullivan or Veliz hit big, the White Sox took a series of Ls here.

Credit to president of baseball operations Chris Getz for acknowledging a mistake with Castillo and acting quickly to unload him. It was costly, though. Martin isn't a star, but cheap back-end starters are very valuable. We'll see what Getz & Co. do with the savings. Presumably they'll invest in more pitching. Having to give up Martin to dump Castillo so soon is a stinker, though. Ouch.

The Rockies need all types of pitching (righty, lefty, starter, reliever, whatever) and it's not often they can convince quality (or even competent) free agents to come to Coors Field. They have to develop their own pitchers or trade for pitching, and in this instance, they took on Castillo's hefty salary to get Martin and his four years of control. Creative, if nothing else.

There is downside potential too. Martin has run below league-average strikeout rates and middling ground ball rates throughout his career. Pitchers who allow a lot of balls in play -- a lot of balls in play in the air -- are a poor match for Coors Field. It's good the Rockies spent and found a way to add controllable pitching. They just might not have picked the best pitcher.

After losing 104 games in 2026, there is no such thing as a bad dart throw for the Rockies. It's unlikely they would have been able to spend the $22.75 million on a free agent (at least not without overpaying), so taking on Castillo to get Martin is the next best thing. I like the thinking, even if I don't love Martin's profile in Coors Field.
