#2601. What's next for the Twins? Three things Minnesota must do to make a postseason push in 2027 season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It has been a surprisingly productive week for the Minnesota Twins. First, catcher Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer on Tuesday. Jeffers turned down a multi-year offer from the Twins, according to The Athletic, so he's betting on himself. Betting that he'll at least maintain his free agent stock and get paid next offseason.

Then, on Wednesday, the Twins brought back veteran righty Sonny Gray with a two-year contract worth $55 million. There's an opt-out after the first year. Gray, 37, finished fifth in the AL Cy Young voting this season and pitched wonderfully for the Twins in 2022 and 2023. He joins a rotation that, on paper, looks like one of the better starting units in the American League.

Here is Minnesota's rotation depth chart:

"I really don't take it lightly that he chose us," GM Jeremy Zoll told the Associated Press about Gray's return. "He had an abundance of options, and given where he's at in his career, I know how important it is to him. He expressed it quite directly how important it is to win, and this isn't just about having a good season or a winning season. It's about winning and going deep in the playoffs and making a real playoff run."

Matthews could land in the bullpen next season and that might be his long-term home. His stuff should be well suited to a relief role. Gray makes the rotation better and potentially the bullpen better as well by bumping Matthews to relief. Jeffers accepting the qualifying offer keeps a key middle-of-the-order bat in place. A good week for the Twins, this has been.

After a disappointing 77-85 finish this year, Minnesota has already improved significantly in the early days of the offseason. They play in the AL Central. With all due respect, it is not the most imposing division. There's no reason the Twins can't be in the division and wild card races next season. Here now is what's left on Minnesota's offseason to-do list.

Teams had until 5 p.m. ET Friday to offer their pre-arbitration and arbitration-eligible players contracts for 2027. They didn't have to sign them Friday, but they had to tender an offer; otherwise, the player immediately became a free agent. Dozens of players were cut loose at the non-tender deadline, as usual, and two players stood out as non-tender candidates for the Twins: Trevor Larnach and Royce Lewis. Larnach was indeed non-tendered, while Lewis was dealt to the Dodgers.

It's not often a player gets non-tendered after posting a .352 on-base percentage and 120 OPS+, but the writing was on the wall. The Twins had an agreement in place to trade Larnach at the deadline (Astros owner Jim Crane nixed the deal) and they have a very crowded outfield. Also, Larnach had wrist surgery earlier this month. That created some questions going into next season, and the Twins opted to cut him loose.

Larnach had one more year of control remaining and was expected to make over $6 million through arbitration in 2027. I reckon the Twins tried again to trade him prior to Friday's non-tender deadline. In the end, he was non-tendered rather than risk tying $6 million or so up in yet another outfielder, particularly one who is coming off wrist surgery.

Things got so bad this summer that Lewis, who has a .288 on-base percentage in over 1,200 plate appearances the last three years, was sent to Triple-A for a spell, and also moved across the diamond from third base to first base. The Twins could not count on him to provide offense and now he's playing a position with a high offensive bar. That made him expendable.

Lewis, 27, was under team control through 2028 and that extra year was an important consideration for the club. His salary would have been in the $5 million range next season through arbitration, which is pricey but not exorbitant. Now, Lewis will receive a fresh start with the Dodgers, where he can be one of the guys, not the former No. 1 overall pick and expected face of the franchise.

The Twins presumably did not want to give up on a player with as much talent as Lewis. At the same time, they kept trying, and it never worked.

The Twins got a head start on their offseason bullpen shopping when they acquired Jeff Hoffman at the trade deadline. He has one more year remaining on the contract and will be in the team's late-inning mix in 2027.

Here is manager Derek Shelton's bullpen unit at the moment:

Morris is not yet a household name, but he has a great arm and was dominant at times in 2026. The Twins have themselves a nice little late-inning trio in Gómez, Hoffman, and Morris. A spare starter like Matthews or Prielipp could wind up in the bullpen as well. Given the quality of their stuff, they have a chance to make a real impact as relievers.

Clearly though, the middle relief could use some help, and the Twins wouldn't need to spend big dollars to improve it. A second-tier free agent like, say, Andrew Kittredge would be a solid pickup. It's worth giving the Miami Marlins a call to see what it would take to get Anthony Bender and/or Michael Petersen. Point is, the bullpen can be improved, for sure.

The Twins have way more outfielders than outfield spots and that is in no way a bad thing. First and foremost, it allows them to use Byron Buxton as the full-time DH, which could help keep him on the field. Secondly, there's no such thing as too many good players. Depth is important and the Twins certainly have plenty of it in the outfield.

More outfielders than outfield spots is not a problem. It's just something the Twins have to figure out. Even if we assume Buxton will DH and is not part of the outfield mix, here are the outfielders Minnesota must sort through:

Rodriguez is one of the game's 50 or so best prospects and he is out of minor league options, meaning he must go through waivers to go to Triple-A. Obviously, the Twins won't waive him. Non-tendering Larnach allows the Twins to play Rodriguez alongside Jenkins and Keaschall in the outfield, keep Kreidler and Martin on the bench, and keep the others in Triple-A.

#2598. Will anyone else sign Aaron Rodgers after he torched Steelers? Breaking down 5 questions, including most logical match

The cognitive dissonance was high and, yet, unsurprising.

Few around the NFL were surprised that the Pittsburgh Steelers released quarterback Aaron Rodgers after he lambasted head coach Mike McCarthy on "The Pat McAfee Show."

And also: Few were ready to say with certainty that the 42-year-old four-time MVP would not get another chance to play in the NFL.

There is a laundry list of reasons why other teams would not sign the man who just aired quite a bit of dirty laundry.

And yet: NFL teams have operated off far less logical desperation before. Rodgers' arm strength has not fully dissipated, nor has his line-of-scrimmage command lost its argument among the best in the game.

So multiple sources weren't ready to fully rule out a Rodgers return to the NFL this season.

One high-ranking AFC executive said they "doubt" Rodgers gets another gig but left the door a crack open, noting "we all are trying to get to the postseason."

It's doubtful Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy will be exchanging holiday cards this year.

An NFC talent evaluator responded to whether they'd sign Rodgers if they were general manager not with a "no" but by asking in this hypothetical "of what team?"

And an NFC assistant coach whose team has realistic odds to make the playoffs did not dismiss the upside of signing Rodgers for a team with strong pieces to support a quarterback.

"If it means we win a Super Bowl? Yes," the assistant said. "Not sure who is in that mode right now."

So could another NFL team sign Rodgers for the rest of the regular season and/or a playoff run? Here are five questions to keep in mind surrounding Rodgers' possible next steps.

1) The Steelers released Rodgers on Wednesday, and he went unclaimed on waivers Thursday. Doesn't that already mean no team wanted to sign him?

Claiming Rodgers off waivers feels like trading for receiver A.J. Brown last year. Sure, any team could have tried to pry the three-time Pro Bowler from the Philadelphia Eagles. But Brown's vocal disruptions in Philadelphia indicated that he would not go quietly to wherever he was told. The New England Patriots knew Brown wanted to reunite with his former Tennessee Titans head coach Mike Vrabel and thus they felt confident that Brown's willingness to accept coaching and embrace his teammates would be stronger with Vrabel in New England than in a place he landed against his will.

And then there were the financial implications to claiming Rodgers off waivers rather than signing him as a free agent: Off waivers, Rodgers' original contract had $8.56 million left this year. As a free agent, a team could sign Rodgers for the prorated veteran minimum and leave the Steelers responsible for nearly all of his pay. It's not hard to guess whether Rodgers would appreciate taking up as much space as possible on the Steelers' books.

Now that he's cleared waivers, teams can pursue Rodgers as a free agent at a lower cost and with a higher ability to research whether they want him.

2) Would Rodgers add value to another team?

Determining Rodgers' net value is complicated: How does one weigh decades of schematic and technical knowledge against the risk of another public embarrassment for which teammates and coaches must answer? How does one project Rodgers' willingness to accept play-calls from a play-caller other than himself — after his ultimatum to McCarthy about the head coach no longer calling plays appears to have first and foremost triggered his benching?

What's indisputable: Rodgers' performance this year. He led the Steelers to a 6-4 record on track for the playoffs (there is plenty of time, and reason, to wonder if they'll go off the tracks now), but Rodgers' individual statistics haven't topped charts. In 10 games, Rodgers completed 60.9% of passes for 2,241 yards, 16 touchdowns and six interceptions. His 86.6 passer rating ranks 19th among 32 qualified quarterbacks, per Next Gen Stats, while Rodgers' 6.2 yards per attempt ranks 26th. Rodgers' EPA/dropback, a measurement for the average amount of expected points added on dropbacks from a quarterback, ranks 29th among 32 quarterbacks.

Rodgers' completions have primarily featured dump-offs. Rodgers' 7 air yards per attempt ranks fourth-lowest in the NFL this season, per Next Gen Stats, and his 36.4% rate of downfield passing (10+ air yards) ranks last in the league.

How much will other clubs view this as a sign of Rodgers' age or unwillingness to run plays? How much will they view this as reflecting the Steelers' cast around him and perhaps the coaching and play-calling deficiencies of which he's accused McCarthy?

Earlier this month, a high-ranking executive from a team that played Rodgers this season characterized the quarterback as "pretty good."

"He wasn't against us, but he's pretty good," the executive told Yahoo Sports. "He can still throw it as good as anybody in the league. And he's got a quick mind and still moves around a little bit. I didn't see anything that would tell me he can't play anymore."

Expect that executive to not stand alone in his assessment.

This question seemed of most interest to executives, talent evaluators and coaches after Rodgers unleashed his allegations. To consider what teams would sign Rodgers, let's start with which teams will not. Teams with established and healthy starting quarterbacks will not sign a declining, disgruntled player on the cusp of his 43rd birthday. Teams outside the range of realistically making the playoffs are also unlikely to waste their time managing a quarterback who plans to retire after this season — nor would Rodgers likely want to join a team with whom he cannot contend.

So which teams on track to make the playoffs, or contend for a final spot, could make sense? Six of the eight division leaders as of Thursday night do not currently need a quarterback: That's the Buffalo Bills, Denver Broncos, Jacksonville Jaguars, Cincinnati Bengals, Chicago Bears and Carolina Panthers. (An injury could make those teams interesting.) The San Francisco 49ers certainly don't need a quarterback when Brock Purdy is healthy. And even if Purdy needs to rest his sprained ankle, there's reason to believe the 49ers' second-string Mac Jones has more to offer than Rodgers, particularly for a team that notoriously revolves around head coach Kyle Shanahan's play-calling system.

The New York Giants are currently patching together a system with J.J. McCarthy and Jameis Winston, but at least some in the league don't believe Rodgers and Giants head coach John Harbaugh would mesh. Harbaugh's team-first messaging hardly aligns with Rodgers' McAfee sound-off.

The Cleveland Browns and Minnesota Vikings are each on track for wild-card positions without clear stability at quarterback, while the New England Patriots are on the bubble and fading in the aftermath of quarterback Drake Maye's injury. The Baltimore Ravens also are intriguing given they've lost two quarterbacks for the season and play the Steelers twice more this year (imagine Rodgers wanting revenge!), but Baltimore's playoff chances currently rest at 6%, per Next Gen Stats, and could fall to 2% if it loses on Sunday to the Houston Texans.

4) Given all of that, who is the most likely to sign Rodgers?

There's a reason to take the field against any team if betting. But executives and coaches across the league seem more suspicious of the Patriots' interest than they are of any other team.

Sources believe newly acquired Kirk Cousins fits the Vikings better than Rodgers, and Rodgers' distraction level and subpar play would be a tough sell for a Browns team that's exceeding expectations with Deshaun Watson at the helm.

Expect the Patriots to give in-house Tommy DeVito a full game with practice reps before looking outside their organization for help. But DeVito's 12-of-24 passing (50%) for 81 yards, one touchdown, one interception and four sacks in a 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions two weeks ago did not inspire confidence. The circumstances were unideal, in the aftermath of Maye fracturing his right fibula, per ESPN, while abroad in Germany.

The Patriots visit the 1-9 Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. While that should challenge DeVito less than an eight-win Lions team did, the Chargers' defense is feisty and a loss could further create questions around Vrabel's recent comments surrounding winning culture. Add to that Rodgers' Green Bay overlap with now-Patriots general manager Eliot Wolf and Patriots receiver Romeo Doubs … front offices around the league are curious, if by no means sure that any move would happen imminently.

5) Say a team wants to consider Rodgers. What would his references say?

Calling the references of a prospective employee who burned his last employer is dicey. Calling McCarthy, in particular, seems like an unproductive task. But Rodgers' head coach immediately prior, longtime Steelers leader Mike Tomlin, shared his perspective Thursday night as part of NBC's halftime show during the Chiefs-Bills game.

Tomlin characterized his primary emotion as "sadness," for multiple reasons including this possibly marking the end of Rodgers' prolific career. Tomlin agreed that Rodgers' McAfee appearance "certainly" shocked him — while also giving Rodgers credit for the relationships the quarterback built last season upon arriving in Pittsburgh.

"He was beloved and I'm not overexaggerating that," Tomlin said. "He worked at it and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates. And particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years, and at times they lose a little patience for the process or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys.

"Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real natural way."

That didn't keep Tomlin from acknowledging the unprecedented nature of Rodgers' week.

"On the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large," Tomlin said, "to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum, those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football."

#2597. Alejandro Garnacho's Premier League career may be over as Aston Villa loan descends into farce

The Argentine winger has already fallen out of favour under Unai Emery, and could spend the next six months in limbo

"We are delighted with Alejandro," Unai Emery said at Garnacho's official presentation as an Aston Villa player. "He is so talented, young and he showed us his wish to help our project. We are really happy." Garnacho, meanwhile, expressed his belief that he'd picked the perfect place to make a fresh start.

"I was looking for a club to get confidence at and to try to be the player I was in my first years at Manchester United," he said. "I spoke with the manager and I think he will give me the confidence to be here and to help the team." There was no question that Garnacho needed a manager to put an arm around him after an underwhelming debut year at Chelsea, who paid £40m to sign the Argentina international from United in the summer of 2025.

Emery has a proven track record for improving young players, including Morgan Rogers at Villa, and Garnacho's arrival was seen as a cost-effective way to bolster the attack after the England international's departure to Chelsea. Johan Manzambi was signed as Rogers' direct replacement in the No.10 slot, but the expectation was that Garnacho would get the chance to nail down a role on the wing and revive his fledgling career.

Here we are at the end of November, though, and Garnacho has already been cut from Emery's "project". The 22-year-old joined Villa on loan with a conditional option to buy for a reported £42.5m based on appearances, but he can't even get in the matchday squad anymore, and his future in the Premier League is now in serious jeopardy.

While Garnacho has obviously not done enough to convince Emery of his worth, it's also fair to say he was sold a dream. In normal circumstances, he wouldn't be completely written off at such an early stage, but Villa have again fallen into a trap that has left them putting financial security ahead of player welfare.

Emery initially used Garnacho as a late substitute in Villa's opening games of the season, but he quickly fell further down the pecking order

Garnacho has only featured in seven games across all competitions for Villa, all off the bench, with the United academy graduate clocking just 95 minutes on the pitch in total. After missing the UEFA Super Cup final due to a concussion sustained in pre-season, he made three late Premier League cameos as Villa opened their campaign with a 4-0 loss at Brighton, a 1-0 home defeat to Arsenal and a 0-0 draw with newly-promoted Hull City.

Former Villa left-back Stephen Warnock accused Garnacho of looking "completely disinterested" when covering the Hull fixture for Sky Sports, and he was an unused substitute in their next three outings, against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Nottingham Forest in the league and Coventry in the third round of the League Cup.

When asked about Garnacho's lack of playing time, Emery publicly challenged Garnacho to do more, saying: "[He has to] continue working. Work, work, train, work. When he can have minutes to play, try and play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now. George [Hemmings] is playing fantastic. Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well. We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind, because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs."

Considering Villa paid a combined total of £57m to sign Alysson and Mbaye in the summer, it was understandable that Emery favoured them over Garnacho, but the fact that he was also behind Hemmings, a 19-year-old academy prospect who only played two Premier League games for Villa last term, spoke volumes. Villa were still winless in the league at that stage, too, and yet Emery never considered that Garnacho might add something different in attack.

Emery did make an effort to bring Garnacho up to speed with his methods, but ultimately decided he still couldn't trust him with a bigger role

Garnacho remained rooted to the bench as Villa wrapped up their September schedule with a 3-2 victory at Tottenham, and Emery took drastic action to try and get him up to speed as the international break took effect. As reported by The Telegraph, the Chelsea loanee underwent an intense "mini pre-season" at Villa's Bodymoor Heath training base, with Emery and his staff putting him through a series of individual tactical sessions.

Emery also held several one-on-one meetings with Garnacho, who scored in friendly wins over Southampton and Sevilla, and he was deemed to be making progress. Garnacho's belief seemed to return, too, as he sent a "ready now" message to his followers on Instagram after the latter contest.

However, he still didn't get a look-in during Villa's first competitive game back, a 2-2 draw with Brentford. In fact, Garnacho has only seen three minutes of Premier League action over the last two months, in a 1-1 stalemate against Fulham at Villa Park, and didn't even make Emery's matchday squad for encounters against Newcastle, Manchester City, his former club Man Utd, and Sunderland.

Garnacho did play in Villa's respective 6-0 and 3-1 wins over Fenerbahce and Viking in the Champions League, but only came on after both games were effectively over as contests, and was introduced for the final half hour of a 3-0 Carabao Cup defeat to Bournemouth when Emery's side were already two goals down. There were some positive signs in the Viking game as Garnacho recorded three shots in a lively display, which Emery described as his "best minutes" in a Villa shirt, but it did not lead to any change in his situation.

Garnacho seems to have reached the point of no return at Villa already after a particularly embarrassing omission from Champions League action

If Garnacho was still under any illusions about Emery's opinion of him, that will no longer be the case after the manager's definitive statement on Tuesday night. Despite having the option to name 12 substitutes for the Lions' trip to Galatasaray, Emery instead selected only 11 - including two goalkeepers.

"Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us," Emery said bluntly after seeing Villa go down 1-0 in Istanbul. In a swift response, Garnacho removed all traces of Aston Villa from his Instagram account, even going so far as to replace his profile picture with an "egg", and pinned an image of him holding the FA Cup trophy after Man Utd's 2024 final victory to the top of his page.

Although the best course would have been no response at all, Garnacho could be forgiven for feeling angry or hurt. Emery will have known full well just how humiliating such a brutal decision would be for Garnacho, but did it all the same. Tammy Abraham has also fallen out of favour with the Spaniard, but he made the bench for the trip to Turkey. There was no good footballing reason to leave Garnacho at home, especially when you consider that Villa have now failed to score in four of their last six matches.

When Villa were chasing the game against Galatasaray, having Garnacho as an option to come on and run at the defence would have been useful. What was the point in signing him in the first place? Emery has a duty of care to Garnacho after making the effort to bring him to Villa Park that he is completely forsaking.

"It's mad, Unai talks about he's got the run of the mill at Aston Villa," former Villa defender Liam Ridgewell has said on talkSPORT. "He's signing the players and bringing them in, no one else is, no sporting directors. He's the one who is picking these players, Harvey Elliott and now Garnacho, what have both of them come in and suddenly done to put them out of the team?"

This is the second time in as many seasons that a talented young player has been forced onto the sidelines at Villa Park

The parallels with Elliott are impossible to ignore. The Liverpool midfielder joined Villa on loan after playing a starring role in England's run to glory at the 2025 U21 European Championship, with an obligation to buy for £35m included in the deal if he made 10 appearances.

Emery decided early on that they did not want to sign Elliott outright, and so he was restricted to just nine appearances across the entire season. The Villa boss described the saga as "embarrassing for everyone involved" in May and added: "To now explain about the reason for this decision is very difficult, or it is easy, but it is not the moment. My apologies for Harvey Elliott are, every day, in my mind."

Those words would have meant little to Elliott after a year of misery that zapped him of confidence and match fitness. He was loaned out again at the start of September, this time to La Liga strugglers Valencia, and it's entirely possible that the 23-year-old's vast potential will now go unfulfilled.

Garnacho is in a similar position because Emery clearly learned nothing from the Elliott deal. Former Villa striker Gabby Agbonlahor fiercely opposed the club's summer swoop for Garnacho, insisting he's "not a good player", but is among those to have been baffled by Emery's treatment of the youngster.

"Why wouldn't you put him on the bench and not bring him on? What are you wasting? Wages? What are you wasting on the loan fee?" Agbonlahor said on talkSPORT. "You talk about season ticket prices going up at Aston Villa for fans that have to fork out so much money and then you go and blow (money on Garnacho). So much as the manager has done a fantastic job at Aston Villa, but recruitment, two seasons in a row, (Harvey) Elliott, Garnacho, what player is going to want to come on loan for Aston Villa?"

It's in Villa's best interests that Garnacho stays in limbo now that Emery has deemed him surplus to requirements, or else they risk falling afoul of UEFA regulations

Just two days after selling Rogers to Chelsea for £117m, Villa sealed the Garnacho loan, with The Athletic reporting that Emery was the "key advocate" of the deal. He wanted a pacey, direct forward who could operate on both flanks, and felt he could "refine the raw materials" that made Garnacho such an exciting prospect in his United days.

It was seen as a low-risk rehabilitation project for a player Chelsea were desperate to offload, and Villa did not have the immediate upfront cash to look elsewhere for a winger of similar pedigree and still comply with the Premier League and UEFA's financial regulations. Because both Villa and Chelsea were operating under UEFA financial settlement agreements after previous breaches, Villa couldn't simply spend the £117m Rogers windfall freely.

Taking Garnacho on loan deferred the amortisation of the £42.5m transfer fee to a future accounting year and kept Villa compliant with UEFA's 70% Squad Cost Ratio rules for the 2026-27 campaign. Meanwhile, the appearance-based obligation ensured Villa retained some control, as UEFA automatically scrutinises permanent transfers - or unconditional loan-to-buy deals - between the same clubs within a 45-day period as potential swap deals. UEFA bars player-swap accounting that inflates or distorts sales figures, but Villa purposely structured the move separately to protect how their incoming transfer revenue was treated.

At the time, ex-Villa CEO Christian Purslow said the Garnacho loan put both clubs in "regulatory minefield territory". From a Villa perspective, triggering the buy option would force them to offset that spending with further player sales or Champions League revenue, so they have to be certain about Garnacho to tie him down to a proposed four-year contract. As it is, Emery has seemingly already decided he is not worth the hassle, and so the winger now faces the same spell in limbo that Elliott did.

"UEFA have very strict rules where clubs are buying players that are moving in both directions and specifically, if they decided those transactions are related, then they can effectively deduct the profits of one from the other," Purslow explained on Sky Sports this week. "Now we all know that Morgan Rogers' sale by Villa generated massive profits for the club. But with their challenges of complying with financial rules and regulations, they absolutely did not want to have those profits reduced by UEFA taking the view that Garnacho was a related deal, so it was structured as a loan.

"UEFA aren't stupid; pretending that it's not a transfer by saying 'loan him now and have him next summer', UEFA would capture that, so they [Villa] had very specific rules. They're really trying to make sure that loan is very conditional; in other words, it might not happen. It looks as though Garnacho will have to make a certain number of appearances. Aston Villa will be arguing to UEFA that he may not make those appearances, in which case it's not related and you absolutely can't reduce our FFP profits.

"There are people who don't like those structures, it can be very harsh on the footballer. He's gone there to get his career back on track, and Aston Villa have got a financial and economic incentive not to play him so that they don't have to give Chelsea £40-45m. Some people don't like those structures but they are a direct consequence of the rules and regulations."

The ultimate blame must lie with Emery. He pushed the club for the Garnacho signing and convinced the player it was the right move for his development. Performing such a swift U-turn instead of affording Garnacho the patience he didn't give Elliott raises serious question marks over Emery's judgement and empathy.

The Argentine has admitted he could have handled things differently at Old Trafford, where he went from fan favourite to villain in the space of six months

There's a real danger that United's last FA Cup success will be the peak of Garnacho's career. He was on the scoresheet as the Red Devils beat arch-rivals Man City at Wembley, ultimately finishing the season with 17 goal involvements in 50 appearances - a mightily respectable feat for a 19-year-old. His numbers in the following campaign were similarly impressive, but the same could not be said of his performances, and his minutes dwindled as then-manager Ruben Amorim publicly questioned his attitude.

The situation reached the point of no return when Garnacho was omitted from United's Europa League final starting lineup, and he came out to criticise Amorim for the decision, backed up by his brother Roberto, who claimed on social media that the forward had been "thrown under the bus". Amorim then told Garnacho to find another club, and he ended up at Chelsea.

Had he shown more maturity, Garnacho would probably still be a United player now. He's been big enough to accept responsibility for his actions, though, saying to Sky Sports in April when asked if he regrets the way he left Old Trafford: "Maybe yes, because I loved that club. They gave me the confidence from the start. From Spain, to bring me to the academy, then they bring me to the first team. So it was like four or five years, and amazing love from everyone.

"In the last six months I was just not playing like before at Manchester United. I started to be on the bench, it's not a bad thing. I was only 20 years old, but in my mind it was like I had to play every game. In my mind, maybe it is also on me, I started to do some bad things."

A frustrating first year at Chelsea obviously prompted some introspection. The grass was certainly not greener for Garnacho at Stamford Bridge, where he registered eight goals and four assists across 43 appearances but made the starting XI only 22 times. Garnacho was particularly poor in the Premier League, scoring just once while coming under scrutiny for his lack of defensive awareness.

Former Blues head coach Liam Rosenior never had any concerns over Garnacho's ability or application levels, though. "He's got huge ability and potential. For any young player, the biggest thing to be challenged on is consistency," Rosenior said in March. "But he's shown really good signs - not just in training, but in meetings - that he's on a really good track."

Eight months on, Garnacho's Premier League future looks non-existent. For all his flaws, that's an indictment of Villa's muddled transfer policy more than him. Fabrizio Romano has reported that clubs from the Saudi Pro League have begun making "calls" over a winter deal for Garnacho, with it possible that Chelsea could try to cut his loan at Villa short. That would be a lucrative path for the Villa outcast, but could also spell the end of his time at the top level in both the club and international game.

Garnacho was once billed as a potential generational talent, and even won the Puskas Award for his stunning bicycle kick against Everton in the Premier League back in November 2023. It's a great shame he's in such a mess, but it's not all his own making. Villa have let Garnacho down, not the other way around, and their reputation will suffer the most damage when he inevitably departs the West Midlands.

#2595. Royce Lewis trade grades: Dodgers land former No. 1 pick; Twins get another arm, arrow-up prospect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have added a former No. 1 overall pick. The Dodgers are set to acquire infielder Royce Lewis from the Minnesota Twins for right-hander Bobby Miller and minor-league catcher Francisco Espinoza, reports the New York Post. Neither team has announced the trade.

Lewis, 27, was a candidate to be non-tendered prior to Friday's deadline. Rather than cut him loose, the Twins were able to find a trade partner and receive something in return. The No. 1 pick in the 2017 draft has battled injuries throughout his career and posted a .288 on-base percentage the last three years. Lewis simply failed to launch with Minnesota.

The Dodgers figure to use Lewis as a platoon partner for Max Muncy at third base and could also move him around the infield as a utility guy. The Twins moved him from third base to first base this past season. Lewis has played every infield position in the big leagues, though he's had only one inning at shortstop since 2022.

Miller, 27, has been unable to build on his dynamic 2022 rookie season, when he threw 124 ⅓ innings with a 3.76 ERA. He has battled injuries and control issues since then, and the Dodgers moved him into the bullpen this past season. Miller has a 7.75 ERA in 134 ⅔ Triple-A innings the last three years and can be optioned down in 2027.

Espinoza, 19, reached Low Class-A in 2026 and hit .317/.411/.422 with three home runs and strong contact rates in 46 games. He does not rank among the top 30 Dodgers prospects at Baseball America or MLB Pipeline, but Espinoza is an arrow-up prospect and a solid return for a non-tender candidate.

Here now are our grades for the two-for-one trade.

At worst, Lewis will be a high-priced utility guy next season. He's projected to make $5 million or so through arbitration and that simply is not much for the Dodgers, who have a history of getting underperforming hitters to the next level (like Muncy). At best, Lewis could be the new Chris Taylor and reach his offensive ceiling while bouncing between positions.

Espinoza is a good prospect, not a great prospect, and Miller is a reclamation project. Those are easy players for the Dodgers to surrender to take a chance on Lewis and his upside. It may not work. Lewis could continue to get hurt and not hit, but it was a low-cost move and the chance of a reward is significant.

It's a very nice upside play for a team that has hit on a lot of upside plays over the year.

It's a bummer things didn't work out for Lewis and the Twins, but the reality is he was a non-tender candidate, and it wasn't a secret. Minnesota was able to get back a solid prospect in Espinoza and a lottery ticket arm in Miller despite having little leverage. Getting two players for Lewis is a very good outcome under the circumstances.

Giving each team an "A" suggests a win-win, and maybe it will be. There's a chance it's a lose-lose, though. Lewis may not hit, Miller may never rediscover his 2022 form, and Espinoza may not pan out. I see the vision for both teams, though and like it.

The Dodgers rolled the dice on a talented player and the Twins were able to fetch two players for someone they might have otherwise cut loose and sent into free agency.

#2594. Kyrie Irving to the Jazz? Why Utah's reported interest in the star Mavericks guard makes no sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NBA teams are remarkably diligent. They will consider almost any path to improving their rosters, no matter how obscure or unexpected. Still, every now and then, a truly bizarre nugget hits the rumor mill and forces us to consider what exactly a team is thinking.

On Thursday, one such rumor arrived as SNY's Ian Begley reported that the Utah Jazz have given Kyrie Irving "internal consideration as a potential trade candidate." Now, this is common. Teams will do due diligence on a wide variety of players leading up to transaction periods in order to make sure they've covered their bases, and Begley gives no indication that there have even been talks between the Jazz and the Dallas Mavericks. Still, as he notes, "you're not gonna spend a lot of time on a player if you don't have any interest in him, so the idea of Utah spending some time internally on Kyrie Irving was interesting."

So, let's consider this rumor in earnest. The Jazz entered this season with playoff expectations after four straight years in the lottery. They are 3-13 due to a combination of injuries, players adjusting to a new roster and simply poor performance. Utah has shown a willingness to trade for players outside of its perceived timeline before. The Jazz looked at then-33-year-old Jrue Holiday early in their rebuild in 2023, for instance, but backed off when Holiday's camp reportedly made it clear he would not be interested in extending.

Irving, still a star-caliber scorer, has the Mavericks at 8-7 through 15 games. He's averaging over 22 points on roughly his standard efficiency for a Dallas team with pretty limited shooting around him. We can't say at this stage whether or not the Mavericks are willing to trade him. The notion that they might depends on the team's asset deficit (Dallas does not control its own first-round pick again until 2031) and the 15-year age gap between Irving and franchise player Cooper Flagg, but Dallas could easily elect to simply build off this early success.

If they do take the long view and consider trade offers, Irving could absolutely help a team trying to win right now. Plenty of teams potentially looking for individual shot-creation, like the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets and Miami Heat, could be planning pursuits of the future Hall of Famer.

The question here is why the Jazz, specifically, would be interested in Irving, because on paper, there is perhaps not a single, high-profile player who makes less sense for this roster than he does. Utah's young core revolves around three perimeter players: Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey. The Jazz are so strong on that front that Bailey came off the bench to start the season, and it's unclear how exactly they plan to handle their starting five when Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. return from injuries. If Utah isn't comfortable with Jackson playing center full time, and the Memphis Grizzlies certainly weren't, then one of those five players either needs to get traded or come off the bench.

Adding Irving to this logjam doesn't make sense. Neither does trading one of those players for Irving. George is 23. Bailey is 20. Peterson is 19. Teams that are 10 games below .500 simply don't trade foundational pieces for players a decade or more their senior. They gave up three first-round picks for Jackson largely to improve their defense, and now that Walker Kessler plays for the Los Angeles Lakers, his presence matters more than ever.

Markkanen is the obvious trade candidate of the group, but he's still five years younger than Irving and plays a less saturated position. If Utah viewed Markkanen's max contract as a negative it needed to escape, that would be one thing, but there's just no evidence at this stage that this is the case. They have rebuffed trade interest in Markkanen at every turn. If Dallas were willing to put substantial draft equity on the table to cover the age and positional gaps here, there could perhaps be a conversation, but Dallas isn't in a position to do so.

There's some merit to the idea that Utah might eventually want to shake up its backcourt. There were rumors during the draft process that Peterson's representatives were skeptical of Utah as a landing spot because they also represent George and felt that two score-first guards would clash. Even if the Jazz were prepared to split them up less than 20 games into Peterson's career, Irving himself has typically fared far better when he has been paired with a high-level passer. He won his championship with LeBron James. He's thriving next to Cooper Flagg now. His best trait is, and always has been, his scoring.

And then, of course, there is the history shared between Irving and Utah's top executive. The CEO of the Jazz is Danny Ainge, who once traded for Irving when he ran the Boston Celtics. Before his second season in Boston, Irving publicly shared plans to re-sign with the Celtics as a free agent in 2019. When the time came, he instead joined the Brooklyn Nets, a divisional opponent. This is the NBA. If LeBron James can reunite with Dan Gilbert, any player-executive reunion is theoretically possible. Nonetheless, Ainge and Irving would seemingly be among the unlikeliest pairings in all of basketball. Put all of this together and this is a puzzling rumor to say the least.

Sometimes a rumor says more about a team's big-picture plans than it does a specific target. For a variety of reasons, some of which we've covered, it seems exceedingly unlikely that the Jazz are going to trade for Irving. However, they've invested the time in considering it, as Begley noted. That means something, even if it doesn't mean a trade is coming.

The simplest read on this is that Utah is concerned enough about its short-term prospects that it is considering investing in win-now help despite its 3-13 start. That, in itself, makes sense. The Jazz don't control their own first-round pick this season. They have no incentive to lose, and while making the postseason despite starting the season 10 games under .500 is improbable, it just happened a year ago when the 4-14 Charlotte Hornets recovered quickly enough to reach the Play-In Tournament. The Jazz are 5.5 games out of the No. 10 seed in the Western Conference right now. If they get healthy in time and make the right addition, perhaps they could still make a real run at it.

Skepticism about the George-Peterson fit, for now, should be on the back burner. Though the two fared far better early on when they played separately, both, at least for now, have better net ratings and true shooting percentages in the minutes they've shared than the minutes they haven't. George's usage skyrockets when he plays without Peterson, but that's to be expected with Markkanen and Jackson out.

There may have been concern early in the season, and that might have been when Irving crossed Utah's mind. There may still be concerns down the line when the Jazz have had a longer sample size to evaluate the pairing with the rest of their roster. For now, though, it's simply too early to consider splitting up such a talented tandem, especially right as the team has actually started winning some games.

However, ball-handling behind them is a valid concern. Utah declined its fourth-year option on backup point guard and former first-round pick Isaiah Collier, and the offense has been 6.5 points per 100 possessions worse with him on the floor this season. Adding a veteran backup point guard, if only to ease Peterson's burden during the minutes George rests, would be sensible. Irving is obviously no backup, but as perhaps the most notable point guard theoretically on the market, it makes sense that the Jazz would at least broach the concept internally.

Ainge hasn't earned the nickname "Trader Danny" for nothing. His teams are almost always at the center of the trade market, and as last year's Jackson deal proved, he's as capable of a stunner as he's ever been. Irving would certainly qualify as one. We shouldn't expect it. It wouldn't really make sense based on what we know now. But in the post-Luka Dončić trade NBA, it would be hard to dismiss basically any rumor involving a player of this stature.

#2593. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2592. MLB rumors: Yankees moves heating up, plus latest on Tarik Skubal, Mets, Padres, Red Sox, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near-certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free-agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Friday's supply just below.

The buzz at the GM Meetings last week was that the Mets offered top free agent Tarik Skubal a nine-year contract worth almost $400 million, reports MLB Network Radio. If the deal is worth at least $390 million, it would set new records for total guarantee and average annual value given to a pitcher. Here are the current pitcher contract records:

Given the player and the deep-pocketed teams involved in the bidding (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), Skubal is well-positioned to shatter Yamamoto's record. He could beat Scherzer's and Verlander's record as well. The expected lockout will begin after the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Skubal is likely to sign before then.

The Diamondbacks are set to acquire righty Johan Oviedo from the Red Sox for minor-league lefty Luke Dotson and a player to be named later, reports the Arizona Republic. Boston had four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Oviedo, Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck) and always seemed likely to trade one to ease the logjam.

Acquired from the Pirates last offseason, Oviedo made just one ineffective appearance around elbow trouble in 2026. He returned from Tommy John surgery in 2025 and looked excellent, and Arizona will hope Oviedo rediscovers that magic as he gets further away from his injuries. Dotson is not a top prospect. It's a low-cost flier for the D-backs.

The Tigers have signed right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year extension worth $46.5 million, reports ESPN. There is a club option for a seventh year and escalators can push the total guarantee to $80 million. Melton still had five years of team control. The new extension buys out his five team control years and one free agent year with an option for another free agent year.

Melton, 26 next month, missed the start of the season with elbow inflammation and finished the season on the injured list with more elbow woes. Between injuries, he made 20 starts with a sub-3.00 ERA with strong under-the-hood numbers. The Tigers know him better than anyone and are obviously comfortable with Melton's medicals to lock him up long-term.

The New York Yankees have agreed to a two-year contract with veteran right-hander Jonathan Loáisiga, ESPN reports. The deal also includes a club option for 2029 and is worth roughly $18 million, according to MLB.com.

Loáisiga, 32, is coming off that strong season above for the Arizona Diamondbacks, and for his career boasts an ERA+ of 128 across parts of nine MLB seasons. He's worked in relief for almost all of that span, and eight of those nine seasons came with the Yankees.

New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman was recently asked if he'd be willing to play Spencer Jones in center field. In response, he told media, including SNY, this:

"I would be comfortable with that. At the same time Jasson Domínguez is pounding the ball in winter ball. The entire industry is noticing that based on the phone calls I'm getting."

The 23-year-old Domínguez still has big-time power potential, and defensively he's best suited to center field. For his career in the Bronx, he has an OPS+ of 93, but his 751 plate appearances have been doled out erratically across four seasons. As things stand now, he'll once again be subject to a playing-time crunch. Aaron Judge and Cody Bellinger are installed at the outfield corners, and Giancarlo Stanton, if healthy, should get much of the playing time at DH. That leaves center field for Jones or Domínguez. Other teams no doubt see that bottleneck and are seeing if Cashman and the Yankees are willing to relieve it through trade.

Lefty ace and two-time American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal remains far and away the top talent on the free-agent market. While the New York Mets and incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers seem like the favorites to secure his services, the San Diego Padres also have significant interest in him. That interest took the next step on Thursday with an in-person meeting, The Athletic reports. The Padres are the fourth team to meet with Skubal, who turned 30 on Friday. Previously, the Dodgers, Mets, and Toronto Blue Jays met with him.

The Padres have a pronounced need in the rotation, especially if free-agent right-hander Michael King signs elsewhere. Last winter, they also lost Dylan Cease to the Blue Jays via free agency.

The Padres and left-handed platoon hitter Gavin Sheets have agreed to a three-year, $11 million contract extension that includes two opt-outs, FanSided reports. Sheets, who'll turn 31 in April, had been slated for free agency after the upcoming season. Instead, he and the Padres will now be potentially committed through the 2029 season, depending on whether Sheets exercises any of his opt-outs. While he's not much of a hitter for average, he does draw walks and hit for power. In two seasons with San Diego, he's tallied 36 home runs and 44 doubles in 855 at-bats while seeing DH, first base, and the outfield corners.

The New York Mets have agreed to a three-year, $12 million deal with right-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández, reports José F. Rivera.

Hernández, who turns 30 in December, hasn't pitched in MLB since 2022 and instead has revived his career with four strong seasons in Japan. Over that span for Softbank of the NPB, he's put up an ERA of 2.46 in 131 ⅔ innings with 168 strikeouts and 42 unintentional walks. Prior to rebuilding himself in Japan, Hernández had a 5.06 ERA and a 1.82 K/BB ratio over parts of four seasons with the Boston Red Sox.

The NBA season started one month ago today. The first stanza of the campaign brought a great deal of excitement at the top of the league with superstars doing superstar things and most of the projected championship contenders getting off to hot starts. But we also saw injuries, a disappointing first handful of games from Mikal Bridges and an Eastern Conference that is not nearly as dominant as it was supposed to be.

Those are three of the biggest letdowns of the young season. Here's our John Gonzalez on why Bridges might be the greatest dud of any individual player:

Another major disappointment: The Kings. How can a team underperform expectations when those expectations are already about as low as they come? Well, Sacramento sure has found a way. With a 1-13 record and after a puzzling trade, the Kings earned their spot in our ranking of the NBA's most hopeless teams.

The College Football Selection Committee is in love with the SEC. Only one time in three different rankings have the bracket-makers ranked a team from that conference lower than AP Top 25 voters. Whether or not you think it's fair, the numbers largely back it up. In fact, two-loss No. 5 Texas even has a better resume score than undefeated No. 2 Utah! Here's how to watch the biggest games of Week 12 and our picks for each of them:

This is easily the most lopsided week of the NFL season. The Bills and Chiefs are three-score favorites. The Bears and Broncos are also favored by double digits. We put a few of them on upset alert, and a handful of our experts are in agreement that the Lions are among the most vulnerable.

First of all, the Buccaneers have just as much to play for as the Lions. Both of them are locked into tightly contested division battles. The motivation will be there for a Tampa Bay team that could somehow sneak into the playoffs even with a losing record. And then there's the Tampa Bay defense, which has forced at least four turnovers in each of its last three games. Our Tyler Sullivan said it would not surprise him if Jared Goff's interception streak continues.

And even though our Jordan Dajani could not bring himself to pick the upset outright, he does see the Buccaneers keeping this one highly competitive.
