#2589. From bible study groups to Ballers in God: The rise and rise of Christianity in modern football

A growing number of high-profile footballers are both joining the religion and making overt demonstrations of their faith on the pitch and online, but is there something more sinister behind the movement?

"I want to thank my Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ."

That phrase, or some variation of it, has often become the first thing to come out of a player's mouth in a post-match interview of late. We had become accustomed to Christian footballers subtly showing their faith by crossing themselves or pointing towards the heavens in celebration in the modern era, but now we are increasingly seeing much more overt demonstrations of Christianity, in the Premier League and beyond.

While the movement might seem harmless on the face of it, as a community forms among previously disconnected Christian players on and off the pitch, we have also seen this wave of evangelism cause friction and land certain individuals in hot water amid ambiguity over the views that they hold. But what is behind the seemingly unstoppable rise of the religion in football?

We are seeing many more players make overt displays of their Christianity on the pitch and online than ever before

"First of all, I want to thank Jesus Christ, my Lord and Saviour," Manchester City's Rico Lewis said in his post-match interview with TNT Sports after the Champions League victory over AEK Athens in October. "Can't even fathom doing anything without him, so all the glory and honour goes to him." That was just one example of the kind of evangelical Christianity that has become prevalent in the English game in recent years.

Lewis is among a growing cohort of English and Premier League-based players who are increasingly vocal about their faith. Alongside Jeremy Doku and a clutch of other City players, he participates in weekly bible study online, according to The Athletic. Marc Guehi is another team-mate who has been open about his beliefs, the son of a former church minister.

Meanwhile, at Arsenal, a group of Christian evangelical players that includes England internationals Bukayo Saka, Eberechi Eze, Noni Madueke and many others has been dubbed the 'Bible Brothers', also gathering on a regular basis to discuss passages of scripture. That was something that was replicated among members of the Three Lions camp at Euro 2024.

There was an unprecedented moment at the end of England's World Cup third-place playoff clash against France in the summer that reflected the relentless growth of this movement among players, as stars from both sides including Saka, Eze and Guehi gathered together in an impromptu prayer circle on the pitch after the full-time whistle.

Away from post-match interviews, social media has increasingly become a platform for these footballers to convey their message. Doku regularly captions his posts using relevant bible verses, Saka often uses the hashtag #GodsPlan and has the moniker 'God's Child', Jurrien Timber will cryptically reference bible passages and Madueke's Instagram bio reads "Follower of Jesus Christ!".

Dr Graham Daniels, a former Cambridge United player and general director of the charity Christians in Sport, believes this is the new normal. "The era that any of our young professionals live in now is an era where you have Instagram," he tells GOAL. "Your life story is told on Instagram. That's how it is. These just happen to be very famous young men who have millions of followers.

"Initially, I'd want to say that this simply is the cultural context of our world now. Your life is lived in the public arena via social media. The fundamental thing isn't whether it's a good thing or a bad thing to share your beliefs, whatever they may be, on social media. It just is. It's normative. That's what these people do. That's what these young men do."

Christianity has declined sharply in wider British society, but in the world of football it is alive and well

What's fascinating is that this swelling wave of Christianity within the football sphere doesn't reflect wider British society, where the religion has declined sharply. In the most recent census in 2021, for the first time ever, less than half the population of England and Wales described themselves as 'Christian' (46%, 27.5 million people) - a 13% decrease from the previous survey in 2011 (59%, 33m people).

In the world of football, at least, Christianity is thriving. According to research commissioned by the charity Christians in Sport that was published in the summer, there are Christian players in the first-team squads of 75% of clubs in England and Wales, while half of Premier League clubs reported regular Christian gatherings which are often led by players.

"Professional football is often portrayed as a world shaped by money, fame and performance. What this research reveals is a different story," Daniels said at the time. "Across the professional game, Christian players are gathering to pray, study the Bible and support one another.

"Perhaps the most striking finding is that, in an environment where identity is constantly tested by success, failure and public scrutiny, many players are looking beyond football itself for meaning, purpose and security. Christianity is not disappearing from the professional game; it is far more present than most people realise."

Daniels believes a number of factors have paved the way for this new wave of the faith in football, including the dawn of the Premier League, respected figures in the game becoming Christians, such as Cyrille Regis, and the overall progression to a more empathetic culture. "When the Premier League came in 1992, that was a sea change in terms of international footballers. There was a whole new dynamic of people who had Christian faith, and Muslims and Christians particularly, who didn't find it culturally difficult at all to express their faith," he tells GOAL.

"There were a handful of really good professionals, not necessarily superstar pros, but very good professionals who said they were Christians. That was a pretty unorthodox thing to do, but their team-mates saw that they remained good professionals, good at their job and good blokes. They had their weaknesses and strengths, but they were good pros and good men in the changing room.

"Finally, there's just been a change in culture. We're in a postmodern world and it's a therapeutic world, and everyone's free to say how they feel. You really can't bully very easily anymore, and rightly so. It's a much more comfortable environment to express your inner emotions in a way that would never have happened 15 years ago."

Dr Graham Daniels was one of very few Christian sportspeople when he found the religion early in his playing career at Cambridge United

Daniels was something of a trailblazer in English football, laying a foundation for the many Christian footballers who enjoy such visibility at the highest level today. The 64-year-old came to the religion during his time at Cambridge United in the 1980s - a time when there were very few openly-religious players anywhere in the game.

"I came to faith, really, because I'd been to Cardiff City as a kid and studied there while I was at university, while at the club," he says. "I moved to Cambridge to play, so I was away from home for the first time in my adult life, really away. Of course, I was in the sharp end of football.

"I'd done philosophy as an undergraduate, so I read quite a lot about a range of things and stumbled upon reading defences of the Christian faith, evidence and historical evidence. Somewhere in that window of a year or two, I started going to church. I've kept going ever since."

Life as a Christian footballer then was a stark contrast to what it is now. "I really did think I was the only one," Daniels continues. "It sounds a bit absurd and a bit full of hubris to say it, but I could say it then because every Saturday you'd play against people you'd met over the years through games, reserve games and youth games.

"I'd ask, 'Any Christians here?' I never got a positive response from anyone. Then a chap showed up at Cambridge who had founded Christians in Sport. He came to my club. He asked whether I knew there were Christians in the Football League. I said, 'No, there really aren't'. He said, 'No, there are'. I was thrilled. There were 92 clubs, so I thought this bloke had an organisation and must know. I asked how many there were, and he said, 'Well, four'. I asked who they were. He named three. I said, 'Well, who's the fourth?' He said, 'You!'.

"It was hard. It was a different cultural era. Aggressive, bullying, really hard. If you were slightly different, wore a pair of glasses or something, let alone having some kind of faith or worldview that would set you apart, there was plenty of what we today call micro and macro aggressions that went on. But, of course, you're in a tough world, in a tough game. I was able to navigate that most of the time."

Players like Arsenal's Noni Madueke have expressed concerns over whether this new wave of evangelical Christianity could become performative

Interestingly, the BBC reports that there has been growth in denominations of the religion like Pentecostalism in wider society - the form of evangelical Christianity that many footballers practise - and most evidently in Greater London, where a number of current Premier League stars hail from, which has been "partly driven by immigration". Several of the English players who have become more candid about their faith come from immigrant backgrounds, with the diversification of the Premier League over the years inherently making all religions more visible.

It has been reported by members of the clergy that people are "expressing their faith with more zeal and vigour" than before. "The discourse, the tenor of the conversation, is different in the last two years. We're seeing a greater confidence among active Christians, particularly those who are younger," Dr Rhiannon McAleer, director of research and impact at the Bible Society, told the BBC.

Sceptics will question whether this more vocal form of preaching is performative, in an age where engagement is undeniably a driver of what players will post on social media, while others will argue that this new loud and proud strain of Christianity among footballers has the characteristics of a trend that might eventually pass.

Speaking on the Four8TV YouTube channel in October, Madueke admitted: "With Christianity and the football, it can become a bit performative. I've definitely been there as well, these times where you're gonna be thinking like 'Cool, let me do a caption for God so that maybe next week I'll score again'. I'm being real bro.

"So I feel like it's important to really make sure your heart posture is honouring, 'Yo, I'm just trying to show you guys what he's done for me so that maybe he can do it for you too', not because I'm trying to ram it down your throat or say I'm better than you or say I'm now a pastor. Nah bro, I'm a footballer. I'm a footballer bro. But it has to come from a place of actual genuine love. I genuinely want to see other people experience this type of love. Power in their life. It's difficult to get the balance, for sure."

Meanwhile, City team-mates Lewis and Doku have both revealed that they only recently discovered their faith; the former told The Athletic that he suddenly made the decision to buy a bible in the past year or so, while Doku said in an interview after an impressive display against Liverpool last November: "What changed for me this season, I have God in my life."

In defence of Madueke and his fellow worshippers, evangelism is quite literally defined by sharing the message and teachings of Jesus Christ, and from that perspective it would be remiss not to use a platform where they can collectively reach millions of people almost instantly to spread the Christian gospel. The aim is also to invite others to the faith, and that is seemingly what has happened with both Lewis and Doku.

London City Lionesses and England star Nikita Parris believes she would not have been able to overcome adversity in her early life without God

Background aside, it's not difficult to see why some footballers might turn to God. Considering just how difficult it is to become an elite-level professional footballer in the first place (it has been estimated that just five percent of academy players will go on to play the game at the highest level), you can understand why some might believe there had to have been some divine intervention.

As Dr Daniels said, many are also "looking beyond football itself for meaning, purpose and security", while others are convinced that they would not have been able to overcome setbacks in their lives and playing careers on their own. Speaking on Four8TV, Nottingham Forest defender Ola Aina says: "There's just some things that's happened in life, in our careers, that you couldn't say, 'Yeah, I manufactured that one'. There's just so many things that I could say that I know that's a higher power, that's God man, that wasn't me. I'm just grateful for it because, who knows? If I tried to manufacture that, I could have collapsed my whole journey."

That was echoed by London City Lionesses and England attacker Nikita Parris, who said: "I think I lean on God's understanding more in the bad years of football and the setbacks. I think you never truly understand or comprehend how he has his hand on you until maybe a couple of years down the line you're like, 'Wow, how have I come so far? Inner-city kid, low-income background, single-parent household, four kids, and I'm the one that made it?!'. For me it's crazy. Now I sit back and think, 'Thank God he's on my side'."

Former Tottenham and Crystal Palace midfielder John Bostock founded Ballers in God in 2015

One of the driving forces behind the rise of evangelical Christianity in football, especially online, seems to be the initiative Ballers in God, which was founded by former Tottenham and Crystal Palace midfielder John Bostock, a devout Christian, in 2015. It describes itself as "a global, player-led community dedicated to supporting professional footballers and their partners to know Jesus deeply and grow in their Christian journey", with a mission to "use the global platform of football to make Jesus known".

Their 600 members meet online on a weekly basis to discuss football and their faith and also occasionally gather in person, while there is also a WhatsApp group that is hundreds strong. Several high-profile players seem to be associated with the group including Eze and Semenyo, who both feature in a social media video about 'who Jesus is' to them.

Professional players are invited to apply to join the community on Ballers in God's website, with a form requiring them to enter a list of their former teams, the highest level they've played at and their Instagram handle. A separate page is dedicated exclusively to merch; there you can buy crucifix shinpads and gloves, base layers with 'I belong to Jesus' emblazoned across them and branded grip socks.

"Ballers in God is a pro-to-pro football ministry," Bostock said in an interview with Premier Christianity last year. "We're a disciple-making, soul-winning movement in the beautiful game. It was birthed in 2015 out of a longing in my heart, really. I moved from Spurs and went to Belgium to play for Antwerp. I felt quite isolated in my faith. I prayed: 'God, what do I do?'

"I sensed that if I was struggling, other players must be going through the same thing. So, I called a few players and asked them: 'How do you fancy coming online once a month just to pray, read the word, encourage each other?' When people see Ballers in God, they might see the online brand, but the heartbeat is a community that serves professional players. We've baptised players, won many to the Lord, sowed even more seeds."

He added: "Football breaks down barriers. There's been Christians in the game for years, but now there's a centralised place where their voices can be heard. And because of that, players see other players being bold, and it encourages them to step out. In the UK, there's talk of young people turning back to the Lord, and I think players are recognising that football is an instrument God wants to use."

The rise of evangelical Christianity and questions over the intent of some of its messaging have already caused friction at the highest levels of the game

In the UK and other European countries where Christianity is on the wane, the emergence of this new strain of very public, outspoken Christian evangelism within football has occasionally caused friction. That has usually stemmed from certain players being accused of holding fundamentalist views that emphasise biblical literalism, which can include being against same-sex relationships and abortion.

In English football, the most infamous recent incident came in December 2024 during the Premier League's LGBTQ+ inclusion initiative Rainbow Laces, when then-Crystal Palace player Guehi scrawled 'Jesus loves you' and 'I love Jesus' on his rainbow armband in two separate games, defying the league's rules on displaying religious messages. The defender ultimately avoided punishment.

Speaking during the controversy Guehi's father John, a church minister, suggested that his son was indeed opposed to the campaign. He told the Daily Mail: "Marc said 'Yes' and did the right thing by ­wearing it but people are having a go at him for what he wrote, he accepted to wear the armband, he was just trying to balance the message. He was saying: 'You gave me the armband, as a Christian I don't believe in your cause, but I will put it on.'"

Last summer during Pride Month, Ballers in God posted on social media questioning whether Christian players should have to wear the rainbow armband, writing: "In football, Pride Month often brings pressure to wear rainbow symbols to show solidarity. But what if that celebration clashes with your convictions and the Word of God?...We don't take this stand because we hate. We stand because we honour God over culture. Because the Bible calls all sexual immorality, straight or gay, out of bounds.

"Sometimes, obedience means kindly saying, 'I can't wear that'. This isn't arrogance. It's worship...We don't see the LGBTQ+ community, or anyone, as enemies. We see people deeply loved by God, just like us, all in need of truth and grace. So while many wear the rainbow this month, we choose to wear the cross." The group later welcomed the decision to discontinue the Rainbow Laces campaign, posting: "We prayed. We fasted. And God heard us...True inclusion makes space for different beliefs, without pressure or judgement."

The outspoken nature of this very online movement also clearly has the capacity to rub people up the wrong way, especially in light of the ambiguity surrounding the overarching message. Earlier this month, a social media post by FC Twente's former Manchester United striker Wout Weghorst, that included an image with the message 'I AIN'T FORCING JESUS ON NOBODY. BUT DON'T EXPECT ME TO HIDE MY LOVE FOR HIM' and was reshared by Ballers in God, drew the ire of ex-Germany and Aston Villa midfielder Thomas Hitzlsperger, who responded by writing: "Well said. How do we feel about 'I AIN'T FORCING HOMOSEXUALITY ON NOBODY. BUT DON'T EXPECT ME TO HIDE MY LOVE FOR MEN'?" The tweet would go viral.

In Germany, there was a significant backlash from sections of Borussia Dortmund's support when midfielder Felix Nmecha - who is among those closely connected to Ballers in God - was signed from Wolfsburg in the summer of 2023, with some even protesting outside the stadium. Earlier that year he had shared homophobic and transphobic posts on social media, including one that equated the concept of 'Pride' in the LGBTQ+ movement to the devil.

Felix Nmecha has sparked controversy in Germany by performing a celebration that is linked to a Ballers in God campaign that seems to promote homophobic and transphobic ideas

Three years on, Nmecha has found himself at the centre of another storm that has also thrust Ballers in God and the perceived ambiguity surrounding its intended message into the spotlight. The Dortmund and Germany midfielder landed himself in hot water for performing the 'Crowns Down' celebration, which involves kneeling, symbolically removing an imaginary crown from your head and placing it on the floor.

The gesture is believed to be a nod to Ballers in God's 'The King's Return' campaign that launched ahead of the World Cup. A video on the official website, which appears to be AI-generated, explains: "We all want the crown, a symbol of status, success, recognition and control...But the crown was never ours to keep...And now we have a choice: to hold on to a broken fading crown or place our trust in the king who reigns forever."

While that might seem innocent on the face of it, an investigation by German media outlet ARD found that the campaign's homepage linked out to a live chat carrying The King's Return's crown logo, which provides counselling from US-based digital evangelism ministry Groundwire. It's claimed that counsellors on that platform told ARD's reporters, who used fake names, that homosexuality is a sin and abortion is "Satan's plan".

The chat is still active at the time of writing and can be accessed through a link in the bio of The King's Return's official Instagram page. When GOAL asked a so-called 'coach' about homosexuality, they responded by saying: "Same sex relationships are not God's plan and sinful. We are all born with sinful, defective desires that manifest themselves in various ways, the goal is to not act on them out of love for Christ." They also pointed to the bible verse 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, which condemns homosexuality in the eyes of God. When asked a question about being transgender, the 'counsellor' replied: "God created you and did not make a mistake."

Nmecha's use of the 'Crowns Down' therefore provoked anger from Dortmund's official fan club, which said in a statement that their ire was "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalised because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices". The statement added: "The investigations further reveal connections to an evangelical-charismatic environment [within Ballers in God] where, among other things, extremely conservative positions against homosexuality and transgender identity are advocated."

Amid another backlash from his club's own supporters, the player insisted the celebration "is about laying my 'crown' before the soon coming King and pointing to Jesus" and "was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form". However, he was told by new Germany boss Jurgen Klopp to stop performing the gesture when playing for his national team, and Dortmund planned talks with him at club level.

After netting against Monchengladbach following the November international break, he pivoted to a new celebration, signalling to the crowd and apparently mouthing 'Jesus loves you'. Ballers in God posted about the change on social media, notably removing Dortmund's club badge, sponsor and kit manufacturer from the images.

Nmecha is not the only player to have done the 'Crowns Down' celebration recently; in the Premier League, both Nottingham Forest's Jair Cunha and Fabio Carvalho of Brentford have performed it, but strangely there has been no uproar in response.

Nmecha has been defended by Ballers in God, but there are still questions over what his views are

Daniels, who is connected to Bostock and advocates for the work he has done, insists there would not have been any ill intent behind Nmecha's actions. "Felix was straightforwardly part of the network called Ballers in God," he says. "They're great guys. They're not looking to cause trouble. They work in changing rooms all the time. I think Felix was straightforwardly wanting to join in with celebrating a goal and using it to express his faith.

"I'm absolutely certain there was no malign desire on his part in doing it. I don't know him personally, but absolutely not." Daniels adds: "I think it's an obtuse link from a website to another website, perhaps without enough research. Possibly. That's what I'm guessing."

Amid the furore, Ballers in God felt compelled to release their own statement that seemingly defended Nmecha's actions without directly addressing the accusations of discrimination against LGBTQ+ that had been levelled against them. "At the heart of our community is the belief that Jesus Christ is King and that He is the hope of the world," it read. "We believe the hope found in Him is for everyone, and our desire is to share this message by making Him known.

"We celebrate players who live out their faith privately, as well as those who choose to express it publicly. We are encouraged by player-led movements such as The King's Return, where footballers themselves take the initiative to express their faith in Jesus. Our heart is to support and celebrate their witness and believe everyone should be free to express their faith respectfully, without fear of prejudice or exclusion.

"Our desire is not only to share our hope, but to demonstrate love and respect towards everyone, including those who do not share our beliefs. Our focus has always been, and will always be, to point people to Jesus with grace and love."

Ballers in God have been accused of failing to properly respond to the accusations levelled at them

That follows what appears to be a trend in Ballers in God's external communications: a message of acceptance and that Jesus loves everyone, even those who disagree with the network's views - but it's still not entirely clear what those views actually are as they face accusations of homophobia, transphobia and anti-abortionism.

Jon Holmes, founder of Sports Media LGBT+, an advocacy organisation and digital publication focusing on the LGBTQ+ community in sports, has been left unconvinced. "I think there have been some questionable social media posts that the organisation has put out in the past," he tells GOAL. "When it comes to the LGBTQ part of this, I haven't really seen them address that. They did make a statement in the wake of the Nmecha goal celebration controversy, but it wasn't really directly responding to a lot of the key points that were being raised. I feel it's up to them to decide whether or not they want to make their position clear."

Anti-discrimination in football organisation Kick It Out has reported that there was a 24% rise in reports of homophobic incidents at professional level in the UK in 2025-26, as well as a 23% increase in reports of online abuse. However, Holmes insists it's impossible to draw a correlation between that sharp spike and the growing visibility of evangelical Christianity at the highest levels of the game.

"I think it's just too difficult to try to draw connections there. There is no question about trying to implicate people on the basis of their faith, because that would be discriminatory in itself. Nobody that I've encountered in this whole conversation has wanted to potentially ostracise people on the basis of their faith. That's the last thing that anyone wants. But clearly, there are questions to be raised over what Ballers in God have said in the past, and the fact they're not really saying anything now.

"It's not that long ago, only last year during Pride Month, that they were putting out social media posts about rainbow armbands and celebrating the fact that the Premier League was dropping Rainbow Laces. Now, they haven't done that this year, even though the Premier League has moved on to a different campaign. It's not like it's dropped its LGBTQ inclusion values. Ballers in God are not making those kinds of statements on social media this year, from what I've seen. So there does seem to be a change in strategy.

"What we all just need to be conscious of is trying to understand more about the motivations of the organisations. Everybody ultimately should want the same thing: for there to be no form of discrimination, whether that's against people's faith or against people's sexual orientation or gender identity. If we truly believe in creating a game free from discrimination, then we should be sharing the same ambitions."

Daniels argues that the diversification of football, including more vocal Christians in the game, has created the potential for more friction, albeit he does not believe that tension exists in the changing room. "When you work inside a changing room, all that matters to you when you sign a player is whether he's a good character. You want a new left-back or a cover left-back, 'is he a good left-back?'. That's all you care about. You really don't care what he does in his private life, as long as it's legal. You really don't. No manager cares, no director of football cares, no team-mate cares. Not at all. Your private life is your own business.

"I've been around the game all my working life. I've never seen, especially in the more modern era we're discussing now, homophobia inside changing rooms from Christians or non-Christians. That doesn't mean it's true universally, but it's a case study of one person here. In my time in the game, people are just interested in the player."

Daniels also points to the furore surrounding Guehi and Ipswich captain Sam Morsy, a Muslim, during the Rainbow Laces campaign in 2024. The latter refused to wear the rainbow armband altogether on the grounds of his faith. "It brought into the public square something of real significance in a liberal democracy: freedom of speech and expression. That's the wonder of living in a country where you're expected, and the bar is that you respect all faiths, all sexualities and all ethnicities. It's a mutual respect in a democratic setting. That has to be balanced against the freedom of expression to say, 'Well, I don't actually agree with your perspective there, or your philosophical or sociocultural take on that issue'.

"The art of living a truly human, interactive life is to be able to say, 'Well, we can't agree on that, but let's be sure that, as human beings, we may sometimes have to agree to disagree, even on significantly profound and difficult things'. What's happened here is that one incident has blown up the whole conversation around that issue of mutual tolerance, mutual acceptance and the flexibility to have different opinions. That's a democracy, isn't it?

"This would absolutely never have been a conversation 10 or 20 years ago, because there wouldn't have been more than five people who said they had a Christian faith in professional football. Clearly, what's happening here is that the entrance of not just Christian faith, but Muslim faith and other faiths into the game has meant that the equilibrium between a secular perspective and a religious perspective has shifted. There's a greater equilibrium now and therefore more tension, in a way, that simply wouldn't have existed before."

Bostock believes it is Ballers in God members and other Christians who face persecution for voicing their opinions

GOAL contacted Ballers in God for a comment on the 'Crowns Down' controversy and allegations against the group but received no response. Bostock has, though, previously addressed the potential backlash to his movement in his interview with Premier Christianity, suggesting that it is members of his network and other Christians who risk being persecuted.

"Scripture speaks about having zeal, but also wisdom," he said. "Not every player has to reveal 'I belong to Jesus' after every single goal. But at the same time, we need to be unashamed of our faith. Was Jesus politically correct? Absolutely not. But the angle he came from was always love, even in his correction.

"We encourage players to be bold. We don't tell them to wear shirts. We have conversations around Pride month. What are our thoughts about the rainbow laces? We talk about these things and pray about them. There will be persecution when you make a stand for Jesus, but he's always worth it."

For now, Ballers in God continue to fly somewhat under the radar in the British media, but Holmes believes that could change as the movement seems to grow unabated. "I think what's played out in Germany is that, even before some of the key individuals connected with the Ballers in God movement signed for their club, Nmecha was already under a degree of scrutiny because of previous social media posts that he shared in the past. That's something that Dortmund have dealt with over time.

"I think maybe because this Crowns Down celebration is still relatively new to the Premier League, that's something we're going to see play out over the course of the coming weeks and months, perhaps. It would be up to those fan groups particularly and the clubs. I expect maybe there have been conversations being had behind closed doors that we're just not aware of yet. Perhaps we will see more of that in the future."

#2588. Luis Gil, Nolan Gorman, Trevor Larnach, more hit MLB free agency after non-tender deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Friday marked the non-tender deadline in Major League Baseball. That important date on the offseason calendar is when clubs must make, or "tender," contract offers for the upcoming season to all their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on the 40-player roster. That's every player who isn't a free agent or isn't presently signed to a multi-year contract. Players who are tendered a contract by that deadline remain with their current organizations. Players who aren't offered a contract become free agents.

Most such decisions are easy and obvious. Others, however, present difficult calls for the organization because of roster crunches, crowded depth charts, or, more commonly, reluctance to retain a player as his salary rises through the arbitration process. While a number of non-tendered players are likely on their way out of the league, a select few others qualify as at least interesting to other teams and, on occasion, a few will even be coveted to varying degrees.

All that sets the stage for what follows, which is our list of the most compelling non-tendered players who are now on the market and available for hire. Let's get to it …

The 2024 AL Rookie of the Year, Gil has been injured and ineffective the last two seasons. He missed time with a shoulder issue this past season and also spent time in Triple-A. The Yankees moved him to the bullpen late in the season to see whether he could contribute that way, though Gil was unable to make a strong impression in that role. Now 28, Gil still has another three seasons of team control remaining. Whichever team signs him will be able to keep him through 2029, and that extra control, plus his Rookie of the Year pedigree, will no doubt land Gil with a new team before Opening Day.

As a 23-year-old in 2023, the infielder and former first-rounder hit 27 home runs in 119 games and looked like a future cornerstone for the Cardinals. Gorman, however, has gotten steadily worse since then thanks largely to his persistent strikeout issues. Last season, he wound up back at Triple-A for an extended stretch and didn't fare any better upon being recalled. Long-term, the Cardinals will likely look to hand the third base position to rising power prospect Jesús Báez, who was recently added to the 40-player roster. Gorman can be a plus at third and probably still get by at second, and no doubt some team will take a chance on his power.

On the downside, Larnach is a defensive minus at the corner outfield spots and probably needs to be a DH, and he's also a platoon bat. On the upside, he's been a steady producer from the left side of the plate. This past season, he put up a .352 OBP and an OPS+ of 120 for Minnesota. For his career, he has an OPS+ of 106 across parts of six MLB seasons. He out-hit his underlying indicators by a bit in 2026, but Larnach is still going to be an appealing part-time bat for some teams.

The Twins cut bait on a right-hander who's made 139 career starts for them since his 2021 big-league debut. Ober boasts a career OPS+ of 102, but that figure has slid over the last two seasons. What's also slid is Ober's fastball velocity, which may be why he's on this list. In his rookie season, he averaged a fringy 92.4 mph with his four-seamer, but last season that figure was down all the way to 88 mph. That put him in the very bottom percentile among MLB hurlers. The 31-year-old Ober still should draw some interest as a depth piece.

A platoon extraordinaire, Raley has always hit for power against righties, including 15 home runs in only 290 plate appearances against them in 2026. He's sneaky fast and a very good athlete for his size (6-foot-3 and 235 lbs.), good enough to handle the corner outfield spots competently. Raley also has first base experience and can patrol center field in a pinch. The Mariners cut him loose even though he will remain under team control through 2028. Raley's power against righties and an extra year of control could make him a solid bench option moving forward.

#2587. Victor Wembanyama has dunked so much he hurt his hand, so he came up with a unique solution: The 'shunk'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Remember at the end of Space Jam, when Michael Jordan launched himself off of the butt of a MonStar to dunk from the half-court line? Well, imagine the exact opposite of that play. Instead of an impossibly long dunk, Thursday night's NBA action gave us an impossibly short jumper.

Let's set the stage here. The San Antonio Spurs are leading the Los Angeles Clippers by 12 points with under four minutes remaining. Victor Wembanyama is alone under the basket. He led the NBA with 71 dunks on the season to that point. Nobody else, as of the beginning of play Thursday, had reached even 50. But Wembanyama does not take this opportunity to slam down dunk No. 72, at least not intentionally. No, San Antonio's Martian with an eight-foot wingspan jumps directly in front of the basket... and flicks his wrist downward in what was seemingly a shooting motion. It swishes through the rim. Two points.

Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8

Officially, it will count as dunk No. 72 on the season for Wembanyama. Unofficially, as coined by Spurs broadcaster Sean Elliott, it was the first "shunk" of his season. Or, well, perhaps anyone's. It takes a perfect storm of circumstances to create a shunk: an uncommonly large basketball player, a lane open enough to ensure no defensive resistance, and perhaps rarest of all, a center disinterested in dunking.

That begs an important question: what compelled this maneuver? Well, as is so often the case, necessity was the mother of invention.

Wembanyama has a blister on his right hand. He doesn't know when exactly it came, but he knows where it came from. "It definitely came from dunking a lot," he told reporters after the game Thursday. The math here checks out. Wembanyama dunked 178 times in 64 games last season. That's around 2.8 dunks per game. Even if we discount the shunk, he's at 71 dunks through 16 games this season, or around 4.4.

Fortunately for the Spurs, Wembanyama has no plans to stop dunking, "but if I can avoid it, I would," he said after the win. The blister, according to Wembanyama, is quite painful. You'd hardly know it from watching him play. Wembanyama is averaging career-highs in points, rebounds, blocks and field goal percentage thus far this season. He is leading a 13-3 Spurs team that is tied for the NBA's best record thus far, and along with Luka Dončić, he is one of the two heavy favorites to win this season's MVP award.

If he's looking for a fringe benefit here, the "shunk" might save him from the "run and just dunk" esque criticism that Giannis Antetokounmpo recevied during his MVP pursuits. This is genuine innovation in the short-distance conversion space. Innovation is rarely in short supply in San Antonio. Earlier this week, Wembanyama threw himself multiple passes off of the backboard in a single quarter. Every time you turn on a Spurs game, there's a real chance Wembanyama does something you've never seen before, and the shunk is no exception.

#2584. Damian Lillard stars in his Milwaukee return in another stark reminder of how bleak things are for the Bucks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- "Stay up! Stay up!" The pleading voice of the Milwaukee Bucks' in-arena host was still echoing around a half-empty Fiserv Forum early on Thursday night when Damian Lillard knocked the ball away from Tyler Herro and coasted the other way for the first points of a 124-114 Portland Trail Blazers victory.

Bucks fans are supposed to stay standing until their team scores. Those who are still proud enough to show up and follow the tradition get much more time on their feet than they did when Lillard was still in a Bucks jersey. They waited nearly two minutes on Thursday, then spent the next two hours watching Lillard pour in a season-high 33 points to send the Bucks to their 12th consecutive defeat and an NBA-worst 1-15 record.

Lillard's return to the court where he tore his Achilles a little more than a year ago -- which came just one night after the Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time -- was yet another reminder of how wrong things have gone in Milwaukee over the last few years, and the grim future the franchise faces. Jrue Holiday's 22 points, seven assists and four steals on Thursday only added to the misery.

Trail Blazers coach Micah Nori joked pre-game that this might be the "first and only revenge game" of Lillard's career. Afterward, Lillard, who was waived by Milwaukee mere weeks after his injury, downplayed its significance. It was just a normal game, he said, "other than it just being the first time that I've played on the court since I got hurt."

Lillard's aggressiveness may have suggested otherwise, but both he and Nori attributed his approach to the Blazers being without Deni Avdija and Ja Morant. "When you're down your next two top scorers, I knew that I would need to be a little more assertive," Lillard said.

No one knew what to expect from the 36-year-old Lillard this season after such an extended layoff, but through 15 games he's averaging 20.9 points and 4.1 assists, and shooting 35.8% from 3-point range.

"He still has the stop and go, which has made him so effective. Obviously, the jumper and his legs. I think the biggest difference would be, 18 months without playing, I don't know if you want to call it rust or timing, that's the only thing you see," Nori said pre-game. "And it's coming back. Every single day, you can see it. But when you're playing against the best athletes in the world, the best players in the world, the best defenders in the world, it is gonna take you a little bit of time to get back up to speed. But as far as from a health standpoint, you really wouldn't know it."

The moment Lillard's Achilles snapped 572 days ago during Game 4 of a first-round playoff series against the Indiana Pacers, everyone knew it was a turning point for the Bucks. But no one could have foreseen everything that's happened since then.

The Bucks waived Lillard not even two months after the injury and stretched the remaining $113 million on his contract over five years in order to create the cap space to sign Myles Turner to a four-year, $107 million deal with a player option for the 2028-29 season.

"I thought it was pretty simple. I was injured. I wasn't gonna be available to play last season, and the team was focused on bringing somebody in here that they could pair with Giannis so that they could still be a competitive team, which is the business side of it," Lillard said Thursday morning at shootaround. "I saw it for what it was, and I moved on."

The desperate ploy to keep Antetokounmpo happy didn't work. Now, both he and Lillard are gone, while Turner is averaging just 7.1 points and six rebounds on 36.2% shooting this season and the Bucks are still paying Lillard $22,516,603 each year through 2030. If you break that figure down by game, they gave Lillard $247,592 for the trouble of beating them on Thursday while Turner sat and watched with a shoulder injury.

Five years ago, Antetokounmpo and Holiday were carrying the Larry O'Brien trophy through the streets of Milwaukee. Three years ago, Holiday was traded for Lillard. Just over a year ago, Lillard tore his Achilles in the most recent playoff game at Fiserv Forum and was waived. Now, Antetokounmpo is leading the 9-6 Miami Heat, who sit in fourth place in the Eastern Conference, while Holiday and Lillard are together in the same backcourt for the 10-5 Trail Blazers, who occupy sixth in the Western Conference.

And the Bucks, who haven't won a playoff series since 2022 and don't own their own first-round pick until 2031, the year after they'll stop paying Lillard? They're 1-15, have the worst record in the league and are in the midst of the second-longest losing streak in franchise history. Oh, and they're also under investigation for salary cap circumvention relating to Gary Trent Jr.'s $64 million contract.

No team has a bleaker present or future than the Bucks.

Just how bad are the vibes in Milwaukee? Major Goolsby's, a sports bar down the street from the arena, has started running a new promotion on game nights: everything's free if the Bucks win.

#2582. Could Chloe Kelly really miss out on England's Women's World Cup squad? Lionesses legend again facing selection battle despite big-game pedigree

The Arsenal winger was the hero at Euros of both 2022 and 2025, despite her participation in both tournaments being in doubt for a long time, and as the summer approaches, a similar story is unfolding

If anyone is experiencing a case of deja vu when it comes to Lionesses star Chloe Kelly right now, it's understandable. In seven months' time - granted they expectedly come through next week's play-off with Ukraine - England should be kicking-off their Women's World Cup campaign. However, as was the case two years ago as the 2025 European Championship loomed, and five years ago as Euro 2022 neared, the chances of Kelly, one of this team's biggest stars, being there appear are far from certain.

It's been a recurring theme in Kelly's career to date, which is especially strange given each of the three cases have been for entirely different reasons. At the end of 2021, Kelly was in the middle of a long recovery from a devastating ACL injury; at the end of 2024, she was dramatically out of favour at Manchester City, to the point that she wasn't even making some matchday squads; and right now, as 2026 nears its conclusion, a puzzling hamstring problem is keeping her on the sidelines, with her most recent minutes coming back in September.

For some, it might seem like an irrelevant topic: If Kelly is fit when the World Cup comes around, she will surely be in the squad, right? She has too much big-game pedigree to be left out by Sarina Wiegman, especially given squads have finally been expanded to incorporate 26 players.

But the longer Kelly's rather vague absence continues, the more that line of thinking is thrown into doubt. She was the match-winner in the Euro 2022 final and it was her penalty that decided the shootout in the showpiece event in 2025. But could the Lionesses' icon really find herself watching the 2027 Women's World Cup from home?

Kelly has accumulated so many big moments in her England career to date, with her winner in the Euro 2022 final the most notable

The catalogue of big moments that Kelly has built up in an England shirt over the last few years is quite remarkable.

To score an extra-time winner against Germany, at Wembley, in the Euro 2022 final to deliver the Lionesses' first-ever major tournament triumph, and on home soil, guaranteed that Kelly would be an England icon no matter what else happened in her career, even if she was only 24 years old at the time.But to follow that up with numerous moments of magic at the subsequent Euros has added massively to her legend.

It wasn't just one big moment like in 2022, but rather several spread out across one of the most dramatic knockout-stage runs in the history of the game. Her decisive spot-kick in the penalty shootout win over Spain in the final was the headline contribution, but she also scored the extra-time winner in the semi-final against Italy and provided the cross that kickstarted the incredible comeback in the quarters, before scoring in the shootout as Sweden's hearts were broken.

There have been other highlights too, such as the thunderous penalty - so powerful it generated headlines aplenty for its speed - that won the last-16 shootout against Nigeria at the 2023 Women's World Cup, as part of England's run to the final.

Regardless of questions about form and a lack of game time, some would argue that Kelly should be on the plane to the World Cup whatever the case, granted she is fit

It all contributes to the reputation Kelly has carved out as a serious big-game player - and it's not as if she is limited to these moments either. After joining Man City in 2020, Kelly would spend the majority of the next five years marking herself out as one of the best wingers in the Women's Super League, before it ended on a strangely sour note.

When she found a way out from her exile via a loan to Arsenal, she reminded everyone of those qualities with a tremendous second half of the 2024-25 season, which served as an excellent response to being left out of an England squad for the first time under Wiegman. Her contributions in the Champions League were particularly notable, helping the Gunners to defy the odds and win the trophy. It paved the way for a return to the Lionesses squad ahead of Euro 2025, where she took centre stage as England retained their title.

Match-winning qualities, penalty-taking expertise and an ability to rise to the biggest of occasions - regardless of form, Kelly will surely be in Wiegman's 2027 Women's World Cup squad... right?!

It feels difficult at this moment to guarantee Kelly's fitness, and there are concerns about her form too, which wasn't at a high level before her ongoing absence began

But none of this is even a conversation if Kelly isn't fit. Her last game came on September 27, when she played 30 minutes from the bench in Arsenal's 1-0 defeat to Chelsea. Two days later, she wasn't in the England squad. Explaining her absence, Wiegman said that Kelly's "levels" on the pitch "weren't what I expected". When asked if there was any injury that contributed to her decision, the England boss replied: "For me, it's just what I saw on the pitch."

Bizarrely, when Arsenal boss Renee Slegers faced the media just a few hours later, she revealed Kelly was unavailable for the next day's Champions League clash with Paris FC. "She's had some issues with her hamstring," she explained. "Nothing we could see from an injury perspective. [She's] been managing something and at the moment not available to play."

Later in the press conference, Slegers confirmed that Kelly had indeed been available for selection for England too: "She played on Sunday. She played 30-plus minutes for us, so at that point she was fit and available."

Such vagueness has endured when Slegers has been asked about Kelly in the two months since. Last week, ahead of Sunday's draw with West Ham, she said the forward was "still managing the same hamstring issues", adding: "There's no timeline [for her return] at the moment."

Will Kelly complete another redemption story ahead of the World Cup - or will this ending come with disappointment rather than glory?

It's all set up for another of Kelly's trademark redemption stories. In 2022, she bounced back from the devastating ACL injury which ruled her out of the Olympic Games in 2021 and the majority of the following season, returning just in time to make the Euro 2022 squad. Once there, she made her mark with the title-winning goal.

In 2024, she endured what she'd later describe as a "dark time" at Man City, where she was completely out of favour and dropped from the England squad due to a lack of game time, with just four months to go until Euro 2025. A loan to Arsenal was secured at the 11th hour in the January transfer window and her road to redemption began, culminating in her becoming a European champion with club and country, providing decisive moments in both triumphs.

Will the difficulties of 2026 have a similar ending? When the 2027 Women's World Cup concludes in July, will we be talking about how Kelly overcame these frustrating fitness issues, and a lack of form before them, to make Wiegman's squad and deliver a moment that helped the Lionesses win the tournament for the first time? Or will it be different this time around? Right now, Kelly is running out of time to book her ticket on the plane to Brazil?

Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong. Freddy Peralta, who'll be going into his age-31 season in 2027, is one of the strongest free-agent starting pitchers on the market not named Tarik Skubal. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form.

#2576. Kimmi Ascanio: The USWNT prospect dubbed 'mini Tobin Heath' but showing Keira Walsh-like traits

The San Diego Wave teenager started life as a promising forward but she's since transitioned into a holding midfielder, and has already caught the eye of U.S. boss Emma Hayes

When Kimmi Ascanio, the San Diego Wave's talented 18-year-old, was a guest on the RE-CAP Show in February, a podcast hosted by United States women's national team legends Tobin Heath and Christen Press, it was always going to be a must-watch. Ascanio has been likened to Heath throughout the early stages of what looks to be a promising career, so to see her actually meet and converse at length with the iconic winger was sure to be interesting.

Funnily enough, in the time since the show came out, Ascanio has actually adopted a position in the Wave line-up that is essentially foreign to Heath. Long an exciting forward like Heath, Ascanio transformed into an integral holding midfielder in the 2026 season - one so important, even, that her absence from the play-offs due to injury was a "serious issue", in the opinion of three-time NWSL champion McCall Zerboni, as the Wave crashed out. "She's more important than people realize," Zerboni added on CBS Sports Golazo.

But Heath's view on the similarities she shares with this teenage phenom were never rooted in a position on the field. "It's more so how she moves with and without the ball," she explained. "I definitely see the comparisons." Press agreed. "You move through space similarly," she observed. However, Press' main takeaway from sharing a conversation with the pair was rooted in their personalities. "I had a 'Freaky Friday' moment," she proclaimed. "I saw Tobin 20 years ago sitting next to Tobin today."

At one point, when Ascanio explained how she likes to meet with the coaching staff to analyse her game, and sheepishly declared that she doesn't like meeting with the head coach but rather those around him, Press interjected with astonishment: "Oh my gosh, you just are like Tobin!"

Understandably, while still just 18, Ascanio is a little shy at points as she chatted to two icons of U.S. women's soccer, one of whom she is obviously flattered to be compared to. "If there's one person I'd want to be compared to, it would be Tobin," she rather heart-warmingly shared.

But none of that is related to a lack of confidence. Ascanio is not just one of the most talented young players coming through in the NWSL and the U.S. youth national teams; as her recent nomination to the NWSL's Second XI for the 2026 season and her inclusion on the USWNT's CONCACAF W Championship preliminary roster shows, she is also a player making her mark at the top level right now.

Though a more dedicated tennis player in her youth, it didn't take long for Ascanio to mark herself as a top soccer prospect once she changed her focus

Incredibly, Ascanio didn't even start playing soccer in an organised format until she was around 10 or 11 years old. Born in Orlando, Florida, to Venezuelan parents from a Spanish background, the sport was a feature in her life before then, with her family always having it on the television and her brother also playing it. "I love Real Madrid and my brother loves Barcelona," she explained.

But it was tennis that Ascanio got into first. While she would play soccer casually with her brother, it was only when she was watching him play one day and his coach needed an extra participant that everything changed. "From then on, I let go of tennis," she said.

Alongside the youth club soccer she played with Florida United, heavy exposure to futsal would help to accelerate Ascanio's potential in a sport she picked up in a more dedicated sense quite late, something which is evident in her outstanding technique. Soon enough, the talented teenager was a mainstay in the U.S. youth national teams, helping her country win continental titles at Under-15 and Under-17 level.

Her contributions at the U17 CONCACAF Women's Championship were particularly notable: As the youngest player in the squad, Ascanio scored a six-minute hat-trick in the semi-final win over Haiti and also netted in the final, a 4-0 victory over Mexico. Later that year, Ascanio also stood out at the U17 World Cup, starting every game in the U.S's best performance at the tournament for 16 years, as the team finished third.

Ascanio signed her first contract with the San Diego Wave when she was just 16 years old and became an important starter the following season

It was just a few weeks after that tournament that Ascanio was catapulted into the limelight, signing a three-year contract with the San Diego Wave just two months after she had celebrated her 16th birthday. The versatile teenager had spent some time with the club in pre-season and they did not hesitate to secure her signature after witnessing up close what she was capable of.

"We saw Kimmi's ability to transition to the professional game and we were thoroughly impressed," Molly Downtain, then the Wave's general manager, noted.

Unsurprisingly, Ascanio's game time didn't come immediately, with her making just six appearances in 2024. But those opportunities increased the following season, with her able to evolve into a consistent starter relatively quickly, setting her up for a big 2026.

Ascanio continued to be a key player for San Diego in the 2026 season, albeit in a brand new role

How Ascanio performed in the 2026 season was tremendous. Only eight players in the NWSL played more accurate passes in the final third than her, only one of whom was a San Diego team-mate. Among the Wave's squad, Ascanio ranked fifth for key passes, fourth for accurate passes and also provided three assists, despite transitioning from a forward role to that of a defensive midfielder during the season.

In that new role, she was able to provide a steady presence in front of the San Diego back line, ranking third in the squad for tackles and fifth for interceptions, while also linking defence and attack in possession. Somehow, she became one of the best in the position in the NWSL almost overnight, as well as one of San Diego's most important players.

Her absence in the post-season hurt the Wave, who lost to the Utah Royals in the quarter-finals. "Losing Ascanio did change their dynamic quite a bit," Zerboni noted after the game.

A place in the NWSL's Second XI on awards night was a consolation, though her absence from the list of nominees for Midfielder of the Year was a surprise, while her presence on the USWNT's preliminary roster for the CONCACAF W Championship showed that she is on Emma Hayes' radar too.

Boasting great technical skill and awareness, Ascanio's seamless transition into a new position has highlighted a lot of her strengths

Ascanio's outstanding technical skill is the first thing that stands out when watching her play. She's simply brilliant with the ball at her feet, something explained wonderfully by Heath on the RE-CAP Show: "I like her relationship with football. I think that's what I always look at when I'm looking at top talent. Are they friends with the ball? It's so clear to me the players that have a relationship with the football and Kimmi absolutely is in love with that thing."

Being so good on the ball no doubt plays a role in how calm Ascanio is when she comes under pressure. That's all the more important now that she has dropped back into a deeper midfield role, where not losing possession is more of a priority when compared to the attacking positions she has occupied in the past.

Aiding Ascanio's strong transition into this new role has been her great awareness, how consistently she keeps her head up and checks her surroundings, and also her strong positional discipline, which is especially impressive given her situation. While still only boasting a slight physique at this stage, she is dogged and scrappy when it comes to putting opponents under pressure, and her work rate out of possession is impactful.

The teenager can still provide an attacking threat from deep too, with a smart pass forward often followed up by a charge up the field to add another number into the final third, while her vision and passing range also still helps carve out opportunities for team-mates.

Still just 18 years old, Ascanio has plenty of room for growth, despite already being an impactful player in a top league

There are still things for Ascanio to get used to in the senior game and also in her new position. She can still sometimes play a slightly riskier or trickier pass to control while in that deeper role, probably because she is still getting used to that smaller margin for error in defensive areas, which can lead to turnovers.

She can - and likely will - grow to demand the ball from her team-mates more often too, especially from the defence and her goalkeeper. After all, she has the ability to dictate games and she should lean into that.

There will also be a natural increase in strength as she spends more time in the senior game and matures as a player in this environment. That said, she does plenty of good work in her defensive actions even with that to come.

Though regularly compared to Heath, Ascanio's move to a holding midfield role has highlighted similarities she shares with England's Walsh

Holding midfielders come in all different shapes and sizes. There are physical, disruptive ones; there are diminutive, scrappy ones; there are players whose strengths are more in out of possession work and winning the ball back for others to then do damage with; there are others whose deeper role is centred around the dictating and controlling of play, rather than being an enforcer.

At this stage, Ascanio appears to align more with a holding midfielder like Keira Walsh. The teenager is the first to admit that she is not particularly strong or fast, things which have made her lean into her technical skill more throughout her development. It means she is instead the sort of midfielder who dictates games and controls them from deep with her great passing range, vision and calmness on the ball.

Like Walsh, she can still be effective in thwarting the opponent, able to cover space well and read the game to intercept passes or recover the ball. But rather than being an all-action holding midfielder with stand-out defensive strengths - like, say, a Lena Oberdorf - the emphasis is more on Ascanio's distribution, while still asking her to snuff out danger as it appears in front of the back line.

Of course, there is also a world in which Ascanio reverts back to a more attacking role and showcases more of the traits that earned her comparisons to Heath. For now, though, she is excelling in midfield.

After a huge 2026, it'll be fascinating to see what 2027 has in store for Ascanio - especially with a senior World Cup on the horizon

It'll be fascinating to see how Ascanio builds on this 2026 season, not least because it looks like she could be about to leave not only the San Diego Wave in this off-season, but the NWSL as a whole. The teenager's contract expires in the coming months, and The Cutback has reported that she is set to leave when it does, amid interest from clubs in the U.S. and Europe. Soccerdonna, meanwhile, believes London City Lionesses are the front-runners for her signature.

It would be an interesting move for several reasons. It'd expose Ascanio to a new league with different styles of play, plus all the off-field baggage that comes with moving abroad for the first time, which could be a valuable experience to further mature this impressive 18-year-old. Joining London City would also put her in a midfield with none other than Alexia Putellas, who won her third Ballon d'Or just last month.

Some have raised concerns that Ascanio might not get the same level of game time at London City, but while the club does have a number of options in that holding midfield role, it is Daniela Arques who has shrugged off most competition for the place, playing 830 of the team's 990 league minutes this term. Ascanio would be a sterner challenger for Arques' spot, which would be good news for a London City side pushing for Champions League football, if not the Women's Super League title.

Minutes will be important if Ascanio wants to push for that first full USWNT call-up. Her place on Hayes' CONCACAF W Championship preliminary roster earlier this month shows that it clearly isn't too far away, though it may not come in time for her to force her way into the picture for the 2027 Women's World Cup. Hayes has some great midfield options to pick from, after all.

However, a lot can change in six months. Wherever she is playing her football in the New Year, if Ascanio starts 2027 like she ended 2026, before that injury frustratingly ruled her out of the NWSL play-offs, then she will surely be rewarded by Hayes - and she will have earned the opportunity.

#2575. Logan Webb landing spots: Five possible destinations for Giants starting pitcher on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Coming off a disaster of a season and with a roster badly in need of an overhaul, the Giants make sense as a team to make a trade or two this offseason. Sure enough, they are "listening to trade offers" for All-Star starting pitcher Logan Webb, per The Athletic, but they'd need a "very strong return" in order to deal him.

Webb, 30, has two years and $47 million left on his current deal. He went 8-9 with a 4.31 ERA and 1.3 WAR last season, but it was his worst year in quite a while. He averaged 4.5 WAR per season in the previous four years with a 3.22 ERA and led the National League in innings pitched from 2023 to 2025, racking up three straight top-six Cy Young finishes.

Which teams might make for a good fit for Webb? Many of them. We're talking about a workhorse under team control for two more years. Let's run through five of the best fits while, again, knowing that basically any contender should be interested in at least a conversation with the Giants.

The Cubs need so much pitching this offseason. Their entire rotation heading into the playoffs last season is in free agency. This isn't hyperbole. Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes and David Peterson are all off the roster. If the Cubs were to try and put together a rotation right now, it would be something like Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Javier Assad and several question marks. Ben Brown and Cade Horton will open the season on the injured list.

Do we really need to spell out what a reliable innings eater would mean for this bunch? Webb is an outstanding fit here.

The upstart playoff team last season was a ton of fun, but also was running bullpen games in the ALDS. The White Sox just attached Davis Martin to Luis Castillo in a trade to the Rockies in order to offload Castillo's contract, too, so they're down a starter. The Dustin May signing means they have him along with Sean Burke and converted reliever Grant Taylor. The White Sox would reportedly like to sign another starter in the May ballpark, but what about trading for someone better like Webb?

A top four in the rotation of Webb, Burke, Taylor and May would be exponentially better than what the Sox had last season.

Returns of Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach at some point will help, but this is still a thin rotation for a team coming off a division title. Chris Sale remains, but he's followed up with Grant Holmes and Bryce Elder before the Spencers return. Youngster Didier Fuentes moving to the rotation is exciting, but there are an awful lot of questions behind Sale, who turns 38 in late March, by the way.

Given that the Padres reside in the NL West with the Giants, there might be a bit of an intradivision tax in terms of the asking price, but Padres boss A.J. Preller is never shy about offloading prospects. There could certainly be a fit. The Padres need rotation help, too, after losing Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Robbie Ray and others to free agency. We know they're in on Tarik Skubal, but that doesn't mean they'll be content with just landing one big fish.

Look at the current Padres rotation. It's basically Joe Musgrove and Randy Vásquez. With three straight playoff berths and zero trips to the World Series, now isn't the time to have Jhony Brito, Ryan Weiss and Ian Koenig make up 60% of the rotation.

Dealing for Webb and signing Skubal would make for a nice offseason for new ownership, no?

One of the most disappointing teams in baseball last season needs to have a prolific offseason. We've heard plenty about the Mets being involved in the Skubal sweepstakes and we've seen them win a monster bidding war before (see: Soto, Juan). Grabbing Webb would make it quite a well-rounded rotation with talented youngsters Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton.
