#2551. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

Author: “MH” is a young analyst who regularly produces content for Spielverlagerung NextGen and TotalFootballAnalysis. On X, he can be found under Mh_sv5.

#2550. As James Harden passes Kobe Bryant on NBA's 50-point game list, Donovan Mitchell says he's underappreciated

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

James Harden is in the midst of his worst scoring season since his second year in Oklahoma City 16 years ago, but the 37-year-old turned back the clock some on Friday night with a 51-point performance in a Cavaliers win over the Pacers.

Harden's vintage scoring night saw him go 15-of-26 from the field and 14-of-14 from the free-throw line in typical Harden fashion for the 26th 50-point game of his career. That moves him into third all-time in NBA history for 50-point games, passing Kobe Bryant and sitting just five behind Michael Jordan.

At 37 years old (and 86 days), Harden is the fourth-oldest player to score 50 points in an NBA game, passing LeBron James on that list and trailing only Bryant, Jordan and Jamal Crawford, who scored 50 at 39 years old.

After the game, Cavaliers' coach Kenny Atkinson offered an eyebrow-raising comment calling Harden "top-10 all-time," which drew immediate pushback from NBA fans, but Harden is an unquestioned Hall of Famer and continues to put his name among the all-time greats on NBA scoring lists.

His co-star in Cleveland, Donovan Mitchell, lamented that Harden doesn't get the appreciation he deserves at this stage of his career, and that he expects, much like Russell Westbrook, that it won't happen until he retires.

"He won't until it's over with," Mitchell said. "I hate it, but that's just the world we live in. We won't appreciate greatness. We didn't appreciate Russ in his latter years until now. It's like, 'Oh man, Russ was this and that.' It's like we forgot he averaged 28, 15 and 16 for a month. It's one of those things where we live in such a negative space. I hate it. At the end of the day, he doesn't care. And for me, seeing that, I don't care. It helps, but at the end of the day, that's just what the world is. It sucks that that's that way, but us in this locker room and guys in this league, we know who he is and we know what he's done for the game. That goes for not just him but a lot of people in this league. We don't appreciate what's in front of us on a consistent basis."

Harden has long been a divisive player among NBA fans. Some have appreciated his ruthless efficiency while others have hated the aesthetics of his mastery of the dark arts of drawing fouls. As Mitchell noted, few players have had as much influence over the game in the last decade-plus as Harden. From his massive stepback 3-pointer to his movement on drives to create contact, so much of Harden's game has made its way into the arsenal of most elite guard scorers.

Fans will debate whether that's a good thing, but his influence is undeniable. As Mitchell said, whenever Harden calls it a career, he will get more appreciation, but there will also be heated debates over his place in NBA history as one of the most divisive stars (from a play-style perspective, at least) of his generation.

#2549. Will Mike McCarthy survive Aaron Rodgers' backlash? Steelers reportedly standing by coach, but for how long?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If a fraction of what Aaron Rodgers said on Wednesday is true, the Pittsburgh Steelers have a lot of things to clean up. If the majority of what Rodgers said is indeed fact, it's a downright miracle that the Steelers are 6-4 entering Friday's game with the visiting Broncos.

Rodgers, in a scorching interview on "The Pat McAfee Show" that lasted roughly 35 minutes, took Mike McCarthy to task, accusing him of falling asleep during meetings, being late or missing them altogether, falling behind on film study, and not connecting enough with players, especially defensive players.

Rodgers said that, as a team leader, he felt compelled to address McCarthy, which he did this week. During those conversations, Rodgers offered McCarthy an ultimatum: either give up play calling or release him.

The Steelers' brass backed McCarthy, who promptly benched Rodgers and made him inactive for Friday's game. Pittsburgh then released him shortly after his public criticism of McCarthy, who defended himself in a press conference Wednesday evening.

"I know how to win," McCarthy said, "and that's the facts. This is my third program, and I plan on winning here because of the men, because of this organization, what we've got started, and the opportunity we have to learn and grow today — because of some of the things that, frankly, should have been talked about earlier. So, this is a growth opportunity that I intend to take full advantage of."

The last sentence might be the biggest takeaway from McCarthy's 12-minute presser.

McCarthy wasn't going to acknowledge Rodgers' accusations Wednesday night for obvious reasons (he did confirm Rodgers' accusation that he accidentally said Packers instead of Steelers during halftime of last week's loss in Philadelphia). He did, however, acknowledge that he needs to make some changes, which is a positive sign for the Steelers moving forward.

McCarthy spoke to the team's leadership council after practice, and based on his comments afterward, it appears that the meeting had an impact on him.

"We had some really unique conversations in the player council meeting, and things I think that I haven't done in the past or haven't done recently," McCarthy said. "I probably should have had more dialogue early in the process when I first arrived here. I do respect Mike Tomlin and his career here and the things that are in place. I don't have a throw the baby out with the bathwater type philosophy. And so, when you have situations that create honest, direct conversation, there's good things that come out of that. Some things that (I) definitely will consider moving forward. Maybe not today or tomorrow, but there's a lot that came out of the meeting."

Really, what happened prior to this week doesn't matter nearly as much as what will transpire from this point forward. What happens moving forward is what will likely determine McCarthy's future in Pittsburgh.

If Pittsburgh rallies and makes the playoffs, it will validate the Steelers' decision to stand behind McCarthy. If the Steelers continue to struggle, however, Steelers president Art Rooney II will be forced to make a tough decision.

Rooney, if he hasn't already, needs to find out exactly what is happening inside his own facility. Is McCarthy falling asleep in meetings? Is he late or not showing up to others? Is he not watching film of future opponents in a timely manner? Is his not connecting well enough with the players? If any of those accusations are true, it raises serious concerns about McCarthy's ability to lead the Steelers.

If Rodgers' accusations are true, and the Steelers spiral and miss the playoffs, it's hard to envision McCarthy being with the team in 2027. If McCarthy comes back in that scenario, it would likely entail significant changes, including relinquishing play-calling duties.

The Steelers haven't fired a coach since 1968, and that streak will likely remain intact for quite some time. Rooney probably won't fire a coach with four years remaining on his contract, but it's possible that he and McCarthy could have a mutual parting of ways if the two sides can agree on a buyout.

The last two days have raised a lot of questions about what is actually happening within the Steelers' facility. One thing that is clear, however, is that McCarthy is at a crossroads just 10 games into his tenure in Pittsburgh. How he and his players handle the next seven games will likely determine his future in Pittsburgh beyond this season.

#2548. So you missed out on Tarik Skubal: The best starting pitchers still available through free agency, trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets' splash record signing of ace lefty Tarik Skubal, who was far and away the top free agent available, has of course reset the market in a major way. Those who missed out on Skubal and those aspiring contenders who otherwise have rotation needs may be left wondering: What's next?

Clubs like the Chicago Cubs, Atlanta Braves, San Diego Padres, Los Angeles Dodgers, Chicago White Sox, Tampa Bay Rays, among others, still have options, even if none of them rise to the skyscraping level of Mr. Skubal. Let's explore some possibilities for you, and let's also move beyond just the current class of free agents and name-check some potential trade targets who could buttress a rotation for next season and beyond. Let's jump in.

Yes, Morejon is a reliever at this writing, but his deep repertoire, excellent velocity and stuff make him a compelling transition candidate for next season, even with recent reporting that he wants to stay in the bullpen. Morejon, who sits triple digits, can give some velocity back while working longer outings and still have plenty in the tank to miss bats in the strike zone. And if starting doesn't work, he can go right back to dominating as a reliever. He doesn't turn 28 until February.

While his ERA ballooned last season thanks to some early season struggles, Rogers' underlying performance indicators are still quite strong, specifically his ability to get chase out of the zone and duck quality contact with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years. He's not a name that leaps readily to mind, but Rogers has a high ceiling and bargain potential.

Peralta, coming off three straight seasons for the Milwaukee Brewers in which he topped 30 starts and 200 strikeouts, wasn't himself with the New York Mets for the first half-plus of 2027. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter, all the way to ALCS MVP. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form. The 2027 season will be his age-31 campaign.

He has a full, five-pitch repertoire with elite spin and movement on almost all of those five offerings and boasts an ERA+ of 129 for his career. King turns 32 in May, and he's experienced a gradual decline at the command-and-control level over the past few seasons. As well, his fastball's not beating hitters in the zone like it used to. That's to say, there's risk here, but even if he's beginning his decline phase, King will be a rotation asset for the near- to mid-term.

The 32-year-old righty was reborn last season after a deadline trade to the Braves. Atlanta ramped up his splitter usage and adjusted his slider shape, and in perhaps related matters, Mahle was much more successful at staying away from the heart of the zone. In 54 ⅓ innings after the trade, Mahle ran a sub-2.00 ERA and struck out 48 batters against nine walks. No, he's not going to put up those numbers over the long haul, but his revival makes him an intriguing option.

The big pre-Skubal hot stove news was the San Francisco Giants' reported willingness to listen to offers on ace Logan Webb. Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong. For his career, the three-time All-Star has a career ERA+ of 115 with three top 10 finishes in the American League Cy Young vote. In three of the past four seasons, he's topped 200 innings. Webb is under contract through 2028.

Will the Rays part with him even though they're the defending American League champs? They're famously comfortable with churning core contributors, and McClanahan is going into his walk year in 2027. McClanahan's long and labored comeback from Tommy John surgery was finally realized this past season, and he turned in a strong age-29 campaign for the Rays. He was pretty much an ace from 2021-23 before the elbow problems took hold.

Teams will pay a lot for a young and controllable starting pitcher with frontline upside, and all of that describes the 27-year-old lefty Detmers. Not eligible for free agency until after the 2028 season, Detmers topped 4.0 WAR this past season and struck out 211 batters in 185 innings. For the Halos, trading him might be an example of selling high, but the pending change in ownership clouds any reading of those particular tea leaves.

Greene has one of the biggest fastballs in the game and a top 10 finish in the NL Cy Young balloting in his recent past. However, he's struggled to stay healthy and realize his potential on a sustained basis – the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2017. He's signed through 2028 with a club option for 2029, and it may be time for a change of scenery. He's been the subject of trade speculation before, and this winter figures to be no exception.

Yes, deGrom is 38, but going into the final guaranteed year of his contract, he remains capable of being a solid rotation presence for a contender. deGrom reportedly used his full no-trade clause to block a swap to the Braves at the deadline, so it's far from certain whether he'd be willing to approve a deal out of Arlington. That said, such things are always negotiations, and a late-career run at the playoffs might prove tempting for him.

#2546. Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren

Tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX)

Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

On the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

The attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim showed some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The issue, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

The half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

Hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

In general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, showed excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He quickly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses

A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

Due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too quickly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

An additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant issues in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

By the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate new build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

Additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

Despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham showed general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

Through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game plan was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

In principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

The extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

The central issue with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

Both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

In general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

Sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

Towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

From there, Hoffenheim attempted to play quickly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

In the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

The biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

There were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

Although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

For Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing issues ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

Towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could quickly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

The conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

However, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”

Postecoglou’s team also showed deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

#2545. Carmelo Anthony calls out Ravens' Marlon Humphrey after controversial Baltimore 'criminals' comment

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Among sports fans, Carmelo Anthony is perhaps most synonymous with New York -- both upstate from his incredible year at Syracuse and in New York City, where he starred for the Knicks. But Anthony was raised in Baltimore and is extremely proud of his roots.

So when Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey made headlines this week when he said that the thing the city of Baltimore was best at creating was "criminals," Anthony felt compelled to respond. Humphrey was admonished by the Ravens, which sent him home for the week and will hold him out on Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. He also received scathing responses from Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott and many other prominent Baltimore figures.

Anthony joined that group on Friday with an Instagram post that called on Humphrey to go beyond the apology he issued earlier in the week. Anthony wants Humphrey to join him, Scott, and others in the community to find ways to lead by example.

I've been sitting with this one for a couple of days, because Baltimore isn't a talking point to me. It's in my blood. I came up on Myrtle Avenue in West Baltimore. I saw what this city can take fro you. I lost friends to the streets, and I watched people I loved get swallowed by a system that was built to swallow them. I know the reputation. I've heard every joke and every headline my whole life.

So when one of our own stands on our name and says the best thing Baltimore makes is criminals, and then laughs that it'll get cut out, that doesn't get cut out for me. It doesn't get cut out for the kid in Baltimore who heard it. It doesn't get cut out for the mother working two jobs to keep her son off the corner. And it doesn't get cut out for the man who did his time, came home, and is fighting every day to be seen as more than his worst moment.

Marlon, I see the apology. I'll take it, man to man. But Baltimore has been apologized to its whole life. Apologies don't build anything. Presence does. I put my time, energy and resources in Baltimore because I want kids to have somebody who believe in them. That's the job when you wear this city on your chest. You don't get to rep Baltimore on Sundays and talk about it like an outsider on Wednesday.

So let me tell you what Baltimore makes. We make fighters. We make builders. We make people who were counted out from the day they were born and showed up anyway. We make teachers who buy supplies out of their own pockets, coaches who become fathers, artists the whole world copies, and returning citizens who turn their pain into purpose. We make Olympians, Hall of Famers, legends. We make ME. We make Tank Davis.

The Mayor opened a door. Walk through it. And when you do, call me. I'll meet you there. Let's sit with these young boys together and let them hear from two men who wear this city that they are not what anybody says they are.

Baltimore doesn't make criminals. Baltimore makes the ones who make it out. And the ones who come back. #B-MORE.

The overwhelming response to Humphrey's comments in Baltimore has been to highlight the incredible work being done by leaders to improve conditions, decrease violence, and provide mentorship and guidance to young people in the city.

Anthony echoed the mayor's invitation to join in that work in the community and offered to be there right alongside him.

#2543. What's next for the Mets after record-breaking deal with Tarik Skubal? Biggest needs for 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets landed the offseason's best free agent and one of the game's top pitchers Sunday evening. The Mets and two-time Cy Young-winning lefty Tarik Skubal have agreed to a record-shattering nine-year contract worth $450 million. The contract obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) and average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million). A 1-of-1 contract for a 1-of-1 pitcher.

New York's offseason work is not complete, however. It's not close to complete, really. The Mets went 74-88 and disappointed every which way this past season. There are still roster needs to address. Here's what's left for the Mets to do this offseason following the Skubal signing.

Yes, the Mets still need another starter even after signing Skubal. They have an excellent 1-2-3 punch. The depth behind that top three is not great, however. Here is New York's updated rotation depth chart:

Manaea and Senga both pitched so poorly this past season that they were demoted to the bullpen. They shouldn't be counted on as anything more than emergency options at this point in their careers. Thornton had some moments this summer and Tong is not too far removed from being a top prospect, but yeah, the Mets need another starter. Clearly.

After landing Skubal, I suspect the Mets will aim lower than the second tier of free agent starters (Michael King, Freddy Peralta, Trevor Rogers, etc.) to fill out their rotation. A Clay Holmes reunion would make some sense. Others in that class of veterans make sense too. Think Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, Casey Mize, pitchers like that.

Year 1 post-Pete Alonso at first base went worse than anyone could have expected. Jorge Polanco barely played and was terrible when he did play. Jared Young was fine and owner Steve Cohen isn't running near-record payrolls for fine. Alonso led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR for the Orioles. The Mets finished dead last at the position with -0.8 WAR. Yeesh.

Here are the best available free agent first basemen by FanGraphs projected 2027 WAR:

It ain't great. I think the projections on France, who had an excellent season in 2026, are a bit low, but the fact of the matter is he's only had one year in line with the kind of contract he's likely to sign. Perhaps there's a Luis García Jr. trade to be made with the crosstown rival New York Yankees? García's a clunky fit for the Yankees and might be most useful as a trade chip.

The good news is it won't be hard for the Mets to improve at first base. Getting even an average first baseman would represent an enormous upgrade. Now the Mets just have to go out and find that average (or, preferably, better than average) first baseman and improve their lineup. This might be the single biggest item remaining on their offseason to-do list.

The Mets traded away several relievers at the deadline this summer (A.J. Minter, Brooks Raley, Luke Weaver, etc.), which allowed them to audition a few young pitchers down the stretch. Left-hander Nate Lavender in particular stood out and cemented his place in the 2027 bullpen. The bullpen pecking order currently looks something like this:

Williams was at best inconsistent during his first season with the Mets. Another late-inning reliever to share the high-leverage load (someone to replace Weaver, basically) seems essential. You don't want to pay Skubal all that money only to have the bullpen blow his starts, you know? President of baseball operations David Stearns is adept at building bullpens on the cheap. Spending money is OK too.

Assuming the Mets don't go to the top of the market for Adrian Morejon, the best available free agent relievers are battle-tested veterans like Bryan Abreu, JoJo Romero, and Alex Vesia. Abreu is an excellent buy-low candidate after his rocky first half. There is no such thing as too many good relievers. The Mets should continue adding to their bullpen this winter.

The case can be made that Skubal's contract is only the second smartest contract the Mets gave out this weekend. They agreed to an eight-year, $95 million contract with a ninth-year club option with center fielder A.J. Ewing on Saturday. The deal buys out his six years of team control and two free agent years with an option for a third. That's a nifty piece of business.

I would expect the Mets to pursue extensions with McLean and outfielder Carson Benge next, if they haven't already. McLean and Benge both had terrific first full seasons in the big leagues and look like keepers, like players who can be centerpieces for a World Series contender rather than just tag along for the ride. Locking up McLean and/or Benge would be fantastic work.

#2541. Is Stephen Curry the real NBA MVP? It's hard not to think so when you watch the Warriors without him

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's easy to forget because of what Stephen Curry has turned the Golden State Warriors into over the last decade and change, but this is an organization with some pathetic history in its books. So it's really saying something to start registering all-time marks of franchise ineptitude, which is precisely what the Warriors have done over the last week.

After battling admirably in a respectable loss to the Houston Rockets on the night Curry went down with an oblique injury in the first quarter, the Warriors have lost their last four games by 20-plus points for just the second time in franchise history. The only other time this has happened to a Warriors team was in February of 1998, a few months after Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo. The total margin of that four-game losing streak was 104 points.

This current one is even worse. These Warriors have lost their last four by 109 points, and what makes it even more jarring is comparing them to the team that had won eight straight prior to Curry's injury. That 1997-98 team was trash all year, starting 1-14 and finishing with just 19 wins without ever winning more than three straight games.

These Warriors, on the other hand, were starting to look like a legitimate playoff-caliber team. A cynic would say that run of victories came against a softer schedule than what they have faced of late, but that qualification doesn't hold much, if any, water. That eight-game run included wins over the Denver Nuggets, Minnesota Timberwolves, Los Angeles Lakers, Miami Heat and an Orlando Magic team that has immediately gone on to win five of its last six.

Perhaps the Warriors would have lost to the 13-3 San Antonio Spurs even with Curry. Hell, maybe they would've lost to the New Orleans Pelicans, Dallas Mavericks and Memphis Grizzlies, too. That feels unlikely, but who knows? Even with Curry, the Warriors aren't good enough to start checking off scheduled wins. But that's not the point.

The point is how utterly incapable they have looked in losing these games. Not only have they lost each of these last four by at least 20 points, but they've also been held under 100 points in all of them. That's a combination of incompetence that stretches beyond a franchise mark. That hasn't happened to a single other team this century.

Before we try to answer that, let's just agree upfront that Curry has little to no chance of actually winning what would be his third MVP. The Warriors almost certainly won't have a good enough record to put him in real contention. His across-the-board counting stats, even if he were to maintain his torrid early pace, are not going to match those of Luka Dončić or Victor Wembanyama.

The only real chance would be if both of those guys, and likely a bunch of others, failed to meet the 65-game threshold, but the chances of Curry, who has already missed six games and isn't expected to be re-evaluated until around Thanksgiving, making it to 65 games himself already feel next to impossible. He may be past the maximum 17 games-missed mark before he even returns from this injury.

Which is to say, what we're asking here is whether Curry, at 38 years old and in his 18th season, is still the most valuable player in the league (has he always been?), not whether he'll actually win the award, and the answer to that question, at least in its simplest form, could very well lie in his absence. Just look at this team without him.

Admittedly, there's some cherry-picking in those numbers. Curry actually didn't play in one of the wins during that eight-game streak, and the Warriors still beat the Los Angeles Clippers 124-112 with a 122.8 offensive rating behind 37 points from rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

We're also leaving out the aforementioned game against the Rockets on Nov. 11 in which Curry only played six minutes and the Warriors looked fine, or even good, in testing one of the best teams in the league to its limit. It also must be noted that Golden State lost its first three games of the season and looked every bit like the team many of us predicted would stink, all of which Curry played in.

Still, the general rule applies. The Warriors go as Curry goes. That was true even in the golden years when the on/off splits, even with the likes of Kevin Durant and Klay Thompson still out there, always pointed to Curry as the clear MVP.

"If I didn't have Steph, I would've been like every other NBA coach and lasted a few years [with the Warriors] and then gone and coached somewhere else," Steve Kerr has said, openly admitting that Curry, and Curry alone, has been the difference between a journeyman coaching career and a Hall-of-Fame one.

He's not lying. Have a look at the numbers.

Even if you want to remove the 2019-20 season from the equation, when Durant had defected, Thompson missed the whole year and Curry only played in five games, Kerr is still a below-.500 coach at 74-96 without Curry in the lineup. This is a coach who has had all kinds of great players at his disposal over the years, and still it was always Curry in control of his and the organization's ultimate fate.

This is still the case for the Warriors, who continue to fall off a cliff without Curry. When he's been on the floor this year, they have registered a 59.6 eFG%, which would rank first in the league. When he's off, they fall to 49.1%, which would rank last.

Even the defensive decline we see in Curry's on/off splits can largely be tied back to his offense. Without him, the Warriors are unable to create the same shots and, when their new brand of shots miss far more often, they end up defending in transition on almost 3% more possessions. That's a big deal. It's meant almost five more points per game surrendered to fast breaks over this stretch.

The Warriors have produced an average offensive rating of 103.8 in games Curry hasn't played this year, which would rank as the second-worst mark in the league. All told, they are 26.3 points per 100 possessions better in Curry's minutes this season, per Cleaning The Glass. By comparison, the Lakers drop by 25.5 points per 100 when Dončić sits. Wembanyama is in his own galaxy with this stat, representing a 37.8-point decline in San Antonio when he's off the floor.

It's fair to say Wembanyama means as much to San Antonio's defense, where most of that decline happens, as Curry does to Golden State's offense, and certainly the Lakers falling off by as much as they do offensively, even with Austin Reaves as a legit secondary star, tells you everything you need to know about his impact. All of these guys are MVP players.

But only one, by subjective definition, can be the most valuable, and the simple truth is the Lakers and Spurs are outfitted with far more functional rosters independent of their respective superstars. In Golden State, there is just nowhere else to turn. Nobody to generate any kind of consistent offensive leverage. No gravity. No shot creation.

After the Warriors took that 38-point beating against the Spurs without Curry, the rookie Lendeborg, who had, in total unfairness, been saddled with filling Curry's go-to-scorer shoes, said "it felt helpless out there," and that is exactly what it has looked like since the Curry variable was removed from Golden State's equation.

To be fair, the absence of a player is an imperfect lens through which to view value for a bunch of contextual reasons, not the least of which is how a team like Golden State is designed to play -- a specific, Curry-centric ecosystem not particularly amenable to abrupt adjustments. These players are not as bad as they have looked without Curry over these last four games.

But by the same token, they aren't close to as good as they looked with Curry, either. I always laugh when my dad calls me saying things like, "This Pat Spencer guy can play!" Everyone looks like they can play next to Curry. And then he goes away and suddenly you're wondering how the hell this guy made the Washington Generals look like one of the best teams in the league. Is he some kind of miracle worker?

In a basketball sense, that's not far off. Curry's individual production is already virtually unmatched, but it's his exponential powers, his ability to compound the returns of those around him, that set him apart. It's early, yes. Perhaps the Warriors will figure things out the longer Curry is away. Probably not. But maybe they at least can return to competitive functionality. Until then, however, it's pretty hard to not think Curry is the most valuable player in the league when you watch the Warriors play without him.

#2540. Lions vs. Bears Thanksgiving prediction: Which team will take control of NFC North?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the first of three Thanksgiving day games, the Detroit Lions play host to the division rival Chicago Bears in one of the biggest games of the NFL season to date.

Detroit enters this game winners of six straight and sitting in first place in the NFC North with an 8-2 record. The Lions sport one of the NFL's most efficient and explosive offenses, and their efense hasn't allowed more than 21 points in a game since all the way back in Week 4. The Lions are dealing with injury issues on that side of the ball, but they've held up surprisingly well. That will be put to the test on Thursday afternoon.

Chicago comes into this game having won five in a row and sporting an 8-2 record that matches that of Detroit, with the Bears sitting in second place in the division by virtue of a tiebreaker. The Bears also have one of the league's best offenses, while the defense has been strengthened by the acquisition of superstar defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons, who seems to have transformed the unit up front and allowed everything else to click properly into place. That unit, too, will be tested more than ever here.

Which of these two teams will keep its winning streak alive and lay claim to sole possession of first place in the division? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.

Chicago is eighth in total yards and eighth in total points this season, but some of that has to do with volume. The Bears rank a surprising 14th in yards per play, 12th in points per drive and 15th in EPA per play, according to Tru Media. Some of that is due to the fact that Caleb Williams missed several games with a hamstring injury, but even with Williams on the field the Bears' EPA per play mark is only the equivalent of the 10th-best offense in the league.

Chicago is one of the league's most run-oriented offenses, ranking ninth in the share of plays that turn into a rush attempt. But D'Andre Swift is averaging just 3.7 yards per carry and Kyle Monangai, who has been more effective (5.0 per carry) has played in only five games.

The Lions have sported a top run defense this season in allowing only 4.0 yards per carry, but that defense took a couple of massive hits over the last few weeks with the losses of Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson to injury. Still, Detroit held Tampa Bay's running backs to 84 yards on 22 carries last Sunday, when Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell had previously been destroying teams on the ground. The Bears will need Swift and Monangai to find more success if they want to control the game in the fashion they have preferred since Ben Johnson became head coach last year.

Chicago's passing game has been relatively inconsistent this year, as there have been times when Caleb Williams has looked like an elite quarterback and others when he has looked ordinary — sometimes within the same game. (Like the Sunday night showdown against the Buccaneers, for example.) Williams has completed 68.3% of his passes at 7.9 yards per attempt, but he's thrown only 10 touchdown passes against six interceptions.

He's 11th in the NFL in EPA per dropback, according to Tru Media, but he's been highly susceptible against the blitz: he ranks fourth in EPA against four-man rushes but only checks in 19th when opponents rush five or more. Detroit has blitzed at a below-average rate this season (30.3%, per Tru Media), but would be wise to turn up the pressure a bit against a quarterback who has shown that he can be pressured into some bad decisions on occasion if you get defenders into his lap.

Still, the Lions have been highly susceptible to opposing passing attacks, even if they have been improved since the return of Brian Branch and should get another lift as Kerby Joseph rounds into form. The Lions are 27th in EPA per dropback allowed, and they're in the bottom third in opponents' explosive play rate through the air.

Detroit is most vulnerable against opposing tight ends, allowing the league's fifth-highest target share to the position, so this could be a game where the Bears finally get Colston Loveland going in a way that they haven't been able to accomplish as much as they likely wanted to this year. The Lions do limit yards after the catch better than any defense in the NFL, though, allowing only 4.0 YAC per completion, according to Tru Media. That could take away from some of Chicago's success in the screen game and possibly limit the effectiveness of Luther Burden III and — to a lesser extent because he's not as big a part of the offense — Kalif Raymond.

The Lions are third in the NFL in yards and fifth in points. They're fifth in both yards per play and points per drive, as well as fifth in EPA per play, according to Tru Media. They're second in EPA per pass attempt and third in EPA per rush attempt. They're third in passing success rate, first in rushing success rate and third in overall success rate. They are, in other words, a top-five offense by almost any measurement, and they can beat you with both the pass and the run.

Jared Goff is having a marvelous season, completing 67.8% of his passes at an average of 8.2 yards per attempt with 20 touchdown passes against six interceptions. He's third in the league behind only Brock Purdy and Joe Burrow in EPA per dropback, third behind only Purdy and Burrow in success rate and fourth behind only Purdy, Burrow and Patrick Mahomes in passer rating. His 8.2 yards-per-attempt average is the second-best of his tenure in Detroit, as are the 52.3% success rate and 107.7 passer rating.

He's of course blessed with one of the best skill-position corps in the league: Amon-Ra St. Brown is a picture of consistency; Jameson Williams is one of the most explosive threats in football; Sam LaPorta is a strong option and tight end; and Jahmyr Gibbs is the best running back in the NFL, leading the league in rushes, rushing yards, first downs, yards from scrimmage and total touchdowns.

St. Brown often gets pigeonholed as a slot guy, but in reality he plays more outside (59.2% of snaps) than he does inside (39.8%), according to Tru Media, and he's equally capable of dominating defenses from either spot. He's Goff's first read more often than not because he runs a lot of short-area routes and the Lions like to get the ball out fairly quickly in their straight dropback game, where St. Brown is often the target.

Williams is the guy the Lions turn toward when they're looking to test defenses in the intermediate and deep areas of the field. His 12.36-yard average route depth is fourth among 199 players who have run 100 or more routes this season, according to Tru Media, and he's generated an explosive gain (16-plus yards) on 26.3% of his targets, which ranks 17th among that same group of players. He and LaPorta are generally going to eat into each other's target shares in any given week, while St. Brown remains the more consistent top target.

The Bears' secondary is beatable, as Chicago ranks 22nd in net yards allowed per attempt, according to Pro-Football-Reference. Jaylon Johnson is not the same player he once was, Tyrique Stevenson is inconsistent, Kyler Gordon has barely played and Malik Muhammad has the ups and downs of a fourth-round rookie. If the Lions give Goff time to throw, he could feast on this group all afternoon.

That's where Chicago's improved defensive line comes in. Since acquiring Jeffery Simmons, the Bears rank seventh in the league in EPA per dropback, per Tru Media, in large part because they have recorded a sack on 10.7% of opponent dropbacks. Prior to acquiring Simmons, Chicago's sack rate was 8.9%. That figure still ranked third in the league through seven weeks, but it's been much improved since the Bears dropped Simmons into the middle of the defensive line.

Detroit is pretty strong up front, allowing pressure on only 32.3% of dropbacks, which ranks sixth in the NFL. The sack rate is a bit worse than that because Goff isn't the world's most mobile quarterback, but he's generally given adequate time to throw.

The Lions' run game is diverse, efficient and explosive. Gibbs is seventh in the NFL in yards per carry, fifth in the share of runs that gain five or more yards and second in explosive run rate, according to Tru Media. The Lions utilize him on plenty of inside runs, but he is obviously at his most dangerous when they get him on the perimeter and he can scoot past opposing defenders.

is seventh in the NFL in yards per carry, fifth in the share of runs that gain five or more yards and second in explosive run rate, according to Tru Media. The Lions utilize him on plenty of inside runs, but he is obviously at his most dangerous when they get him on the perimeter and he can scoot past opposing defenders. The Bears have allowed 4.7 yards per rush since acquiring Simmons, but that number is 5.9 per rush on attempts off tackle or off end, per Tru Media. Simmons plays inside, and the Bears can be tested on the perimeter.

These are two incredibly evenly matched teams, but it seems like Detroit has more matchup advantages offensively against Chicago's improved defense than the Bears do against the Lions' own improved unit. With Detroit also getting the benefit of home-field advantage, we're rolling with the Lions to win a close one as a home underdog. Pick: Lions 31, Bears 30
